areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 8.3 million km2 for 800 and 1.0 million km2 for 900 (after the provinces broke away). In 850 Khurasan (Tahirids) and Ifriqiya (Aghlabids) were autonomous but still recognised the caliph, so most of the 800 extent applies (mid); low drops them. The world_800 polygon measures 8.40 million km2.

population.note: Seshat codes 23-33 million for 800 and 9-11 million for the reduced core in 900. 850 sits between: Iraq declining, Egypt rising (HYDE/OWID Iraq 2.5M in 800, Egypt 3.8-4.4M in 800-900). Mid 25 million includes autonomous Khurasan and Ifriqiya; low drops them.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Baghdad 300,000-900,000 (Seshat, disputed) and Samarra, Basra, Fustat, Nishapur, Merv; the most urbanised large state west of China.

activePersonnel.note: Sum of: Samarra central army 20,000-30,000 (Toellner, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ushrusaniyya), half of them Turks; shakiriyya cavalry a few thousand, not more than 5,000 (Kennedy 2001 pp. 201-203, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakiriyya); Baghdad abna and Tahirid forces, frontier (thughur) garrisons in Cilicia and the Jazira, Egypt, Armenia (Bugha the Elder's 852-855 campaign) and the Tahirid army of Khurasan, guessed at 30,000-100,000 together.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Frontier volunteers (mutatawwi'a), Bedouin, Kurdish and provincial levies.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Fleet crews (Egyptian fleet rebuilt after the Byzantine raid on Damietta in 853, Tarsus and Syrian squadrons), engineers, naffatun.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. A salaried army drawn from imported slave soldiers and specific groups; the general population was no longer a military reservoir.

abbasid-caliphate-850.notes: Snapshot = 850, under al-Mutawakkil at Samarra, eleven years before his murder opened the Anarchy at Samarra. Army size is the weakest number: no register total survives for the Samarra period; Toellner's 20,000-30,000 for Samarra and Kennedy's shakiriyya figures are the only modern anchors found, and the provincial and Tahirid forces are guessed. The chronicle figure of 70,000+ for al-Mu'tasim's 838 Amorium army (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'tasim) is noted but not used. Population convention: all lands recognising the caliph, including autonomous Tahirid Khurasan and Aghlabid Ifriqiya (low excludes them); Umayyad al-Andalus and Idrisid Morocco excluded.

Audit follow-up 2026-10-29: 6.0 -> 8.3, 6.0 sat below anchor 7, where powered military aviation starts; re-rated from the helicopters and light aircraft it flies.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.0 -> 0.05. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/AFG/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 51.63% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.55 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.53-0.56). Mid 1 - 0.516/0.55 = 0.05. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.53 = 0.01. High: s 0.56 = 0.07. Low floored at 0.01 (formula below 0): never 0 while agriculture exists. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 55% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Chronic food deficit; dependent on aid and imports after the 2021 aid cut-off.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 22,142,579 x share of males aged 15-19 11.274% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 499,278. Male population from SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10% for single-year cohort variation.

afghanistan-2026.notes: Modern snapshot asOf 2025-26. The armed forces are the Taliban's 'Islamic Emirate Army' since August 2021: a former insurgency organised into nominal corps, with captured US/ANA equipment (much unserviceable). Doctrine archetype-insurgent: they would fight any invader as dispersed light infantry. Conventional counts from the Wikipedia equipment list (IISS 2024 as quoted) are paper holdings; serviceable mids are educated guesses (grade D). Population inside ne:AFG (World Bank 2025). Money via derived:ppp-rebase-2011 (World Bank GDP 2024). Border clashes with Pakistan in October 2025 and February-March 2026 (Pakistani airstrikes on Kandahar, Bagram, Paktika). Ministry of Interior forces excluded. The Taliban government is recognised only by Russia (2025).

areaKm2.note: world_1715 polygon "Safavid Empire" = about 2.52 million km2 on the sphere (Iran, the Caucasus khanates, Herat and Kandahar), the last basemap before the Afghan conquest of 1722 and the nearest to Nader's restored realm. In 1739 Nader also held Kabul and the lands west of the Indus ceded by the Mughals (high); low allows for the loose hold on the Caucasus and the Persian Gulf coast. The world_1783 Persia polygon (Zand era) postdates the empire's collapse and is not used.

population.note: Infobox: about 9 million in 1736-1747 (Axworthy 2008 p. 160) (mid); about 6 million after 1747 (Axworthy 2008 pp. 160, 167) (low). High: OWID Iran 1740 = 5.55M plus Afghanistan 1740 = 2.74M (HYDE 3.3, modern borders, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population) = 8.29M, plus the Caucasus khanates, rounded up to 10M.

urbanization.note: Educated guess: Isfahan was still depopulated after the Afghan siege of 1722; Tabriz, Mashhad, Shiraz, Herat and Kandahar were sizeable caravan cities.

activePersonnel.note: Paper strength (Axworthy 2007 p. 639, via the article): 1736 = 150,000 (low), 1743 = 375,000 (peak). Linear interpolation to 1739 gives about 246,000 (high, rounded to 250,000); mid 200,000 because paper strengths overstate. The Indian expedition left Persia with about 80,000 and fought at Karnal with about 55,000 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Karnal, Sarkar p. 38, Rustam Ali).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: tribal and provincial contingents not under arms. High: the army grew from about 200,000 in 1739 to 375,000 by 1743 (Axworthy 2007 p. 639), the pool Nader could still draw on.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: gunners, zamburak crews, engineers and the Persian Gulf fleet; the camp servants (about a third of the 160,000-strong Karnal camp) are not counted.

mobilizationRatio.note: Peak paper strength 375,000 in 1743 (Axworthy 2007 p. 639, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Afsharid_dynasty_of_Persia) over 9 million people (Axworthy 2008 p. 160) = 0.042 (mid); low/high +/- about a quarter.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: 1744 breakdown (Axworthy 2007 p. 644, via the article): 13,000 guard cavalry (low) and 20,000 Afshar cavalry = 33,000 regular state horse (mid). High allows for other regular Khorasani horse (20 fowj of 1,000, uncited there).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: mail, sabre, lance and firearms; well mounted.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: long-service regulars trained under a uniform system in a decade of continuous campaigning.

count.note: Most of Nader's troops were light cavalry (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Afsharid_dynasty_of_Persia): 50,000 Afghan cavalry in 1744 (Axworthy 2007 p. 644) plus Turkmen, Uzbek, Kurdish and Lur tribal horse. Mid = active less the other roles and support (200,000 - 33,000 - 15,000 - 30,000 - 8,000 = about 114,000), rounded down.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: tribal horse with lance, sword, bow and matchlock.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: experienced tribal cavalry under Nader's discipline.

count.note: Jazayerchi, uniformed and drilled heavy musketeers: 20,000 at Karnal (Ghafouri 2008 p. 383, via the article) (high); 12,000 in 1744 (Axworthy 2007 p. 644 and Hanway, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Afsharid_dynasty_of_Persia) (low).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: heavy-calibre jazayer muskets that broke Mughal and Ottoman cavalry charges.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: drilled volley fire; Karnal and Yeghevard.

count.note: Ordinary foot musketeers (tofangchi): 40,000 in 1744 (Axworthy 2007 p. 644 and Hanway, via the article) (high); fewer in 1739 before the 1740s expansion.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: matchlock muskets.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: provincial musketeers, less drilled than the jazayerchi.

count.note: Educated guess within sourced bounds: the field army had 18 field pieces at Samarra in 1733 (von Hammer, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_the_Afsharid_dynasty_of_Persia) (low); "hundreds of cannons and zamburaks" at Karnal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Karnal) (high). The many hundreds of zamburak camel swivel guns are not counted as pieces.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: lighter and more manoeuvrable than the Mughal guns (Battle of Karnal article); siege guns cast for the sieges of Kandahar and Baghdad.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75.

count.note: Educated guess: Nader built ships at Bushehr and bought thirty ships in India (Encyclopaedia Iranica, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afsharid_Iran), mostly in the 1740s; in 1739 the Gulf fleet was a few bought European-built ships.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: second-hand merchantmen armed as warships.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25. Evidence: no naval tradition; hired crews.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 1.0 (best-in-era) minus. Evidence: Nader Shah beat Afghans, Ottomans and the Mughals in a decade; at Karnal 55,000 men routed a far larger Mughal army in a few hours.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5-0.75. Evidence: a multi-ethnic army (Persian, Afghan, Turkmen, Uzbek, Kurd) held by pay, success and harsh discipline; it broke up after Nader's murder in 1747.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: unbroken victories since 1729 and the Delhi plunder of 1739.

weapons.note: Anchor: 5 (1600, musket, field cannon) to 6. Evidence: heavy jazayer muskets, matchlocks, mobile field guns and zamburaks; no bayonet-flintlock infantry.

armor.note: Anchor: 5 (half-armour). Evidence: mail and helmets for the horse.

ships.note: Anchor: 4-5. Evidence: a few European-built ships bought for the Gulf.

fortification.note: Anchor: 5 minus. Evidence: walled cities and citadels, the siege town built before Kandahar (1737-38); no trace italienne.

logistics.note: Anchor: 5 (magazines). Evidence: camel trains and depots that carried an army from Kandahar over the Khyber to Delhi (1738-39).

communications.note: Anchor: 5 minus. Evidence: mounted couriers on the caravan roads.

isr.note: Anchor: 5. Evidence: light-cavalry screens and spies; Karnal was won by luring the Mughals out of their entrenched camp.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: silk, carpets and crafts, damaged by two decades of war.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Qanat-irrigated oases and dry farming; the army requisitioned heavily.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: Safavid caravan roads with caravanserais and stone causeways; mostly unpaved.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: Bushehr (Nader's naval base) and Bandar Abbas; Caspian landings.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Gulf trade was carried mostly by European, Indian and Arab ships.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Cavalry-heavy armies with camel trains campaigned from Mashhad to Delhi and to Bukhara and Khiva (1740).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: camels, horses and mules of a pastoral and caravan economy (about 10% of the population); no count found.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: plateau ringed by mountains, walled cities and local supply; population support weakened by heavy taxation.

afsharid-iran-1739.notes: Snapshot = February 1739, Nader Shah's realm at the Battle of Karnal. Personnel: paper strength of the standing army (Axworthy) is activePersonnel, with the role split from the 1744 breakdown and the Karnal jazayerchi count; tribal contingents not yet raised are trainedReserves; camp servants are not counted. Territory = the world_1715 Safavid Empire polygon; the Mughal lands east of the Indus taken in 1739 were returned in May 1739 and are not included; includes is empty. Weakest values: activePersonnel mid (paper figures interpolated between 1736 and 1743), artillery and navy counts, GDP per capita (no Maddison value before 1820) and the economy and logistics guesses. Doctrine archetype-gunpowder-linear follows the safavid-empire-1600 precedent.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Polity Territory 450,000-1,000,000 km2 for 2270-2083 BCE (mid = midpoint). Taagepera 1978 gives 0.8 million km2 at 2250 BCE (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_empires). Border = union of the historical-basemaps world_bc3000 polygons 'Ur' (southern and central Mesopotamia incl. Susa, 341,000 km2) and 'city-states' (Upper Mesopotamia and north Syria incl. Mari, Nagar, Ebla, 228,000 km2), computed from the GeoJSON at ~569,000 km2; bc3000 is the nearest file at or before 2250 BCE and has no Akkad polygon.

population.note: OWID historical population (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true, McEvedy-Jones/HYDE series): Iraq 0.5 M in 3000 BCE and 0.875 M in 2000 BCE, linear to 2250 BCE = 0.78 M; plus roughly half of Syria's 0.69 M (2000 BCE) for the Upper Mesopotamian and north Syrian provinces (Mari, Nagar, Ebla) and Susiana. Seshat codes the Akkadian population as undecided (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/476). Wide range.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Southern Mesopotamia was the most urban region of its time (Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish); the northern and Zagros provinces much less. Seshat codes the largest settlement at 20,000-40,000.

activePersonnel.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Low = the 5,400 standing troops plus support; mid adds governors' garrisons in the subject cities and city levies for a campaign; high = a full imperial muster.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. City levies callable within a month along the river network.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Boat crews, onager-wagon drivers, scribes and quartermasters.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Agrarian temple-and-palace state with corvee obligations; Sumerian city levies were large relative to population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Split: close-order spear, axe and mace infantry ~57%.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: copper/bronze axes, spears and maces; lighter kit than the Early Dynastic phalanx but well equipped for the era.

training.note: Core of 5,400 professionals (0.75) diluted by city levies (0.25-0.5).

count.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Split: archers ~29%; the Akkadian reliefs introduce the bow (probably composite) into Mesopotamian battle scenes (Lafont et al. 2001 cited in the fetched page).

quality.note: Composite bow, an advanced weapon for 2250 BCE (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Mixed professionals and levies.

count.note: Field force of Naram-Sin c. 2250: no modern total exists. Anchors: a Sargon inscription says 5,400 men ate daily before him, read as a standing royal army (Westenholz 1999 pp. 65-68, cited in the fetched page); Naram-Sin's inscription names the 'Nine Regiments of Akkad' as the core. Rimush claims 16,212 enemy slain in one battle (royal inscription, quoted in Hamblin 2006, not used as a size). Split: javelin and skirmish troops, Amorite and highland auxiliaries ~14%.

quality.note: Light traditional equipment.

training.note: Levies and auxiliaries.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Sargon and Naram-Sin were proven conquerors with generals (shakkanakkum) commanding organized corps; no evidence of a staff system.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: repeated 'Great Revolt' of Sumerian and Akkadian cities against Naram-Sin; loyal royal core.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: long run of victories and a divine-king ideology.

weapons.note: Anchor 1 (2500 BCE copper/bronze maces, spears) plus the composite bow seen on Akkadian monuments, a step toward anchor 2. audit 2026-10-30: mid 1.3 -> 1.23, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -2250 (1.227); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

armor.note: Anchor 1: leather capes and copper helmets; little body armour.

ships.note: Anchor 1: oared riverboats; Sargon claims ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moored at Akkad (sea trade, not a war fleet).

fortification.note: Anchor 1: mudbrick city walls (Uruk, Ur) and fortified outposts such as Nagar.

logistics.note: Anchor 1: donkeys, onager wagons, river and canal transport; redistributive granaries.

communications.note: Anchor 1: runners and river messengers; Akkadian adopted as an administrative language across the empire.

isr.note: Year anchor (2250 BCE ~ 1.1): scouts and informants.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Iraq 1 CE = 1,116 (2011 int$), Iraq 730 CE = 1,466. Applied 2,250 years earlier and scaled down (lower agricultural productivity, no coinage, but highly productive irrigated cereal farming).

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. The standing army was fed from palace rations; no fiscal data.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Craft production (metal, textiles) concentrated in temple and palace workshops.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated barley agriculture in the alluvium produced high yields per seed and fed large dependent workforces.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No engineered road network is attested; movement followed rivers, canals and caravan tracks.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. River and Gulf harbours: Akkad quay, Ur, Lagash, Mari on the Euphrates.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gulf trade ships of a few tons to ~20 t and river craft.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Armies moved along rivers with boat supply; away from water, donkey trains limited range.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.06-0.12 donkeys, oxen and onager hybrids per inhabitant.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: local supply and familiar alluvial terrain; walled cities argue for 1.2, but the cities themselves were the rebels.

akkad--2250.notes: Snapshot = reign of Naram-Sin c. 2250 BCE (middle chronology), empire at greatest extent. Archetype doctrine is bronze-chariot but the Akkadian army had no horse chariots: the four-wheeled onager battle-wagons of the Early Dynastic period appear to have lost importance in favour of infantry, so no chariots role is listed. All army numbers are reconstructions; royal inscriptions (5,400 men fed daily; enemy dead in the thousands) are not used as mids. Population convention: everything inside the border, McEvedy-Jones-type regional series interpolated.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.03 -> 0.71. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/DZA/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 9.48% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.33 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.29-0.35). Mid 1 - 0.095/0.33 = 0.71. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.29 = 0.58. High: s 0.35 = 0.73. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 33% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Major cereal importer.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.05 -> 0.34. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/AGO/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 51.95% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.79 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.77-0.80). Mid 1 - 0.519/0.79 = 0.34. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.77 = 0.19. High: s 0.80 = 0.35. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 79% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Net food importer despite large arable potential. Not from FAO balance sheets.

population.note: OWID (UN WPP) Argentina 1982 = 28.92M; COW NMC v7 tpop 1982 = 28,966k; World Bank SP.POP.TOTL 1982 = 28.92M; MB 1981-82 = 28,000,000 (low).

urbanization.note: OWID urban share Argentina 1982 = 83.6%. COW upop/tpop 1982 = 12,460/28,966 = 0.43 (cities over 100,000 only), not used.

activePersonnel.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): total armed forces 185,500 (118,000 conscripts): army 130,000 (90,000 conscripts), navy 36,000 incl. 3,000 naval air and 10,000 marines, air force 19,500. COW NMC v7 milper 1982 = 175,000 (mid). Low: the 1962 conscript class had been released and the 1963 class was only weeks into training in April 1982; the 1962 class was recalled. Gendarmerie, coastguard and federal police (43,000) excluded.

trainedReserves.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): RESERVES 250,000 (200,000 National Guard, 50,000 Territorial Guard) = recent conscript classes. Low discounts classes not recalled; high adds the 1962 class.

supportPersonnel.note: Everything outside the P roles: navy 36,000 less ~3,000 marine riflemen, air force 19,500, army armoured cavalry, artillery, 6 AD battalions, engineers, aviation, logistics, 5 corps staffs and conscripts in basic training (~85,000) = ~135,000.

mobilizationRatio.note: Active 185,500 + reserves 250,000 (MB 1981-82) = 435,500 of 28.9M = 1.5% of population on a fast call-up; a total-war mobilisation of the 18-40 male classes (CIA World Factbook 1990: 6.37M males fit for service, 1990) would reach several times that. Range 3-8%.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 3 infantry brigades (1 mech, 2 mot, 3 regiments each) plus corps and independent infantry regiments, and the marines' 5 infantry battalions. Argentine regiments were battalion-sized (~500-800 riflemen; the 25th Regiment that landed at Stanley was ~681 men, Falklands War article). ~25-35 battalion-equivalents x ~800. Reconstruction.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: FN FAL, MAG, 81/120 mm mortars, Cobra and Bantam ATGW (MB 1981-82); some night sights; era-typical.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: one-year conscripts, the 1963 class barely trained; harsh field punishments and poor rations on the islands (Falklands War article). Marines (5th Bn) better (high).

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 3 mountain brigades, 1 jungle brigade, 1 airborne brigade, marine commando battalion; plus 601/602 army commando companies. ~16 battalion-equivalents x ~800. Reconstruction.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: as line infantry, plus mountain and airborne kit.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.75. Evidence: commando companies and marines professional (high); mountain and airborne brigades conscript-based.

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): army 200 105 mm incl. quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: mostly towed 105/155 mm of 1940s-60s design.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: 3rd Artillery Group fought competently at Stanley; conscript gunners.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: TAM (1980 design, 105 mm gun, light armour) era-typical; Sherman and AMX-13 obsolete.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript crews; armoured cavalry brigades trained for the Chilean border.

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 300 AMX-VTP, some TAM VCTP, 75 M-3, 5 BDX, 250 M-113, 50 Mowag Roland (army) + 22 LVTP-7 and 6 Roland (marines) = ~710.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: VCTP modern; AMX-VCI, M-3 half-tracks old.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscripts.

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 1 interceptor sqn with 19 Mirage IIIEA + 2 IIIDA; 2 sqn with 26 Dagger (IAI Nesher) = 47. quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Mirage III and Dagger contemporaries of the Harrier but with only R-530/Shafrir AAM and no all-aspect Sidewinder (MB lists R-530).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: skilled pilots; Daggers pressed low-level attacks on the San Carlos fleet (Falklands War article).

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): air force 9 Canberra B-62 + 2 T-64, 68 A-4P Skyhawk, 32 MS-760A Paris, 45 IA-58A Pucara = 156; naval air 11 A-4Q; plus 5 Super Etendard delivered by April 1982 (Falklands War article: the five Etendards at Rio Grande) = 172. quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: subsonic A-4s without ECM, Pucara COIN aircraft; only 5 Super Etendard with 5 AM39 Exocet.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: Super Etendard-Exocet sank HMS Sheffield and Atlantic Conveyor; low-level bombing sank Ardent and Antelope and hit Sir Galahad, although many bombs failed to explode (Falklands War article).

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): army ~70 (A-109, UH-1H, Lama, CH-47C, Puma, Bell 206/212, FH-1100), air force ~60 (Hughes 500M, UH-1H, Puma, S-61R, CH-47C, Bell 212), navy ~19 (S-61D, Alouette III, Lynx, Puma) = ~150; mid discounts unserviceable airframes.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: mostly utility types, no dedicated attack helicopter.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: army aviation sustained island garrisons until grounded by British air superiority.

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 1 ex-British Colossus carrier (Veinticinco de Mayo), 1 ex-US Brooklyn cruiser (General Belgrano), 9 destroyers (2 Type 42 with Exocet and Sea Dart, 3 Fletcher, 3 Sumner, 1 Gearing) = 11. Low allows Fletchers paid off before April 1982. Falklands War article: Belgrano sunk by HMS Conqueror 2 May.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: 2 Type 42 modern; carrier, cruiser and 7 destroyers WWII hulls (some with Exocet refits).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: professional cadre, half conscripts (18,000 of 36,000).

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 2-3 A-69 corvettes with Exocet (2 in MB, a third delivered 1981), 7 patrol ships, 3 large patrol craft, 2 TNC-45, 4 Dabur, 2 Higgins FAC(T), 6 Ton MCM = 26-27.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: A-69 corvettes modern; the rest old patrol craft.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: as major ships.

count.note: IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): 2 Type 209 (Salta, San Luis), 2 ex-US Guppy (Santa Fe, Santiago del Estero). Low: Santiago del Estero was non-operational and Santa Fe was disabled at South Georgia on 25 April (Falklands War article losses list a Balao-class submarine).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Type 209 modern diesel boats; Guppies WWII-era.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: San Luis was the only Argentine unit to keep operating at sea after the Belgrano sinking (Falklands War article) but scored no hits.

count.note: Batteries. IISS Military Balance 1981-1982, Argentina entry (samlib.ru full-text transcription; data as of July 1981, the last edition before the war): army 6 AD battalions (30/35/40/90 mm AA guns, Tigercat, 10 Roland SAM), marines 1 AD battalion (30 mm, 10 Tigercat); at ~3 batteries per battalion = ~21, plus air force Oerlikon/Skyguard 35 mm batteries (~4). Reconstruction from battalion counts.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Roland and Skyguard-directed 35 mm modern; Tigercat and 40/90 mm guns old.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Stanley air defences kept the airfield usable through the five Black Buck raids and Harrier attacks (Falklands War article).

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: junta command with no joint staff; after the Belgrano sinking the entire fleet except the submarine San Luis returned to port (Falklands War article); Veinticinco de Mayo could not launch her aircraft for lack of wind.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.25-0.5. Evidence: conscript army with an officer-conscript divide and harsh punishments (Falklands War article); marine and commando units held together better.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: the Malvinas cause had broad popular support and lifted the junta in April 1982; conscript morale on the islands fell under cold, hunger and isolation.

weapons.note: Anchor: between 8 (1943) and 9 (1985). Evidence: AM39/MM38 Exocet, Sea Dart, Roland, Tigercat, FN FAL; but Sherman tanks and WWII naval guns (MB 1981-82).

armor.note: Anchor: 8 (rolled armour). Evidence: TAM light-armoured medium tank, AMX-13, M-4 Sherman.

ships.note: Anchor: between 8 and 9. Evidence: Type 42 destroyers with Sea Dart, Type 209 submarines; a WWII carrier and cruiser; no nuclear submarines.

fortification.note: Anchor: 8 (concrete lines). Evidence: dug-in positions on the hills around Stanley; no hardened air bases.

logistics.note: Anchor: 8 (motor transport, rail) to 9 (airlift). Evidence: 7 C-130 + 2 KC-130 tankers (MB) sustained an air bridge to Stanley; sea resupply cut by the blockade.

communications.note: Anchor: between 8 and 9. Evidence: HF/VHF radio networks; no satellite communications or tactical data links.

isr.note: Anchor: ISR 8 = radar, 9 = satellites. Evidence: SP-2H Neptune and Boeing 707 maritime reconnaissance, AN/TPS-43 radar at Stanley; no satellites.

air.note: Anchor: air 9 = 1985. Evidence: Mirage III, Dagger, Super Etendard; no AEW or modern AAM.

cyber.note: No military computer networks with attack capability before ~1985; anchor cyber 9 = 1990 networks.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of the labour force (share of food output not eaten by the farm population; no calorie self-sufficiency adjustment). World Bank WDI Database Archives (version 1999 Apr), SL.AGR.TOTL.ZS "Labor force in agriculture (% of total)" (ILO-based) Argentina 1982 = 12.8%. CIA World Factbook 1990: 12% (1985). Argentina was a major food exporter. Share 12.8% (range 10.0-15.0%) -> 0.872 (0.85-0.9).

armor.note: Educated guess: TAM and VCTP vehicles per year from TAMSE (120 more TAM on order in MB 1981-82).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: CIA World Factbook 1990 (https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/14/pg14.txt): 131 ships of 1,693,540 GRT / 2,707,079 DWT in 1990 (low). The ELMA and YPF fleets were larger in 1982 before the late-1980s contraction.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: Stanley lies ~700 km from Rio Gallegos; the garrison was supplied by C-130 air bridge and, until the blockade, by sea. Mainland operations near Chile would sit on rail and road.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: horses (~3M) and mules in the pampas economy; mountain brigades used mule trains.

nuclearWarheads.note: FAS stockpile series (OWID) lists no Argentine warheads; the nuclear programme (Pilcaniyeu enrichment plant, announced 1983) produced no weapon.

homeDefense.note: 1.1 row: familiar terrain and local supply on the mainland; high 1.2 for population support and Andean barrier against Chile. The occupied Falklands get no home bonus.

argentina-1982.notes: Snapshot date 2 April 1982 (invasion of the Falklands); force data from IISS Military Balance 1981-82 (data July 1981; read in the samlib.ru full-text transcription at http://samlib.ru/t/temezhnikow_e_a/mb1981.shtml), cross-checked with COW NMC v7 and the Falklands War article (land forces on the islands about 10,000-13,000 at peak per the infobox; ~681 men of the 25th Regiment landed first). Personnel: active = army, navy (incl. naval air and marines) and air force incl. conscripts; National and Territorial Guard (recent conscript classes) in trainedReserves; gendarmerie, coastguard and federal police excluded. Population and territory: continental Argentina; the occupied Falklands and South Georgia are listed as bases abroad, not territory. Freedman's official history and the Military Balance 1982-83 (post-war) were not used for counts. Logistics bounds come from the 1990 CIA World Factbook and are adjusted for 1982 by judgement.

areaKm2.note: Hansen 2006 p. 55: Attika could sustain ~100,000 at a carrying capacity of just over 40 per km2, i.e. ~2,400 km2 of mainland Attika; with Salamis ~2,550 km2 (Hansen & Nielsen Inventory gives c. 2,500 km2; not fetched).

population.note: Hansen 2006 (pp. 55-56, nn. 126, 136-137): 4th-century Attika at 150,000 (21,000 adult male citizens) to 210,000 (31,000 adult male citizens; his preferred model: x3.5 for all citizens, +30,000 metics, free:slave 2:1), with Whitby at 250,000-300,000. For 480 BCE, Patterson's 25,000-30,000 adult male citizens (cited in the Hansen literature; Herodotus 5.97 gives 30,000 c. 500) plus fewer metics and slaves than in the 4th century give ~190,000. Citizens, metics and slaves of Attika incl. Salamis.

urbanization.note: Educated guess: Athens (with Phaleron/Piraeus) held perhaps a quarter to a third of Attika's population in the classical period; 480 likely at the lower end.

activePersonnel.note: Sum of hoplites (8,000), archers (~700), light-armed (~4,000) and fleet crews (~33,500). In 480 Athens mobilised nearly all men of military age (Hansen 2006 p. 10); this is ~25% of population, above the validator's 20% warning by design.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: oldest and youngest year classes left for guard duty; in 480 nearly everyone else was already serving. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3,000 -> 2,000 so that active (47,000) + reserves fit inside mobilizable (49,400); this is an educated guess either way.

supportPersonnel.note: Trireme crews: 170 oarsmen + ~16 deck crew/officers per ship (marines and archers are counted as P roles). Low 180 x 170; mid 180 x 186 (the 20 ships lent to Chalcis were crewed by Chalcidians, Herodotus 8.1); high 200 x 186. Rowers included citizens, metics and slaves (Hansen 2006 pp. 10-16).

mobilizationRatio.note: Hansen 2006 p. 10: in 480 perhaps 90% of the year classes 20-49 (Figueira: up to 55) were called up to man the fleet, metics and slaves included. Males 20-55 are ~half of all males, i.e. ~25% of the population; the ratio of the actual 480 effort to total population is ~0.25.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Herodotus 9.28: 8,000 Athenian hoplites at Plataea (479); ~9,000-10,000 at Marathon (490, later sources). Lazenby 1993 accepts figures of this order. In 480 many served as epibatai (10 per trireme) instead. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Bronze hoplite panoply among the era's best heavy infantry (0.75).

training.note: Citizen militia without state drill before the ephebeia (rubric 0.25-0.5).

count.note: Athenian archers fought at Plataea (Herodotus 9.22, 9.60); triremes carried 4 archers each (180 x 4 = 720). Thucydides 2.13.8 gives 1,600 archers for 431 (upper bound). audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - a / s (a = agricultural share of employment, s = calorie self-sufficiency). s from the cited source: Hansen 2006 p. 55 n. 125, Attika "in normal years could sustain a population of ca. 100,000"; with this snapshot's ~190,000 people s = ~0.53 (Moreno, cited there, 52,000-106,000: s 0.27-0.56). a: no fetched occupational figure; ~0.5 (0.42-0.6) assumed, bounded by the urban share (~0.3) and Hansen's point that most of the population lived from farming. Mid 1 - 0.50/0.53 = 0.06; high a 0.42, s 0.56 = 0.25; low 0 where a >= s (the farms only feed the farm population; towns and fleet live on imported grain). Grade D. audit 2026-10-30: was 0/0/0.05 (read as no domestic surplus); recomputed with the formula, which gives a similar value because s is low.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical snapshots. Citizen year class alone ~1,000 for 30,000 adult male citizens (Hansen 2006 p. 35).

roadKm.note: Educated guess: a few engineered routes (Sacred Way to Eleusis ~20 km), otherwise tracks.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Phaleron and Piraeus (being fortified from 493; shipsheds for the Themistoklean fleet).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: grain imports for ~90,000 people at ~200 kg/person/year = ~18,000 t a year, carried by a merchant fleet making several voyages a season.

supplyRangeKm.note: Hoplite armies marched with ~3 days' rations x ~20 km a day; by sea the fleet's range was a few days' rowing between beaching places.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.02-0.06 oxen, mules and donkeys per inhabitant x population.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: familiar terrain and local supply; the city walls did not yet stand in 480 (Athens was evacuated and sacked), so not 1.2.

athens--480.notes: Snapshot = 480 BCE, the Salamis year. Border "none": historical-basemaps world_bc500 only has a single "Greek city-states" polygon (all of Greece incl. Macedonia, plus Magna Graecia and Massalia as further features), which would overstate Athens' territory ~50-fold. Population convention: Attika incl. Salamis, citizens + metics + slaves; no allies. Population for 480 extrapolated from 4th-century models; every Athenian demographic number is disputed (Hansen's "shotgun method"). Active personnel is ~25% of population (validator warning expected): in 480 nearly every able man, incl. metics and slaves, rowed in the fleet. Fleet crews are supportPersonnel per schema; hoplites serving as marines are counted under infantry_line.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.55 -> 0.99. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/AUS/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 2.18% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 2.50 (mean 2021-2023, range 2.47-2.53). Mid 1 - 0.022/2.50 = 0.99. Low: a x 1.5 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 2.47 = 0.99. High: s 2.53 = 0.99. Net exporter: production is about 250% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Exports roughly 70% of agricultural output (wheat, beef, wool, barley); not computed from FAO balance sheets.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 13,702,766 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share of males aged 15-19 6.371% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 174,614. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10%.

australia-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2024-25 data with 2026 order of battle. doctrineId archetype-modern-regional (archetype-coldwar-western is outdated for a 2026 force). Population convention: everything inside ne:AUS (World Bank; external territories such as Christmas Island are separate NE units). Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011. Force counts: IISS Military Balance 2024 (personnel) as quoted; Australian Army equipment list (deliveries as of Apr-May 2026), RAAF inventory and the active RAN ships list. The force is mid-transition: Tiger/MRH-90 retired, Abrams/Apache/Black Hawk/HIMARS/AS9 deliveries running, so counts carry a delivery-timing range. ships_major = LHD + destroyers + frigates; ships_minor = LSD, OPV, patrol, MCM; drones = Group 2+ UAVs (MQ-28 test airframes counted at half). Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Tech note on armour: active protection on Australian Abrams is not confirmed, so armor stays below anchor 10.

areaKm2.note: world_1914 Austro-Hungarian Empire polygon = ~650,000 km2 computed on the sphere (low); published area incl. Bosnia ~676,600 km2 (B&H Table 2: 0.6M km2).

population.note: Broadberry and Harrison 2005 Table 2: Austria-Hungary 1913 = 50.6M (low); COW tpop 1914 = 52,594k (high). Includes Bosnia-Herzegovina.

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share 1910: Austria 40%, Hungary 25.6% (present-day borders; the Galician and Balkan lands were far less urban). Mid 0.25 for the empire. Low = COW upop/tpop 1914 = 4,405/52,594 = 0.08 (cities over 100,000).

activePersonnel.note: Cited page: after war was declared 3.35 million men (incl. the first call-up of the reserves and the 1914 recruits) gathered for action. Navy (~20,000 peace, ~35,000 mobilised) included. Snapshot month: August 1914. Check: COW NMC v7 milper 1914 = 839k, 1915 = 3,800k (annual averages, not the snapshot-date strength).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Rothenberg, The Army of Francis Joseph (isbn:0-911198-41-5), not read from a fetched source. Trained Landsturm and Ersatz reservists not called in August; low conscription (only ~20-25% of each class trained, Rothenberg ch. 10) left a small trained pool.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Rothenberg, The Army of Francis Joseph (isbn:0-911198-41-5), not read from a fetched source. Artillery, engineers, trains (the B-Staffel shuttle between Serbia and Galicia), fortress garrisons (Przemysl ~130,000), Landsturm rear units, navy, staffs.

mobilizationRatio.note: Total mobilised: 9,000,000 (Austrian government reply to the ILO) or 7,800,000 (US War Dept) on the cited page; / ~51.5M = 0.15-0.175.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Rothenberg, The Army of Francis Joseph (isbn:0-911198-41-5), not read from a fetched source. 48 infantry divisions of the common army, Landwehr and Honved plus Landsturm brigades (~12,000 rifles per division) and march battalions. Reconstruction from Rothenberg ch. 11 and Herwig ch. 2.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Mannlicher M95 and Schwarzlose MG good; fewest guns per division of the powers (~42)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: short-service conscripts, ~20-25% of each class trained; officers could not speak their men's languages

count.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Rothenberg, The Army of Francis Joseph (isbn:0-911198-41-5), not read from a fetched source. Tiroler Kaiserjaeger (4 regiments), Landesschuetzen (3 regiments) and ~32 Feldjaeger battalions.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: colourful uniforms, saddles that galled the horses; cavalry ruined in the August 1914 reconnaissance

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: tiny air arm

gdpPerCapita.note: B&H Table 2: 1,986 in 1990 int$; x ~1.6 (the 2011/1990 int$ ratio of Maddison 2023 vs 2001 for Germany and France) = ~3,180. Cross-check, population-weighted Maddison 2023 (OWID CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv) 1913 values: Austria 5,523 (6.6M), Czech lands ~3,800 (10M), Hungary 3,344 (7.7M), Slovakia/Transylvania/Croatia ~2,200 (12M), Galicia/Bukovina ~2,000 (8.8M), Bosnia/Dalmatia ~1,500 (2.5M) = ~3,110.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Ferguson, The Pity of War (isbn:0-7139-9246-8), not read from a fetched source. Low: defence ~2.8% of NNP in 1913, the lowest of the great powers (Ferguson table 6). Mid/high: wartime share; B&H Table 5 gives no Austro-Hungarian government series.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Industry and mining ~30% of output, concentrated in Bohemia, Lower Austria and Budapest; Galicia and the south-east agrarian.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of employment. Cited page: 67% of the workforce in agriculture in 1870 and 60% in 1913. 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 (mid). The Austrian half depended on Hungarian grain.

annualCohort.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Rothenberg, The Army of Francis Joseph (isbn:0-911198-41-5), not read from a fetched source. Men reaching 21 per year ~0.45-0.55M; only ~160,000-200,000 per year were actually inducted before 1912 (Rothenberg ch. 10).

artillery.note: Educated guess. Field and heavy guns per year 1915-1917 (Skoda Pilsen, Steyr; output limited by steel and coal).

aircraft_fighter.note: Educated guess. Fighters per year 1916-1917 (Hansa-Brandenburg D.I, Aviatik D.I, Albatros licence); total Austro-Hungarian aircraft output ~5,400 over the war.

aircraft_strike.note: Educated guess. Reconnaissance and bomber aircraft per year 1915-1917.

ships_major.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Szent Istvan completed 1915; no capital ships after.

ships_minor.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Destroyers and large torpedo boats per year.

submarines.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Submarines completed per year 1915-1918 (~25 over the war).

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Metalled roads of Austria and Hungary; poor in Galicia and the Carpathians.

railKm.note: Educated guess. CHAT railline Austria 1913 = 22,981 km (Cisleithania, read from https://data.nber.org/chat/chat.dta); CHAT has no Hungarian value before 1921, so the Hungarian and Bosnian lines (~22,000 km) are recalled.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Recalled from Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships 1906-1921 (isbn:0-85177-245-5), not read from a fetched source. Trieste, Pola, Fiume, Cattaro, Sebenico, Spalato.

merchantTonnage.note: Lloyd's Register returns 1914: Austro-Hungarian flag 1,011,414 GRT (steam and sail, 100 tons and over, Register Book 1913-14). Converted to deadweight at x1.5 (low x1.3 of the low GRT, high x1.6 of the high GRT).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Austro-Hungarian armies in Serbia and Galicia struggled beyond ~100-150 km of the railheads; Carpathian winter campaign 1915 a logistic disaster.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses of Austria (~1.8M) and Hungary (~2.3M) plus Bosnia; ~0.6M requisitioned in 1914.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before July 1945.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: Carpathian and Alpine barriers, fortresses (Przemysl, Krakow), population support in the core lands.

austria-hungary-1914.notes: Snapshot date August 1914 after mobilisation (partial mobilisation against Serbia 25 July, general 31 July). Territory = the Dual Monarchy incl. Bosnia-Herzegovina; includes is empty (Austria and Hungary as later states are separate nationIds). Forces are the whole army; ~1M men went to Galicia against Russia and ~0.3M against Serbia in August (Herwig ch. 2). Aircraft in aircraft_strike (no fighters in 1914). Ship convention per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: battleships, carriers, cruisers and destroyers = ships_major, torpedo boats and smaller craft = ships_minor (role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries). Book figures (Rothenberg, Herwig, Conway's) not fetched online, graded at most B.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes Axum II (350-599) at 600,000-700,000 km2 and Axum I (to 349) at 300,000-400,000 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208, low). High 1.25 million km2 for 350 is Turchin, Adams and Hall (2006) in the infobox of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum, which counts the claimed Nubian and Arabian lands. The world_300 Axum polygon measures only 89,000 km2 (the Tigray and Eritrean highland core), so the map understates the realm.

population.note: Seshat codes Axum II (350-599) at 500,000-600,000 and its Axum I page quotes "at the outside half a million" for the kingdom without its Arabian and Nubian territories (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208). High: HYDE via OWID (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population) has Ethiopia 861,709 (300) and 1,053,627 (400) and Eritrea 36,036-38,808, about 1.0 million for both modern countries in 350, a ceiling since the kingdom held only the north.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Aksum covered 80-100 ha in the first four centuries CE, 4,500 to 20,000 people at 50-200 per ha (Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/208); Seshat codes its largest settlement at 50,000-60,000 for 350-599 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/210, high). Adulis, Matara and Qohaito were smaller towns.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. No army size survives. The inscriptions name royal armies (sarawit) sent out as separate columns, and the RIE 186 passage on the road Ousanas built for tribute and troop provisions names four sarawit (Hatke 2013, pp. 32-34). RIE 189, Ezana's Nubian campaign of c. 360, tallies 602 men and 156 women and children killed, 629 prisoners, 10,560 cattle and 51,050 sheep; an earlier campaign resettled some 4,400 Beja (Hatke 2013, Aksum and Nubia, pp. 124-130, https://dlib.nyu.edu/awdl/isaw/hatke2013-aksum-and-nubia/). Tallies of that order fit field armies of a few thousand to about 10,000.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.05 -> 0.5. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/AZE/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 34.23% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.68 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.67-0.70). Mid 1 - 0.342/0.68 = 0.5. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.67 = 0.38. High: s 0.70 = 0.51. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 68% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Imports most wheat; exports fruit and vegetables. aztec-empire-1519.notes: Snapshot = November 1519, Cortes entering Tenochtitlan under Moctezuma II. Personnel convention: there was no standing army, so activePersonnel is only the noble warrior orders and frontier garrisons; the trained commoner levy of the calpolli is trainedReserves. No horses and no gunpowder: cavalry, artillery and draft animals are absent. Population is disputed: estimates for central Mexico run from ~3 million to 25 million; the 6 million mid follows the population history article. Chronicle army sizes (200,000-400,000) are rejected as mid values per the brief; Hassig (Aztec Warfare, 1988) not consulted directly. Population convention: the Triple Alliance core and tributary provinces; independent Tlaxcala, Metztitlan, Yopitzinco and the Tarascan state excluded.

The historical-basemaps world_bc2000 polygon 'Ur' (nearest file before 1750; covers Babylon, Sippar, Larsa, Eshnunna and Assur) measures ~341,000 km2 computed from the GeoJSON. Mari and the middle Euphrates are outside that polygon.

After 1763-1761 Hammurabi held Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, so he could field roughly what three kingdoms combined could. count.note: Hamblin 2006, Warfare in the Ancient Near East to 1600 BC, ch. 7 (Mari archive): Shamshi-Adad wrote that 6,000 men from Mari, 10,000 from Assyria and 6,000 from allied Eshnunna would make 'a strong army' of 20,000, implying most armies of the age were smaller; a Mari report puts an enemy force at 15,000; Hammurabi himself warned that 1,000 troops sent are rumoured as 10,000. After 1763-1761 Hammurabi held Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, so he could field roughly what three kingdoms combined could. Split: archers and slingers ~28%. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Composite bows in use.

training.note: Levies with some specialists.

count.note: Hamblin 2006, Warfare in the Ancient Near East to 1600 BC, ch. 7 (Mari archive): Shamshi-Adad wrote that 6,000 men from Mari, 10,000 from Assyria and 6,000 from allied Eshnunna would make 'a strong army' of 20,000, implying most armies of the age were smaller; a Mari report puts an enemy force at 15,000; Hammurabi himself warned that 1,000 troops sent are rumoured as 10,000. After 1763-1761 Hammurabi held Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, so he could field roughly what three kingdoms combined could. Split: Amorite tribal auxiliaries and skirmishers ~17%. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Light equipment.

training.note: Tribal warriors, experienced but undrilled.

count.note: Educated guess. Horse-drawn chariots existed in the Mari period but were rare and largely royal; chariot armies only spread after ~1600 BCE. Crews are in supportPersonnel.

quality.note: Early, heavier chariots, a generation before the Late Bronze Age light chariot.

training.note: Elite crews but no chariot tactics yet.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Hammurabi was a proven strategist (sequenced wars against Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari; flooding tactics); generalship good, no staff system.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: coalition warfare of shifting Amorite kingdoms; core Babylonian troops more cohesive.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: string of victories 1764-1755 BCE.

weapons.note: Between anchor 1 and 2: tin bronze, composite bows, early chariots but no chariot armies.

armor.note: Between anchor 1 and 2: helmets, some leather and early scale armour.

ships.note: Anchor 1: river boats used for troop and grain transport.

fortification.note: Between 1 and 2: massive mudbrick walls (Babylon, Mari, Eshnunna), siege towers and rams attested in Mari texts.

logistics.note: Between 1 and 2: river transport, palace granaries, ration lists; ilkum supply system.

communications.note: Between 1 and 2: dense royal correspondence by courier (Mari letters) and fire signals.

isr.note: Year anchor ~1.4: envoys, spies and informant reports are frequent in the Mari letters.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Iraq 1 CE = 1,116, 730 CE = 1,466 (2011 int$). Old Babylonian contracts show a monetised silver economy with hired labour; scaled slightly below the 1 CE value.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Soldiers were mostly paid in field allotments (ilkum), not cash.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Craft and trade economy (textiles, metal, long-distance trade).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated agriculture; recurrent salinisation in the south.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No engineered roads; river, canal and caravan routes.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. River ports at Sippar, Babylon, Ur, Mari.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. River boats of a few tons and Gulf trade via Dilmun.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Armies followed the rivers with boat supply; Mari letters show armies short of grain away from them.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.1-0.13 donkeys and oxen per inhabitant.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: familiar alluvium, walled cities and canals that could be used for flooding.

babylon--1750.notes: Snapshot = 1750 BCE (middle chronology), after Hammurabi's conquest of Larsa (1763), Eshnunna and Mari (1761). Chariots are listed only as a token royal arm because the horse chariot was not yet a mass weapon in Mesopotamia; the chariot-archetype doctrine fits poorly. Army numbers are reconstructed from Mari-archive letters as discussed by Hamblin (2006), not from any census. Population convention: everything inside the border.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.05 -> 0.4. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BGD/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 44.26% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.74 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.72-0.75). Mid 1 - 0.443/0.74 = 0.4. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.72 = 0.26. High: s 0.75 = 0.41. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 74% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Near self-sufficient in rice, imports wheat; dense population leaves little surplus.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.55 -> 0.95. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BRA/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 7.63% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 1.57 (mean 2021-2023, range 1.49-1.64). Mid 1 - 0.076/1.57 = 0.95. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 1.49 = 0.93. High: s 1.64 = 0.95. Net exporter: production is about 157% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. World-leading net exporter of soy, beef, chicken, sugar and coffee; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 104,657,408 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share of males aged 15-19 7.149% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 1,496,472. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10%.

aircraft_strike.note: Educated guess. Embraer A-29 Super Tucano line (export orders), surge feasible. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_active_Brazilian_military_aircraft)

merchantTonnage.note: asOf 2025: 5,922 thousand DWT under the Brazilian flag (4,210 thousand GT), largely Petrobras/Transpetro tankers and offshore vessels. High is an educated allowance for Brazilian-owned foreign-flag tonnage.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Truck-based sustainment; Amazon operations depend on river transport and airlift.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses (~6 million), mules and donkeys; not from FAO data. Some Army cavalry and Amazon pack use.

nuclearWarheads.note: Brazil is a non-nuclear-weapon state (NPT); not listed by FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces. Party to Tlatelolco and the ABACC safeguards agreement with Argentina; naval nuclear propulsion programme only.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: vast territory and population support; high 1.3 because the Amazon offers deep strategic depth and a climate few invaders are adapted to.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/BDI/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 85.34% (2025). s = 1 assumed: no self-sufficiency figure is fetched for auto-base states, which overstates the value for a net food importer. Mid 1 - 0.853/1 = 0.15. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count) = 0.01 (floored at 0.01: never 0 while agriculture exists). High: kept at mid (no s range).
