burundi-2026.notes: AUTO-GENERATED BASE SNAPSHOT. Population, economy, personnel and infrastructure from the World Bank (grade A/B). Force mix, ratings and tech copied from researched regional analogues (Republic of Angola, Democratic Republic of the Congo, State of Eritrea, Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Republic of Kenya, Federal Republic of Nigeria, Republic of South Africa, Republic of the Sudan, United Republic of Tanzania, Republic of Uganda) and graded D. Replace with a researched snapshot when one exists.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 0.81 million km2 for 1000 CE (before Bulgaria) and 1.15 million km2 for 1050 CE. The historical-basemaps world_1000 polygons "Byzantine Empire" (0.84 million) + "Bulgar Khanate" (0.37 million, annexed 1018) measure 1.21 million km2 on the sphere, computed from the GeoJSON (mid).

population.note: Seshat (Byzantine Empire II) codes 10-14 million for 1000 CE, before the annexation of Bulgaria in 1018 (low). Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (isbn:0804726302, p. 570; via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_of_the_Byzantine_Empire, pointer) gives 12 million in 1025 (mid). High adds Bulgaria and the eastern annexations (Iberia, Vaspurakan, 1000-1022) to Seshat's upper value. Everything inside the border.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Constantinople (Seshat largest settlement 200,000-300,000, disputed, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/75) and Thessalonica; most towns were small kastra. Lower than the 6th century.

activePersonnel.note: Army: Haldon 1999 (Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World, p. 103) ~110,000 for 1025 (low); Madgearu 2013 (Byzantine Military Organization on the Danube, isbn:9789004252493, ch. II) cites an estimate of 250,000 (high, Treadgold's school); both via the manpower table at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_army (pointer). Mid army 160,000 between them. Navy: Treadgold (isbn:0804726302, p. 576, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy) puts oarsmen at 34,200 in 959 and 1025 plus up to 8,000 marines (supportPersonnel). Counted: tagmata (incl. the Varangian Guard), thematic soldiers on the military rolls (registered and paid, mustered seasonally), and the fleets. Allied Rus', Pecheneg and Armenian contingents are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Allied and mercenary contingents hired for campaigns (Rus', Pechenegs, Georgians, Armenian nobles) and thematic households not on the active rolls; militias of fortified towns.

supportPersonnel.note: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (p. 576) and Byzantium and Its Army (isbn:0804731632, p. 67) via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy (pointer): 34,200 oarsmen in 1025 and up to 8,000 marines at the 911 peak; mid 34,200 + ~4,000 imperial-fleet marines + staff. Low allows for the decline of the thematic fleets after 949 (Makrypoulias, as cited there).

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Thematic military lands obliged registered households to provide soldiers; an emergency call on all stratiotic households and militias could perhaps double or triple the registered army.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Army mid 160,000 (range 110,000-250,000, see activePersonnel) split ~70% infantry / 30% cavalry. Infantry split by the taxiarchy of the Praecepta Militaria (c. 965; McGeer, Sowing the Dragon's Teeth, isbn:0884022242): 400 hoplitai + 100 menaulatoi (line) + 300 archers + 200 light per 1,000 = 50/30/20. Includes the ~6,000 Varangians (sent by Vladimir in 988, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_army).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: lamellar or quilted armour, large shields, spears and menaulia; Varangians with axes and mail.

training.note: Tagmata and Varangians professional (0.75-1.0); thematic infantry part-time (0.5).

count.note: Archers = 30% of the infantry per the Praecepta Militaria taxiarchy; see infantry_line.

quality.note: Composite bows (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Thematic archers, drilled in the manuals' formations.

count.note: Javelinmen and slingers = 20% of the infantry per the Praecepta Militaria taxiarchy; see infantry_line.

quality.note: Era-typical light kit (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Thematic light troops.

count.note: Tagmata cavalry (Scholai, Exkoubitoi, Hikanatoi, Athanatoi and provincial tagmata) and thematic heavy horse including kataphraktoi; ~60-65% of the ~48,000 cavalry (30% of the 160,000 mid army).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: kataphraktoi in lamellar with barded horses and maces, among the best heavy cavalry of the era.

training.note: Tagmata were full-time professionals under a strong drill tradition (rubric 0.75-1.0).

count.note: Thematic light horse, horse archers and scouts (trapezitai, prokoursatores); ~1/3 of the cavalry.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: lighter armour, bows and lances.

training.note: Border light horse experienced in raiding warfare (De velitatione).

count.note: Educated guess. Traction trebuchets (manganika), bolt-throwers on walls and siege trains of Basil II's Bulgarian campaigns; no count survives.

quality.note: Traction trebuchets and torsion bolt-throwers, era-typical to good.

training.note: Specialist engineers of the tagmata and themes.

count.note: Treadgold (Byzantium and Its Army, p. 85, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy, pointer) extrapolates ~240 warships for the 10th-century navy and 307 for the 960 Cretan expedition, probably the standing strength. Bireme dromons ~100 (the 960 fleet had 100 dromons + 200 chelandia per the same page).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: bireme dromons with Greek fire siphons, the era's best war galleys.

training.note: Professional imperial fleet and marines; thematic fleets declining.

count.note: Chelandia, ousiakoi and galeai: the rest of Treadgold's ~240-307 warships (see ships_major). audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Lighter galleys, some with Greek fire.

training.note: Thematic crews.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: a trained officer corps working from military manuals (Praecepta, Taktika of Nikephoros Ouranos), proven commanders (Basil II, Ouranos, Xiphias) after half a century of victories.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.75 for the tagmata and Varangians; thematic levies of landholding soldiers lower; the revolts of Skleros and Phokas (976-989) showed aristocratic factionalism.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, decades of victories (conquest of Bulgaria 1018, Armenian annexations).

weapons.note: Between anchor 3 and anchor 4: traction trebuchets, Greek fire, composite bows, kontarion lances and maces; no crossbow until the 1090s.

armor.note: Near anchor 4 (plate-and-mail, barding): klibanion lamellar, mail, horse barding for the kataphraktoi.

ships.note: Anchor 4 (galleys) with bireme dromons and Greek fire siphons.

fortification.note: Theodosian walls and a network of kastra; near anchor 4 short of concentric castles.

logistics.note: Anchor 3-4: aplekta staging camps, thematic supply system and sea transport; granaries of the capital.

communications.note: Anchor 3-4: the beacon chain from Cilicia to Constantinople (9th c.) and the public post (dromos).

isr.note: Year anchor 3-4: organised border scouting and spies described in De velitatione.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true (2011 int$): Turkey 1000 CE = 768, Egypt 1000 CE = 956, Iraq 1000 CE = 1,307. Byzantine Anatolia and the Balkans were closest to the Turkey value; the capital, Greece and southern Italy were richer. Mid ~800.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. The army was paid partly in cash (roga) and partly through military lands; Basil II left a treasury surplus. State revenue perhaps 5-10% of output, the largest part going to the army.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy; silk, textiles, metalwork and shipbuilding concentrated in the capital and Thebes.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Thrace, Bithynia and the Balkans fed Constantinople; recovering agrarian economy in the 10th-11th centuries.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Surviving Roman roads (Via Egnatia, the military road across Anatolia to the eastern frontier) plus maintained routes; much reduced from antiquity.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Constantinople, Thessalonica, Abydos, Attaleia, Bari, Dyrrachium, Trebizond, Cherson, Corinth.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Coastal and Black Sea shipping of the capital's grain supply; Venetian and Amalfitan shipping not counted.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying grain on pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot; Byzantine campaigns used prepared aplekta and seasonal campaigning.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.07-0.11 horses, mules, oxen and donkeys per inhabitant x population; imperial stud farms (metata) in Anatolia.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: fortified cities and kastra, local thematic supply and population support; Anatolian plateau and Taurus passes give depth.

byzantine-empire-1025.notes: Snapshot = December 1025 at Basil II's death, the territorial peak of middle Byzantium (Bulgaria annexed 1018, Iberia and Vaspurakan 1000-1022). Force convention: activePersonnel = tagmata, Varangian Guard, thematic soldiers on the paid military rolls and the fleets; hired allied contingents in trainedReserves. Army size is genuinely disputed: Haldon ~110,000 vs Treadgold-type estimates of ~250,000 (Whittow argued for far fewer per unit); the mid 160,000 is between them and every P-role count inherits that spread. Haldon, Treadgold and Madgearu are cited by ISBN (not fetchable); their figures were read from Wikipedia tables (pointer only), hence grade B at most. Border = historical-basemaps world_1000 "Byzantine Empire" + "Bulgar Khanate" (Bulgaria annexed 1018). Ancient/medieval chroniclers are not used for counts.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 1.3-1.5 million km2 for 500 CE (East only); adding reconquered Africa (~0.4 million) and Italy (~0.3 million) gives the low. The historical-basemaps world_500 polygons used for the border measure 1.93 (Eastern Roman Empire) + 0.36 (Vandals) + 0.56 (Ostrogoths) = 2.84 million km2 on the sphere, computed from the GeoJSON (mid; they include Provence and Raetia, never recovered). Treadgold's table (isbn:0804726302, p. 278, via the Wikipedia pointer above) has 3.4 million km2 for 565 (high).

population.note: Seshat (East Roman Empire) codes 20 million for 500 CE and 12.5-15 million for 600 CE (East only, before and after). Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (isbn:0804726302, p. 278; figures as tabulated at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_of_the_Byzantine_Empire, pointer only) gives 26 million in 540 with Africa and part of Italy, before the plague of 541-542 (high), and 20 million at Justinian's death in 565. Mid 21 million for 555: after the first plague wave, with Italy, Africa and southern Spain now included. Everything inside the border.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Constantinople (Seshat largest settlement 500,000 in 500 CE, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/72), Alexandria, Antioch and a dense network of Levantine and Anatolian cities; plague and the Persian sack of Antioch (540) cut urban populations. Set below the Principate's 17%.

activePersonnel.note: Field army: Agathias puts the effective army at the end of Justinian's reign, incl. Italy, Africa and Spain, at "barely 150,000" (contemporary; Jones, The Later Roman Empire, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, pp. 684-685, reads it as the field army excluding the limitanei). Frontier troops: Soto Chica 2015 (https://gladius.revistas.csic.es/index.php/gladius/article/download/277/281/285, p. 71) uses 150,000 field + 100,000 frontier; Treadgold (Byzantium and Its Army, pp. 59-64, 161-162, as summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Roman_army, pointer) gives 150,300 field army + 229,000 frontier troops, guards and oarsmen = 379,300 for 565 (high). Low = Agathias' 150,000 read as the whole army (Bury) + 15,000 oarsmen + guards. Counted: comitatenses, foederati and bucellarii in imperial pay, limitanei (salaried garrison soldiers, though Procopius says Justinian stopped their pay in places), palace guards and the fleet. Allied Lombard, Herul and Ghassanid contingents are in trainedReserves. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Allied and federate contingents called up for campaigns: Ghassanid Arab phylarchs, Lombards and Heruls (5,500 Lombards and 3,000 Heruls served Narses in 552 per Procopius, ancient), Moorish allies in Africa; discharged veterans.

supportPersonnel.note: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (p. 277; via the Treadgold table at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_navy, pointer) estimates 30,000 oarsmen in 518 and 540 (mid). Low allows for Pryor and Jeffreys' smaller single-banked dromon crews; high adds staff and engineers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Recruitment was voluntary plus barbarian federates; the state struggled to fill units after the plague (Jones, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 684-685: Agathias' 150,000 field army for a huge area). 0.025 assumes an emergency levy roughly doubling the paid army.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Infantry ~75% of the 180,000-350,000 army (field armies about 1/3 cavalry, e.g. Belisarius' 10,000 foot + 5,000 horse in 533 (Procopius, ancient); limitanei mostly infantry; Elton 1996 pp. 105-106 puts late Roman cavalry at about 1/5 of effectives, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Roman_army, pointer). Line ~70% of infantry, the rest archers and light troops (Strategikon proportions of a generation later).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: mail or lamellar, helmets, large shields, spears; well equipped from state fabricae.

training.note: Field-army infantry professional (0.75); limitanei part-time garrison soldiers (0.5).

count.note: Archer share of the infantry (~20%); see infantry_line for the arithmetic.

quality.note: Composite bows (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Professional and frontier archers.

count.note: Educated guess. Javelinmen and skirmishers, Isaurian and Thracian light foot; ~10% of infantry.

quality.note: Era-typical light kit (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Mixed professionals and hill levies.

count.note: Field-army cavalry (~1/3 of Agathias' 150,000 = ~50,000) less light allied horse: regiments of lancer-archers, bucellarii of the generals (Belisarius had some 7,000) and guards.

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: armoured lancer-archers with composite bows, the decisive arm of Belisarius and Narses; on a par with the savaran.

training.note: Long-service professionals and generals' household troops (rubric 0.75-1.0).

count.note: Hunnic, Herul and Moorish horse archers among the foederati in pay, plus limitanei cavalry units (cunei, equites) on the eastern and Danube frontiers.

quality.note: Steppe horse archers and light lancers (rubric 0.5-0.75).

training.note: Foederati professional but loosely disciplined; frontier units lower.

count.note: Educated guess. Ballistae and stone-throwers mounted on fortress and city walls (Procopius describes them at Rome in 537) and siege engines; Justinian built or rebuilt hundreds of forts (Procopius, Buildings). No count survives.

quality.note: Late Roman torsion artillery, still the era's best before the traction trebuchet arrived (c. 580s).

training.note: Garrison crews.

count.note: Educated guess. Single-banked dromons of ~50 oars; 92 dromons escorted the 533 Vandal expedition (Procopius, ancient). 30,000 oarsmen (Treadgold) divided over dromons and smaller craft.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: the dromon was the new standard war galley and the empire had no naval rival after 552 (Sena Gallica).

training.note: Standing professional fleet since Anastasius (513-515).

count.note: Educated guess. Danube flotilla, patrol and light craft; the transports of the expeditions (500 in 533) are merchant ships, not counted.

quality.note: Standard oared craft.

training.note: Professional crews.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75: a trained staff hierarchy (magistri militum, duces) and proven commanders (Belisarius, Narses at Taginae 552 and Casilinum 554, John Troglita in Africa).

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5: regimental identity in the field units, but bucellarii loyal to their generals, mutinies over pay in Africa (536) and Italy, many barbarian federates.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: recent victories in Italy (552-554) and Spain (552), offset by plague losses, arrears of pay and the Lazic war.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 plus refinements: composite-bow lancer cavalry, torsion artillery; no traction trebuchet or crossbow yet.

armor.note: Anchor 3 exceeded: mail and lamellar standard, some horse armour; short of anchor 4 plate-and-mail.

ships.note: Anchor 3 plus the dromon (fully decked, lateen-rigged, single-banked); no Greek fire yet.

fortification.note: Above anchor 3: Theodosian land walls of Constantinople, Dara, the Anastasian Long Wall and Justinian's fort network; below anchor 4 concentric castles. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.7 -> 3.55, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 555 (3.552); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 plus state supply in kind (annona, coemptio) and seaborne transport supporting overseas expeditions.

communications.note: Anchor 3: cursus publicus, partly curtailed by Justinian (Procopius, Secret History 30).

isr.note: Year anchor 3: scouts (cursores), spies, frontier informants.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true (2011 int$): year 1 CE Greece 1,275, Egypt/Levant/Tunisia 1,116, Turkey 897, Italy 1,407; Egypt 730 CE 1,164. The 6th-century East (Levant, Egypt, Asia Minor) was at a late-antique peak; Italy was devastated by the Gothic war. Mid ~1,000.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Army pay was the largest item of a budget Treadgold puts at a few million nomismata a year; land tax ~ a fifth to a quarter of output, of which the army took the largest part. Peacetime share; Justinian was also at war in Lazica in 555.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy; state fabricae, silk (sericulture introduced c. 552), mining, textiles, building programme.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Egypt still shipped ~8 million artabas of tax grain a year to Constantinople (Justinian Edict 13, ancient); surplus regions in Egypt, Africa and Sicily.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (https://orbis.stanford.edu/orbis2012/ORBIS_v1paper_20120501.pdf) models 84,631 km of principal Roman roads and desert tracks c. 200 CE for the whole empire. The 555 empire held roughly 55-65% of that network (Balkans, Asia Minor, Levant, Egypt, Africa, Italy), less where roads had decayed (mid ~50,000 km).

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites for the Roman Empire; ports able to supply a fleet or army in 555: Constantinople, Alexandria, Carthage, Ravenna, Syracuse, Thessalonica, Seleucia Pieria, Caesarea, Ephesus, Rhodes, Naples, Septem, Cartagena... estimated at ~15.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. The Egyptian grain fleet to Constantinople (~8 million artabas, ~200,000 t a year) plus Mediterranean trade; scaled below the rome-117 estimate for a smaller annona.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies with grain carried on soldiers and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; Justinian's expeditions moved by sea.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.075-0.11 draft and pack animals per inhabitant x population.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: fortified cities and fort networks, local supply and population support; Constantinople nearly impregnable. Recently conquered Italy and Africa gave less support.

byzantine-empire-555.notes: Snapshot = 555 CE, Justinian I after the end of the Gothic war (Casilinum 554) and the landing in Spain (552), with the Lazic war against Persia still running (551-557). Force convention: activePersonnel = comitatenses, foederati and bucellarii in imperial pay, limitanei, guards and fleet; allied contingents (Lombards, Heruls, Ghassanids) in trainedReserves. Agathias' 150,000 (contemporary, end of the reign) and his 645,000 for the "old days" are ancient figures; the mid follows Treadgold for structure and Jones for the reading of Agathias. Treadgold's two books are cited by ISBN (not fetchable); his numbers were read from Wikipedia tables (pointer only), so they are graded B at most. Border = historical-basemaps world_500 Eastern Roman Empire + Vandals + Ostrogoths polygons (the nearest file before 555 shows the pre-reconquest empire); this includes Provence and Raetia (not recovered) and misses the Spanish strip. Population inside the border after the first plague wave of 541-542.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CMR/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 41.85% (2025). s = 1 assumed: no self-sufficiency figure is fetched for auto-base states, which overstates the value for a net food importer. gdpPerCapita.note: asOf 2025. Rebased GDP 1,933,497,120,784 / population 41,651,653 = 46,421 2011 int$. Range +/-10%. Corrected 2026-10-29: values x1.0376 because the rebase factor was an arithmetic error (0.8005); the right factor is 0.8306 (FRED GDPDEF, 2017=100: 2011 91.478 / 2021 110.130). Figures quoted above are before the correction.

gdp.note: asOf 2025. World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.KD (constant 2021 int$) 2,415,361,799,855 x 0.8005 (US GDP deflator 2011/2021) = 1,933,497,120,784 2011 int$. Range +/-10% for PPP benchmark uncertainty and the relative-price drift the rebase ignores. Series: https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CAN/indicator/NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.KD?format=json Corrected 2026-10-29: values x1.0376 because the rebase factor was an arithmetic error (0.8005); the right factor is 0.8306 (FRED GDPDEF, 2017=100: 2011 91.478 / 2021 110.130). Figures quoted above are before the correction.

milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via World Bank: 1.63% of GDP in 2025. Low is 2023 (CIA Factbook 1.3%); high 2.0% is the 2025 estimate after Canada declared the NATO 2% target met for FY2025-26 (CIA Factbook).

industrialShare.note: asOf 2022: industry incl. construction 27.35% of GDP (NV.IND.TOTL.ZS).

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.5 -> 0.99. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CAN/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 1.10% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 1.71 (mean 2021-2023, range 1.62-1.78). Mid 1 - 0.011/1.71 = 0.99. Low: a x 1.5 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 1.62 = 0.99. High: s 1.78 = 0.99. Net exporter: production is about 171% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. One of the largest net exporters of wheat, canola, pulses and beef; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 20,681,413 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share of males aged 15-19 5.617% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 232,349. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10%.

ifv_apc.note: Educated guess. GDLS-Canada London (Ontario) builds LAV 6.0/ACSV and LAV for export (Saudi contract); wartime rate limited by components. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_equipment_of_the_Canadian_Army)

ships_major.note: Educated guess. River-class destroyer construction at Irving Halifax only started; first hull not before 2030. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Navy)

artillery.note: Educated guess. No domestic gun line; could assemble light guns or HIMARS kits only with US supply chain. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_equipment_of_the_Canadian_Army)

roadKm.note: CIA World Factbook as quoted: 1,042,300 km total (2020), of which 415,600 km paved and 626,700 km unpaved (mostly engineered gravel). Low is paved only.

railKm.note: asOf 2021: 48,150 route-km (World Bank IS.RRS.TOTL.KM); CIA Factbook 49,422 km (2021, high). Standard gauge, two transcontinental systems (CN, CPKC).

merchantTonnage.note: asOf 2025: 3,305 thousand DWT under the Canadian flag (2,909 thousand GT), largely Great Lakes lakers. High is an educated allowance for Canadian-owned foreign-flag tonnage.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Analogy to NATO mechanized brigade sustainment; Canada sustains a brigade in Latvia through allied host-nation support and strategic airlift.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses, mules and donkeys (not from FAO data). Militarily irrelevant in 2026.

nuclearWarheads.note: Canada is a non-nuclear-weapon state (NPT); not listed by FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces. Hosts no nuclear weapons since 1984.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: familiar terrain, local supply and population support; high 1.3 because the Arctic/sub-Arctic climate and continental depth punish an invader not adapted to it.

canada-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2025 data with 2026 order of battle. doctrineId nato-european-2026: no Canada-specific profile exists; this is the closest NATO middle-power profile (expeditionary brigade inside allied formations). Population convention: everything inside ne:CAN (World Bank). Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011. Force counts from IISS Military Balance 2025 as quoted on Wikipedia and the Canadian Army equipment list, RCAF and RCN articles (Government of Canada fleet pages as cited there). ships_major = carriers/LHD + cruisers + destroyers + frigates; ships_minor = AOPV, coastal defence vessels; drones = Group 2+ UAVs only. Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Readiness is the main caveat: DND reported large personnel shortfalls and low aircraft availability in 2025. ~2,000 troops deployed in Latvia (CIA Factbook 2025). Coast Guard is civilian and excluded.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 1.1 million km2 for 752-840 (low); Wikipedia infobox 1.2 million km2 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Empire); the world_800 polygon measures 1.19 million km2.

population.note: Seshat codes 20 million (disputed) and 15 million (expert, 811). Wikipedia gives 10-20 million (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Empire); the Medieval demography article puts Europe at 25-30 million under Charlemagne, about half in the empire (12-15 million).

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Largest settlement 20,000-30,000 (Seshat, Rome); most "towns" were episcopal seats of a few thousand.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. Standing element only: palace household troops (scara), vassi dominici in attendance and march garrisons (Saxon, Avar, Spanish and Breton marches). Lot (via https://www.medievalists.net/2026/03/size-armies-early-medieval-warfare/) held that even Charlemagne rarely assembled 5,000 men. audit 2026-10-30: date basis: a year without a general muster, so only the household element is active and campaign levies are trainedReserves (france-1415, dated to the Agincourt campaign, counts its assembled army instead).

trainedReserves.note: Werner (1968) estimated Charlemagne could raise 30,000-35,000 heavily armed horsemen and up to 100,000 lighter troops north of the Alps (high, via medievalists.net summary of the debate); the small-army school (Lot, Verbruggen) puts campaign armies at a few thousand. Mid between the schools. These are vassal and free-man obligations under the capitularies, callable for the annual May muster.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Household officials, engineers, carts and coastal guard crews ordered in 800-811.

mobilizationRatio.note: Werner's total (30,000-35,000 heavy horse + up to 100,000 lighter troops = ~135,000) over 15 million inhabitants = 0.9%. Low reflects the small-army school.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Scara and royal vassals with mail byrnie, lance, sword and shield, as required by the capitularies of 792-805.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Frankish swords and byrnies were export-banned (Capitulary of Thionville 805) as the best in the West.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: noble warriors trained from youth, no drill.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Charlemagne ran annual campaigns with multi-column convergent operations (Avar war 791) and written mobilisation orders; no staff system.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: thirty years of victories (Lombards 774, Saxons, Avars 796).

weapons.note: Anchor 3-4: pattern-welded and early crucible swords, lance, bow; no crossbow or counterweight trebuchet.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail): the byrnie, scarce and expensive.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

gdpPerCapita.note: Educated guess. Analogue: Maddison 2023 (via OWID) UK 1000 = 1,151, France 1 CE = 956, Italy 1 CE = 1,407 (2011 int$); the 9th-century West was poorer than Roman Gaul or Italy and than England in 1000.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Service in kind by vassals; no monetised budget.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Estate crafts, swords and textiles.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Manorial agriculture with low yields.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; medieval age structures were similar (high mortality, young population).

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Surviving Roman roads in Gaul, Italy and the Rhineland; none east of the Rhine.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Dorestad, Quentovic, Marseille, Arles, Ravenna area.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Frisian and Mediterranean coastal shipping.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies with carts and pack animals operated ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.1-0.25 oxen and horses per inhabitant.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: familiar terrain and local supply; few fortified towns.

carolingian-empire-800.notes: Snapshot = December 800, Charlemagne's imperial coronation. Army size is the most disputed number of the early Middle Ages: Lot ("rarely 5,000"), Verbruggen and Delbrueck argue for small armies, Werner (30,000-35,000 heavy horse + up to 100,000 others) and Bernard Bachrach for large ones (summary at https://www.medievalists.net/2026/03/size-armies-early-medieval-warfare/; Bachrach, Charlemagne's Early Campaigns, 2013, builds on Werner). activePersonnel counts only the standing household and march garrisons; the vassal and free-man host is trainedReserves and mobilizable, per the feudal-host convention. Population convention: everything inside the empire including Lombard Italy and the Spanish March; papal Rome counted, tributary Slavs and Bretons not.

areaKm2.note: Africa ~72,500 km2 (Scullard, https://erenow.org/ancient/a-history-of-the-roman-world-753-to-146-bc/44.php: about 28,000 square miles, directly ruled and tributary land) + Barcid Spain south of the Ebro 120,000-300,000 km2 (educated guess: coastal Andalusia, Murcia, Valencia and the Guadalquivir valley firmly held, the Meseta tribes only as allies) + Ebusus. The historical-basemaps world_bc300 polygon (689,939 km2 measured on the sphere) predates 218: it still shows western Sicily (lost 241) and Sardinia (lost 238) and has only a small Spanish holding, while its African part runs far into the Libyan desert coast; it is used for the map only.

population.note: African territory 3-4 million (Scullard, A History of the Roman World 753-146 BC, ch. VII, https://erenow.org/ancient/a-history-of-the-roman-world-753-to-146-bc/44.php: "an area of about 28,000 square miles and a population of three to four million"; that figure includes the Libyan subjects and Libyphoenician towns) + Barcid Spain 0.5-3 million (educated guess: Andalusia, Murcia and the Levante coast south of the Ebro; no modern count exists). Mid 3.5 + 1.5 million. Western Sicily and Sardinia were lost by 238 BCE and are not counted.

urbanization.note: Carthage city ~250,000 (low end of modern estimates; the Britannica-derived survey at https://warhistory.org/article/pre-roman-north-africa-ii?amp=1 gives ~400,000 incl. slaves and reports Strabo's 700,000 as probably including the Megara suburb and Sahel) + Utica, Hadrumetum, Gades, New Carthage, Hippo and the Libyphoenician towns (~300,000-400,000 together, estimate) = ~0.6-0.7 million of ~5 million.

activePersonnel.note: Sum of the P roles (93,000 / 121,000 / 153,000) and supportPersonnel (20,000 / 28,000 / 40,000), rounded. P roles from Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html) as read by Lazenby and Goldsworthy; see infantry_line. Convention: the mercenary, Libyan, Numidian and Spanish contingents already under arms in spring 218 are counted as active; Spaniards dismissed to their cities in winter 219/218 and discharged veterans are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Polybius 3.35.6 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html): after the Pyrenees Hannibal sent home a number of Spaniards equal to the 10,000 foot and 1,000 horse he left with Hanno, and in winter 219/218 had dismissed the Iberians to their cities (3.33.5) to recall them later. Plus discharged Libyan and Numidian veterans. Range is an estimate.

supportPersonnel.note: Crews: quinqueremes ~300 rowers each (Polybius 1.26.7, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/1*.html, for 256 BCE) x ~87 crewed hulls (32 of the 50 Spanish quinqueremes per Polybius 3.33.14 standard text, + 55 sent against Sicily in 218 per Livy 21.49, https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt) = ~26,000, + trireme crews, engineers, elephant drivers and staff. High allows more hulls crewed in Africa.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Carthage fought with mercenaries, Libyan subjects, Spanish and Numidian allies; citizens served mainly as officers, in the fleet and in emergencies (the citizen levy of 255 and 202). In 215-207 Carthage kept armies in Italy, Spain, Sardinia, Sicily and Africa at once, perhaps 1.5-3x the 218 total.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Libyan heavy infantry, Spanish scutati, Celtiberians, Ligurians. Hannibal's field army line infantry ~72% of his foot (36,000 / 50,000 / 64,000; at the Trebia 20,000 line to 8,000 light per Polybius 3.72) + Spain 12,150 (Libyans, Ligurians) + Africa ~9,000 of the 13,850 Spaniards + 4,000 Metagonians + 0-10,000 garrisons. Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). Spring 218 BCE: (a) Hannibal's field army, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse crossing the Ebro per Polybius 3.35.1, 50,000 foot and 9,000 horse after the Pyrenees (3.35.7); Lazenby thinks the higher figure possible, Goldsworthy treats it as inflated, so low/high span 50,000-90,000 foot; (b) left in Spain with Hasdrubal (3.33.14-16): 11,850 Libyans, 300 Ligurians, 500 Balearians, 450 Libyphoenician and Libyan horse, 300 Ilergetes, 1,800 Numidians, 21 elephants; (c) sent to Africa (3.33.9-13): 1,200 Spanish horse, 13,850 Spanish foot and 870 Balearians (Paton's text runs the last two together; standard reading), plus 4,000 Metagonian foot sent to Carthage; (d) unrecorded garrisons in Libya and the city, 0-10,000 (educated guess). audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Libyan infantry well armed (later re-equipped with captured Roman kit); Spanish infantry with the falcata and scutum, era-typical to good.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: long-service mercenaries and subjects hardened by 18 years of Barcid wars in Spain (Polybius 3.35.8 calls the army "highly trained"); Africa garrisons lower.

count.note: Spanish caetrati and Libyan javelinmen: ~25% of Hannibal's foot (12,500 / 18,000 / 23,000) + ~4,850 of the Spaniards sent to Africa (split estimated). Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). Spring 218 BCE: (a) Hannibal's field army, 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse crossing the Ebro per Polybius 3.35.1, 50,000 foot and 9,000 horse after the Pyrenees (3.35.7); Lazenby thinks the higher figure possible, Goldsworthy treats it as inflated, so low/high span 50,000-90,000 foot; (b) left in Spain with Hasdrubal (3.33.14-16): 11,850 Libyans, 300 Ligurians, 500 Balearians, 450 Libyphoenician and Libyan horse, 300 Ilergetes, 1,800 Numidians, 21 elephants; (c) sent to Africa (3.33.9-13): 1,200 Spanish horse, 13,850 Spanish foot and 870 Balearians (Paton's text runs the last two together; standard reading), plus 4,000 Metagonian foot sent to Carthage; (d) unrecorded garrisons in Libya and the city, 0-10,000 (educated guess).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: javelins, small shields.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: experienced skirmishers.

count.note: Balearic slingers: 500 in Spain + 870 sent to Africa (Polybius 3.33.11, 3.33.16) + 1,500-3,000 with Hannibal (estimate; slingers fought in the 8,000 light screen at the Trebia, Polybius 3.72.7).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Balearic slingers were the era's best slingers.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: professional mercenary specialists.

count.note: Spanish and Libyphoenician close-order horse: ~60-65% of Hannibal's 9,000-12,000 cavalry (split estimated; Hannibal's horse in Italy mixed Spanish and Celtic shock cavalry with Numidians) + 750 Libyphoenicians, Libyans and Ilergetes in Spain + 1,200 Spanish horse sent to Africa. quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Spanish heavy cavalry outclassed the Roman citizen cavalry at the Ticinus and Cannae.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: veteran professionals.

count.note: Numidian light horse: 3,500-4,000 with Hannibal (estimate from his ~2,000-3,000 surviving Numidians in Italy) + 1,800 Numidians left in Spain (Polybius 3.33.15). Polybius 3.33-35 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/3*.html), whose figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's own bronze tablet at Lacinium and are accepted as reliable by Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978/1998, isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) and Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (isbn:0304366420, ch. 7). quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Numidian javelin cavalry, the best light horse of the western Mediterranean.

training.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: raised in the saddle, veterans of the Spanish wars.

count.note: 37 elephants crossed the Rhone with Hannibal (Polybius 3.42.11) + 21 left in Spain (3.33.16) = 58 (low) + an unknown number in Africa (Carthage's stables are described by Appian, Pun. 95, for 149 BCE as holding 300; in 215 Carthage sent 40 to Italy, Livy 23.13). Counts animals.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: small North African forest elephants, era-typical.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: trained mahouts; elephants panicked against light troops.

count.note: Quinqueremes and quadriremes: 50 quinqueremes and 2 quadriremes left in Spain (Polybius 3.33.14) + 55 quinqueremes sent against Sicily in 218 (20 + 35, Livy 21.49, https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt). Low counts only the 32 Spanish quinqueremes crewed; high allows hulls in the Carthage harbour (whose ship sheds held 220, https://warhistory.org/article/pre-roman-north-africa-ii?amp=1). Lazenby (isbn:0806130040, ch. 2) stresses how small the Punic navy was compared with 264-241.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Punic quinqueremes were the design Rome copied in 261.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: many hulls laid up after 241; crews short (only 32 of 50 Spanish quinqueremes manned).

count.note: Educated guess: the triremes in Spain (Polybius 3.33.14) plus patrol and dispatch craft in Africa.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: era-typical light warships.

training.note: Rubric 0.5.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 1.0 for Hannibal's own army (best-in-era generalship, Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae) and 0.5 for the Spanish and African commands (Hasdrubal, Hanno); mid 0.75.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5 for a mercenary and multi-ethnic host (Mercenary War 241-237 shows the risk), raised toward 0.75 for the Barcid army bound to its general by long service.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, recent victories (Saguntum 219, conquest of Spain).

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (300 BCE): iron weapons, torsion artillery used at Saguntum 219.

armor.note: Anchor 3: bronze and iron cuirasses, mail for some; many Spanish and Libyan troops lightly armoured.

ships.note: Anchor 3 exactly: triremes and quinqueremes.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 (ashlar walls) and above: Carthage's triple land wall and the cothon war harbour; New Carthage fortified.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (depot system) at the low end: Barcid supply bases in Spain, sea supply; few engineered roads.

communications.note: Between anchors 2 (couriers) and 3: couriers and fire signals; no relay-post network documented.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: Numidian scouts, spies in Italy and Gaul before the invasion (Polybius 3.34).

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE Tunisia 1,116, Spain 886 (2011 int$). Punic Africa was a rich agricultural and trading economy; Barcid Spain less developed but with large silver mines. Mid 1,000 weights Africa about two-thirds.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: a mercenary state paying for a large standing army in Spain from Spanish silver , while still paying the 1,200-talent indemnity of 241 and Sardinia indemnity of 237; low is the peacetime level.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: shipbuilding, metalworking, purple dye, ceramics, Spanish mining in a mostly agrarian economy.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: fertile Bagradas valley and Sahel estates (Mago's agronomy) exported grain; high relative to the era.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: tracks in the Libyan hinterland and coastal routes in Spain; no engineered road network like Rome's.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Carthage, Utica, Hadrumetum, Hippo, New Carthage, Gades, Ebusus, Malaca (count of fleet-capable ports is an estimate).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: the leading western Mediterranean trading power; ~500-1,000 merchantmen of 40-100 t.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or the sea; Hannibal's march from the Ebro to the Po relied on Gallic supplies and foraging.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.06-0.09 horses, mules, oxen and camels per inhabitant x population.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: Carthage itself was heavily fortified and supplied by sea, but the Libyan subjects revolted in 241-237 and the Spanish dominion was recent; between 1.1 and 1.2.

carthage--218.notes: Snapshot = spring 218 BCE, Hannibal leaving New Carthage at the outbreak of the Second Punic War; forces are the Barcid field army at the start of the march plus the troops left in Spain and Africa. Polybius' figures for Spain and Africa come from Hannibal's Lacinium inscription and are accepted by modern historians; the 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse he gives for the army crossing the Ebro is disputed (Hannibal reached the Po with 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse, Polybius 3.56.4) so the infantry ranges are wide. Population convention: everything ruled from Carthage in 218 (Punic Africa with its Libyan subjects, Barcid Spain, Ebusus); Numidian kingdoms and Iberian allies beyond the Barcid dominion are not counted. Border uses historical-basemaps world_bc300 (nearest file at or before 218), which predates the loss of Sicily (241) and Sardinia (238) and the Barcid conquest of Spain (237-219); areaKm2 is researched separately. Navy numbers are low because the Punic fleet had not been rebuilt after 241.

Figures quoted above are before the correction.

industrialShare.note: asOf 2025: industry incl. construction 31.42% of GDP (NV.IND.TOTL.ZS). Mining (copper, lithium) is the largest component.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.3 -> 0.9. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CHL/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 6.07% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.60 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.60-0.60). Mid 1 - 0.061/0.60 = 0.9. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.60 = 0.87. High: s 0.60 = 0.9. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 60% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Large exporter of fruit, wine, salmon; imports cereals; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 9,871,188 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share of males aged 15-19 6.318% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 124,726. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10%.

china-1937.notes: Snapshot date July 1937 (Marco Polo Bridge incident, 7 July; full-scale fighting at Shanghai from 13 August). Forces are the National Revolutionary Army plus provincial armies under the Nanjing government; the Communist Eighth Route Army (formed August 1937) is counted only in the high bounds. Manchukuo (since 1931-32) and Japanese-held Hebei/Chahar zones excluded; includes empty. The world_1930 basemap is the nearest file at or before 1937. Ship convention per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: battleships, carriers, cruisers and destroyers = ships_major, torpedo boats and smaller craft = ships_minor (role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries).

High: COW NMC v7 tpop 1979 = 985,467k (https://correlatesofwar.org/wp-content/uploads/NMCv7.zip). audit 2026-10-30: mid was ~975M from memory; now the fetched OWID value.

activePersonnel.note: COW NMC v7 milper 1979 = 4,600k (high). Yang, The Modernization of the Chinese PLA (Naval Postgraduate School thesis, June 1980, DTIC ADA092422), tables citing the IISS Military Balance 1979-80, Table II-1: Army strength 3,600,000 (main forces 115 infantry, 11 armoured, 40 artillery and 16 railway divisions; local forces 85 infantry divisions). Navy ~0.3M and Air Force ~0.4M added for the mid.

china-1979.notes: Snapshot date 17 February 1979, start of the Sino-Vietnamese War. Forces are national totals; the invasion force was ~200,000 troops with 400-550 tanks (Sino-Vietnamese War article, Chinese data), while ~1M troops faced the USSR. Key order-of-battle numbers come from a 1980 Naval Postgraduate School thesis (Yang, DTIC ADA092422, archive.org full text) whose tables cite the IISS Military Balance 1979-80. Population convention: mainland PRC, Taiwan excluded. Militia: armed core militia counted as trainedReserves; the ordinary militia falls under mobilizable. Many economic and logistics values are educated guesses (grade D) because no fetchable 1979 statistical yearbook was available.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.15 -> 0.73. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CHN/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 21.68% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.80 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.79-0.80). Mid 1 - 0.217/0.80 = 0.73. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.79 = 0.64. High: s 0.80 = 0.73. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 80% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess: large domestic production but net importer of soybeans, feed grain and meat; low surplus over subsistence under blockade.

Male population from SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10% for single-year cohort variation.

china-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2025 data with 2026 order of battle. Population convention: mainland China inside ne:CHN; Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan excluded. Infantry P-role splits and air_defense batteries are educated guesses. People's Armed Police (~500,000), China Coast Guard and maritime militia excluded. chola-1030.notes: Snapshot 1030, late in Rajendra I's reign, after the Ganges expedition and the 1025 Srivijaya raid. Army numbers in inscriptions (900,000, 955,000) are court and enemy claims and are not used; all force counts are educated guesses. foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.15 -> 0.81. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/COL/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 14.16% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.76 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.76-0.76). Mid 1 - 0.142/0.76 = 0.81. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.76 = 0.76. High: s 0.76 = 0.81. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 76% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Exports coffee, flowers, bananas, palm oil but imports most cereals; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

areaKm2.note: The 11 seceded states cover ~1.95M km2; Confederate-controlled territory in mid-1863 was smaller after Union gains in Tennessee, Louisiana and Arkansas. No historical-basemaps file has a Confederate polygon.

population.note: 1860 census, 11 seceded states: ~9.1M incl. ~3.5M enslaved (McPherson, isbn:0-19-503863-0, ch. 10). By mid-1863 Union armies held much of Tennessee, Louisiana, northern Arkansas, coastal enclaves and West Virginia, leaving ~7.5-8.5M under Confederate control.

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) United States 1860 = 19.8% for the whole country; the South was far less urban (~7-10%; New Orleans, the largest southern city, fell in 1862).

activePersonnel.note: Page: C.S. War Department reports 449,439 (1862) and 464,646 (1863) on the rolls; Livermore p. 47: 446,622 on Confederate returns 1 January 1863. Present for duty ran at ~55-65% of the rolls, so mid = ~300,000 present plus the navy.

trainedReserves.note: State troops, home guards and irregulars: Livermore estimates ~98,720 irregular troops not always carried on the returns.

supportPersonnel.note: Artillery ~18,000, engineers, ordnance and quartermaster ~6,000, navy and marines ~4,000. Reconstruction.

mobilizationRatio.note: Page: enlistment estimates range from ~750,000 to 1,227,890-1,406,180 over the war, from ~5.5M free inhabitants, i.e. 8-15% of the total population incl. the enslaved.

count.note: Infantry present, all departments, mid-1863. Army of Northern Virginia ~75,000 at Gettysburg, Army of Tennessee ~45,000, Vicksburg garrison ~30,000.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: scratch crews

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75. Evidence: Lee and Longstreet in Virginia; weaker western command (Bragg, Pemberton)

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5-0.75. Evidence: state regiments with strong identity; desertion rising after July 1863

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: defence of the homeland after Chancellorsville, shaken by Gettysburg and Vicksburg

weapons.note: Anchor: between 6 (1805) and 7 (1905). Evidence: rifle-muskets, imported Whitworths, fewer breech-loaders

armor.note: Anchor: 6 (none / cuirass). Evidence: casemate ironclads

ships.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7. Evidence: improvised ironclads, first successful submarine attack (Hunley, 1864) still ahead

fortification.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7. Evidence: Charleston and Vicksburg earthworks, naval mines (torpedoes)

logistics.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7. Evidence: decaying railways, gauge breaks, Tredegar the only big iron works

communications.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7. Evidence: telegraph, signal corps

isr.note: Anchor: between 6 and 7. Evidence: cavalry scouting, Stuart absent before Gettysburg

air.note: No military aircraft before 1911; balloons, where used, are counted under ISR.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Analogue: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID) United States 1863 = 4,734; southern income per head incl. the enslaved was ~80% of the national mean in 1860 (Engerman), less after blockade and war damage.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: Confederate war spending, financed largely by paper money and inflation, absorbed roughly a quarter or more of output in 1863; low = US antebellum peacetime share.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: the South had ~10% of US manufacturing capacity in 1860.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: cotton economy; food shortages and Richmond bread riot (April 1863).

annualCohort.note: Analogue ratio of the France 1805 snapshot (males reaching military age ~1.05% per year) applied to the ~5.5M free population only, as the enslaved were not conscripted.

artillery.note: Educated guess: field guns per year, mostly from Tredegar (Richmond) and Selma.

ships_major.note: Educated guess: ironclads completed per year.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: few engineered roads; dirt roads impassable in rain.

railKm.note: About 9,000 miles (14,500 km) in the 11 states in 1861 (McPherson ch. 10; CHAT US total 1861 = 49,412 km, https://data.nber.org/chat/chat.dta); lines lost in Tennessee, Louisiana and Virginia by mid-1863.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: Charleston, Wilmington, Mobile, Savannah, Galveston (blockaded).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: blockade runners and coastal craft.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: thin wagon and rail supply.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: horses and mules under Confederate control; heavy losses by 1863.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: familiar terrain, fortified ports and cities, white population support.

confederate-states-1863.notes: Snapshot = Confederate States in July 1863. Territory and population = the area under Confederate control (1860 census base of the 11 seceded states, less Union-held areas); includes is empty. Border: no historical-basemaps polygon exists for the Confederacy at any year, so border is none. Personnel: troops present and navy = active; state troops, home guards and irregulars = trainedReserves. Of the ~8M inhabitants ~3.5M were enslaved and not armed; mobilizable is computed on the total population, so the ratio is set against the total. Strengths from the Confederate States Army page (War Department reports), Livermore (1900) and McPherson; branch split is a reconstruction (grade C/D).

ships.note: Anchor 8: converted trawlers, Osa/Pauk craft, midget submarine.

communications.note: Anchor 8-9: Soviet-era radio, Chinese/Russian assistance (Bejucal SIGINT site).

gdpPerCapita.note: GDP below / population 10,937,203. The Factbook per-capita line ($23,700, 2024) is inconsistent with its own GDP and population and is not used.

gdp.note: World Bank has no PPP GDP for Cuba and the IMF does not cover it. CIA Factbook real GDP PPP 2024 $81.165 bn (2015 dollars, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/factbook/factbook.json/master/central-america-n-caribbean/cu.json) x US GDP deflator 2011/2015 (FRED GDPDEF 91.478/97.315 = 0.940, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=GDPDEF&fq=Annual) = 76.3 bn 2011 int$. Range +/-25% (no PPP benchmark for Cuba; 2025 contraction during the energy crisis).

milSpendShare.note: CIA Factbook: 4.2% of GDP (2020), 3.2% (2019); SIPRI via World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS 2.88% (2018, last value) low. Opaque budget; mid an educated middle.

industrialShare.note: asOf 2024: industry incl. construction 23.85% of GDP (NV.IND.TOTL.ZS).

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.05 -> 0.78. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CUB/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 15.53% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.69 (mean 2017-2019, range 0.68-0.72). Mid 1 - 0.155/0.69 = 0.78. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.68 = 0.7. High: s 0.72 = 0.78. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 69% of domestic calorie supply. FAO balance sheets for Cuba stop at 2019; the post-2020 output collapse is not in s, so the true value is likely lower. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Imports most of its food (rice, wheat, chicken); rationing in place; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 5,393,966 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share of males aged 15-19 5.554% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 59,916. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-15%.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. No road figure on the fetched Factbook record or the road-network table; older Factbook editions gave ~60,000 km total with roughly 20,000 km paved (2015). Mid is the derived midpoint.

railKm.note: CIA Factbook 8,367 km (2017; 8,195 km standard gauge, incl. sugar-industry lines); World Bank IS.RRS.TOTL.KM 5,076 km (2007) low.

majorPorts.note: CIA Factbook 2024: 34 ports, 6 large + 3 medium = 9 (Havana, Mariel, Cienfuegos, Santiago de Cuba, Nuevitas, Matanzas...).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Cuba is below the 1 million GT threshold of the merchant-fleet table (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_merchant_navy_capacity_by_country); CIA Factbook 2023 counts 65 merchant ships (13 general cargo, 10 tankers).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Island defence on interior lines; fuel shortage limits motorized movement.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses (~900,000) and draught oxen widely used in agriculture since the 1990s Special Period; not from FAO data.

nuclearWarheads.note: Cuba is a non-nuclear-weapon state (NPT); not listed by FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces. Party to the NPT since 2002 and Tlatelolco; no Russian nuclear weapons stationed since 1962.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: island fortified with tunnels and militia, population mobilization doctrine; high 1.3 for the tropical climate and dense organised resistance.

cuba-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2024-25 data with 2026 order of battle. Most data are IISS estimates (Military Balance 2024 personnel, 2025 equipment via the List of equipment of the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces) with many "n/a" quantities, so counts are grade C/D and heavily storage-inflated; serviceability is very low. Population convention: everything inside ne:CUB (World Bank). GDP from CIA Factbook (World Bank/IMF give no PPP series), rebased to 2011 int$ via FRED GDPDEF; grade C. ships_minor = patrol ships, missile craft, MCM; missiles = coastal anti-ship launchers. Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Territorial Troops Militia and Youth Labour Army (~1.12 million reserve paramilitary) excluded from active and P roles; they feed mobilizable.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.15 -> 0.98. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/CZE/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 2.71% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 1.24 (mean 2021-2023, range 1.22-1.26). Mid 1 - 0.027/1.24 = 0.98. Low: a x 1.5 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 1.22 = 0.97. High: s 1.26 = 0.98. Net exporter: production is about 124% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Near self-sufficient in cereals, imports fruit/vegetables.

areaKm2.note: League of Nations Statistical Year-Book 1939/40, Table 2: Czecho-Slovakia 140 thousand km2 within the 1937 boundaries (low, mid). world_1930 Czechoslovakia polygon = 141,071 km2 computed by the pipeline (high). Pre-Munich territory incl. the Sudetenland and Carpathian Ruthenia; the world_1938 polygon (90,899 km2) already shows the post-Munich state and is not used.

population.note: League of Nations Year-Book 1939/40, Table 2: official estimate vi.1937 = 15,239k, 1937 estimate column 15,270k (mid); census 1.xii.1930 = 14,729k. COW NMC v7 tpop 1937 = 15,250k. OWID Czechoslovakia 1938 = 14.60M (low; COW 1938 also 14,600k, already net of the Munich cessions). High allows for growth to September 1938.

urbanization.note: HYDE 3.5 (OWID) urban share, present-day borders: Czechia 1930 36%, 1940 42%; Slovakia 1930 15%, 1940 20%. Weighted by OWID 1938 population (Czechia 10.88M, Slovakia 3.29M): 1930 = 0.31 (low), 1940 = 0.37 (high), ~0.35 in 1938 (mid); rural Ruthenia (~0.7M) is outside both series. COW upop/tpop 1937 = 1,619/15,250 = 0.11 counts cities over 100,000 only and is not used.

activePersonnel.note: Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45): strength after the general mobilisation of 23 September 1938 = 1,280,000 men (mid, Shishkin); the same page gives "about 1.5 million" in 42 divisions (high) and the 1936 mobilisation plan figure of 972,747 men (low). Peacetime army 200,000 (17 infantry and 4 mobile divisions). COW NMC v7 milper 1938 = 163k is an annual peacetime average. Snapshot date 30 September 1938. Grade C, not B: the source is a self-published compilation, and the primary works it cites (Shishkin, Osprey MAA 554) were not checked.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. After the general mobilisation of 23 September 1938 nearly every trained class was with its unit; older classes and State Defence Guard (SOS) men not yet called are counted here.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Everything outside the P roles in the 1.28M mobilised army: 2,330 guns, 1,177 AT guns, 1,379 mortars and the AA arm (272 heavy and 227 light AA guns), 80 engineer companies, the air force (6 regiments, ~1,300 aircraft), signals, fortress artillery, 17 armoured trains, trains and services (equipment counts from Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45)). Roughly 45% of the mobilised strength, the share in the Polish 1939 snapshot.

mobilizationRatio.note: Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45): 972,747 (1936 plan) to 1,280,000 (mobilised) and ~1.5M of ~15.2M = 0.064-0.1; mid 0.085 = 1.28M plus the remaining reserve classes.
