commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: French-trained general staff under Krejci; partial mobilisation in May and general mobilisation in September 1938 completed in days; untested in war, and a defensive plan that relied on French and Soviet help (cited samlib page).

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5 (national conscript army) minus minorities. Evidence: the 1936 mobilisation plan counted 718,230 Slavs, 192,844 Germans and 61,671 Hungarians, i.e. a quarter of the mobilised men from minorities whose loyalty was doubtful (cited samlib page).

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75 (motivated). Evidence: Czech and Slovak reservists answered the September 1938 call-up in full; defence of the homeland behind a new fortified line; German and Hungarian reservists less willing.

weapons.note: Anchor: between 7 (1905) and 8 (1943). Evidence: ZB vz.26 and ZB-53 machine guns, 37 mm vz.37 AT gun, 105 mm vz.35 gun, 81 mm mortars, ZK-383 SMG entering service (cited samlib page).

armor.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8 (rolled homogeneous armour). Evidence: LT vz.35 riveted 25 mm armour with a 37 mm gun; LT vz.38 not yet in service.

ships.note: Anchor: 7. No sea-going navy; a river flotilla of two artillery boats and patrol craft under the engineers (cited samlib page). Value only matters if ships are added.

fortification.note: Anchor: 8 = concrete lines (Maginot). Evidence: by September 1938 264 heavy blockhouses and 10,014 light pillboxes, a line modelled on the Maginot Line, about 20% of the planned heavy and 70% of the light objects (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovak_border_fortifications).

logistics.note: Anchor: 7 (railways) toward 8 (motor transport). Evidence: 26,000 motor vehicles and tractors and 217,000 horses after mobilisation (cited samlib page); 13,548 km of railway.

communications.note: Anchor: 7 (telephone), radio partly. Evidence: signal battalions at army and corps level; radio below divisional level scarce (inferred from the organisation tables on the cited samlib page).

isr.note: Anchor: between 7 and 8. Evidence: 22 reconnaissance squadrons with 483 aircraft, sound-ranging; no radar.

air.note: Anchor: between 7 (1914) and 8 (1943). Evidence: B.534 biplane fighters, SB-2 monoplane bombers; no modern monoplane fighter in service.

cyber.note: No military computer networks before ~1990 (cyber anchor 9 = 1990 networks).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID CSV) Czechoslovakia: 1937 = 4,594 (mid, high), 1936 = 4,143 (low), 2011 int$. No 1938 value.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Global Military Spending Dataset via OWID, Czechoslovakia: 1937 = 3.08% (low), 1938 = 4.36% (mid), 1939 = 5.32% (high). Mobilised but not at war on the snapshot date, so the 1938 annual share is the mid. COW milex 1938 = 201,459 thousand current US$, 1937 = 156,591.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Industry and mining share of output. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Czechoslovak_Republic: in Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia 39% of the population worked in industry and 31% in agriculture and forestry; Slovakia and Ruthenia were mainly agricultural. Czechoslovakia had inherited 70-80% of Austria-Hungary's industry.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of employment (s = 1 assumed). Czech lands 31% agriculture and forestry (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Czechoslovak_Republic); Slovakia and Ruthenia assumed ~60% (not fetched). Weighted by population (10.9M / 4.4M): ~39% -> 0.61. Roughly self-sufficient in grain and a sugar exporter.

annualCohort.note: Educated guess. Men reaching military age (21) per year: the 1917 birth cohort, depressed by the First World War (pre-war births ~30 per 1,000 of ~13.5M, roughly halved in 1915-18), half male, ~75% survival.

armor.note: Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45): LT vz.35 deliveries 15 (1936), 262 (1937), 21 (1938) for the army, plus export tanks for Iran, Peru, Switzerland and others from CKD and Skoda (high). Mid = the 1937 peak.

aircraft_fighter.note: Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45): B.534 / Bk.534 deliveries 100 (1935), 149 (1936), 174 (1937); 568 built in all. Range spans the 1936-37 rates.

aircraft_strike.note: Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45): Letov S.328 445 built 1935-39 (~90 a year), Aero MB.200 124 built (1936), Avia B-71 (licence SB) 161 built 1937-39; ~150 bombers and reconnaissance-bombers a year combined.

artillery.note: Temezhnikov, Armed forces of Czechoslovakia 1930-1939 (samlib.ru compilation citing Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle series and Osprey MAA 554 Czechoslovak Armies 1918-45): 37 mm vz.37 AT guns 1,131 built 1937-39 (~450 a year), 150 mm vz.25 345 (1930-39), 100 mm vz.30 188 (1932-39), 105 mm vz.35 106 (1935-39); field and AT pieces combined ~250-700 a year.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. State, district and municipal roads with hard surfaces; dense in Bohemia-Moravia, sparse in Slovakia and Ruthenia.

railKm.note: CHAT railline Czechoslovakia: 1936 = 13,595 km (high), 1937 = 13,548 km (low, mid); no 1938 value.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Landlocked. Danube port of Bratislava and the leased Czechoslovak zone in the port of Hamburg (Versailles treaty) were the only water outlets; neither can supply a fleet.

merchantTonnage.note: League of Nations Year-Book 1939/40, Table 113 (merchant vessels of 100 GRT and more, June 1929-1938) lists no Czechoslovak fleet; the first sea-going ships came in the 1950s.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Defensive war on interior lines from a dense railway net; 26,000 motor vehicles gave more reach than the Polish army had.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Low = 217,000 horses with the mobilised army (cited samlib page); national horse stock of roughly 0.6-0.8M guessed.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before July 1945.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row: mountain rim, a new fortified line and population support among Czechs and Slovaks; low 1.1 because the fortified borderlands were German-speaking and Austria (annexed March 1938) outflanked the line from the south.

czechoslovakia-1938.notes: Snapshot date 30 September 1938: general mobilisation of 23 September complete, the day the Munich Agreement was signed. Territory and population are the pre-Munich republic (Sudetenland and Carpathian Ruthenia included); the world_1938 basemap already shows the reduced state, so the border uses the world_1930 polygon. Personnel: active = the mobilised army and air force (1.28M, range 0.97-1.5M); no navy. Equipment counts come from a samlib.ru compilation (Temezhnikov) that cites Shishkin's 1938 order-of-battle articles and Osprey MAA 554; they agree with the fort counts of the Wikipedia fortifications article. P-role counts are reconstructions from the division structure (grade D). Weakest values: the P-role split, support personnel, roads and horses (educated guesses). Ship convention per SOURCES.md: no ship roles, since the river flotilla cannot reach the sea.

areaKm2.note: The world_1300 Sultanate of Delhi polygon measures 1.95 million km2 on the sphere (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_1300.geojson, mid). The Delhi Sultanate infobox gives 1.5 million for 1300 (low) and 3.2 million for 1312 (high, with tributary Deccan); Seshat codes 2.8-3.2 million.

population.note: Educated guess. India had ~85 million in 1200 and 101-110 million in 1500 (Maddison 2001 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Sultanate); HYDE gives 123.7M for 1300 (OWID https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true). The Sultanate directly ruled Punjab, the Gangetic plain, Gujarat, Malwa and Bengal (Deccan kings tributary), perhaps 35-50% of the subcontinent.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Delhi 200,000-400,000 (Seshat 135), Lahore, Multan, Gujarat ports.

activePersonnel.note: Historians state the Khalji Sultanate kept 300,000-400,000 cavalry and 2,500-3,000 war elephants as a standing army (Tripathi, Digby 1971 p. 24 via the Delhi Sultanate page), echoing Firishta's 475,000 horsemen (16th c., Alauddin Khalji page). The Catalan Atlas (1375) credits the sultan with 100,000 horsemen and 700 elephants (Tughlaq dynasty page). Mid: ~150,000 cavalry + ~80,000 infantry + support, after the 1320 civil war.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Iqta-holders' retainers and Hindu chiefs' contingents callable within a month.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Mahouts (2 per elephant), siege engineers, the barid postal service and commissariat.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. A Turkic and Afghan military elite paid in cash and iqta, plus Hindu paik infantry; mass mobilisation of the peasantry was not the model.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Mounted archers of the iqta-holders and paid regulars.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: imported Central Asian and Arab horses, composite bows

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional mounted archers

count.note: Educated guess. Armoured household cavalry (khasakhail, largely of slave origin) and lancers (Delhi Sultanate page).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75-1.0. Evidence: mail and lamellar, barded horses

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: elite household troops

count.note: Educated guess. Paik infantry, largely Hindu, for sieges and garrisons.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 minus. Evidence: light equipment

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: paid footmen

count.note: Educated guess. Foot archers.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: bows

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: mixed

count.note: Catalan Atlas 700 (low, Tughlaq dynasty page) and 2,500-3,000 for the Khalji standing army (Digby 1971 via the Delhi Sultanate page, high); mid assumes losses in the 1320 succession war. Platform count.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: large royal elephant stables fed by tribute from the Deccan and Bengal

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: royal elephant establishment

count.note: Educated guess. Manjaniq (trebuchets) and arradas in siege trains (Chittor 1303, Ranthambore 1301).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Islamic-world trebuchets

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: siege specialists

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, a veteran of the Mongol wars, won the 1320 civil war; Khalji generals had beaten the Mongols 1298-1306

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: factional Turkic, Afghan and convert nobility; three dynastic changes 1290-1320

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5-0.75. Evidence: new dynasty after a civil war; long run of Deccan victories

weapons.note: Anchor: 4 (1250). Evidence: composite bows, trebuchets, high-quality steel blades

armor.note: Anchor: between 3 and 4. Evidence: mail and lamellar, barded horses for the elite

ships.note: Anchor: between 1 and 2. Evidence: river craft; Gujarat ports had merchant ships but no royal navy

fortification.note: Anchor: about 4. Evidence: Siri and Tughlaqabad walls, captured Rajput fortresses

logistics.note: Anchor: between 3 and 4. Evidence: Alauddin's price controls and state granaries, banjara grain carriers

communications.note: Anchor: 4 (relay horses). Evidence: barid relay post with horse and foot runners

isr.note: Anchor: between 3 and 4. Evidence: barid news-writers and spies

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Analogue: Maddison 2023 (via OWID grapher CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) has India only from 1600 (1,264) and China 1000 = 1,225, 1150 = 1,181; Egypt 1000 = 956, 1300 = 972 (2011 int$). Medieval South Asia placed in that band.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Land revenue taken at up to half the produce under Alauddin largely paid the army.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Textiles (Gujarat, Bengal), metalwork.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Doab and Punjab grain, heavily taxed.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Royal roads Delhi-Daulatabad, Delhi-Lahore-Multan, Delhi-Lakhnauti.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Khambhat, Bharuch, Satgaon.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gujarati and Bengali merchant shipping.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Cavalry armies campaigned 1,500 km into the Deccan (Warangal, Madurai) living partly off the land.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Oxen, banjara pack herds, camels in the west.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: 1.1-1.2 row: fortified cities and summer heat against steppe invaders.

delhi-sultanate-1320.notes: Snapshot September 1320, when Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq took Delhi from Khusrau Khan; Warangal fell in 1323. Army figures in the sources (Firishta's 475,000, the 300,000-400,000 cavalry repeated on the Sultanate page) are chronicle-derived and taken as the high end; the mid is a composite with the Catalan Atlas figure. Population convention: directly ruled provinces; tributary Deccan kingdoms excluded. GDP per capita is a regional analogy. Personnel: active = cash-paid household and regular cavalry, paid paik infantry, royal elephants; trainedReserves = retainers of iqta-holders and Hindu chiefs' contingents; mobilizable = population x ratio.

Figures quoted above are before the correction.

milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via World Bank: 1.38% of GDP in 2025. Much security spending is off-budget or channelled through the presidency (high is an allowance).

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.0 -> 0.36. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/COD/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 58.52% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.92 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.90-0.94). Mid 1 - 0.585/0.92 = 0.36. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.90 = 0.22. High: s 0.94 = 0.38. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 92% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Chronic food insecurity (over 20 million people acutely food insecure) despite vast arable land; subsistence farming.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 55,984,510 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share aged 15-19 10.533% / 5 = 1,179,338. Males only (conscript-pool convention). Range +/-10%.

roadKm.note: Road list (2015): 152,373 km total (high, mostly unusable in rainy season), 3,047 km paved (mid). World Bank IS.ROD.TOTL.KM 153,497 km (2004).

railKm.note: asOf 2021: 3,641 route-km (World Bank IS.RRS.TOTL.KM). CIA Factbook 4,007 km (2014) spans the range. Disconnected networks (Katanga, Matadi-Kinshasa), largely dilapidated.

majorPorts.note: CIA Factbook 2024: 3 ports (Matadi, Boma small; Banana very small).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. CIA Factbook: 24 ships under the DRC flag (2023). (context page: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/factbook/factbook.json/master/africa/cg.json)

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Road network almost non-existent in the east; sustainment by air and river.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Few draft animals (tsetse zone); porters used instead.

nuclearWarheads.note: Non-nuclear-weapon state (NPT); not listed by FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1: vast, forested terrain hard for any invader; little population support for the FARDC in the east.

dr-congo-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2025 World Bank data, 2026 order of battle. War in the east: the Rwanda-backed M23/AFC took Goma (January 2025) and Bukavu (February 2025); US- and Qatar-brokered peace frameworks were signed in 2025 but fighting continued. ADF (ISIS-DRC), CODECO and 100+ other armed groups are active. FARDC strength figures are inflated by ghost soldiers; counts from the Wikipedia Land Forces equipment list and Air Force inventory (grade C) with educated guesses where nothing is published. Population convention: everything inside ne:COD including M23-held territory. Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011 (+/-20%). Wazalendo militias, Burundian troops and foreign contractors excluded. Doctrine archetype-insurgent: the war is fought largely by irregulars on both sides.

areaKm2.note: Infobox: 2,000,000 km2 (undated; the whole empire with Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh) (high). Mid: the world_1783 Afghanistan polygon used as the border, about 1.15 million km2 on the sphere (Kandahar, Kabul, Herat, Balkh, Khorasan to Mashhad, Baluchistan); the 1783 file draws Punjab (Lahore), Multan and Sind as separate polygons. Low allows for the loose hold on Balkh and Khorasan.

population.note: Low: OWID Afghanistan 1760 = 2.87M (HYDE 3.3, modern borders, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population). Mid: that plus Iranian Khorasan and the Baluch and Pashtun lands inside the polygon (educated estimate of about 1.5M from OWID Iran 1760 = 5.79M and Pakistan 1760 = 15.2M). High: infobox 14 million for the whole empire with its Indian provinces (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durrani_Empire). The phase-3 formula gave 47 million for this polygon, far too high.

urbanization.note: Educated guess: caravan cities Kandahar, Kabul, Herat and Mashhad in a pastoral and oasis-farming country.

activePersonnel.note: Panipat field army (14 January 1761): 41,800 Afghan cavalry, 28,000 of them regular, plus 2,000 camel-gun troops in the reserve (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Battle_of_Panipat); the 32,000 Rohilla infantry and Shuja-ud-Daula's 3,000 men and 50-60 guns were allies and are not counted. Mid adds a few thousand for garrisons of Kandahar, Kabul, Herat and Lahore. Low: the 28,000 regulars plus the 10,000 ghulam core (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durrani_Empire) overlap, so about 30,000.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: Pashtun, Baluch, Uzbek and Qizilbash tribal contingents callable for a campaign but not under arms.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: gunners, camel and baggage men of the royal army.

mobilizationRatio.note: Regional analogy: Mughal Empire 1690 and Maratha 1760 snapshots (Barua 2005 p. 47 via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire: about 3% of the population were armed men). A tribal society where most men bore arms could reach more; kept at the analogy.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: 19,000 mailed Afghan horsemen under Shah Wali Khan at Panipat (mid); 28,000 regular cavalry (infobox) (high); low = the 10,000 mounted ghulams of the royal guard (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durrani_Empire).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: mail, lance, broadsword and blunderbuss (sher-bacha ghulams); good horses.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: long-service ghulams, a third of them former Qizilbash of Nader Shah's army.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: tribal lance and sword cavalry with some matchlocks; camel swivel guns.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: experienced raiders of five invasions of India since 1748.

count.note: Educated guess: tribal jezail infantry and fort garrisons; infantry played a very small role in the Durrani army (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durrani_Empire).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: matchlocks.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: tribal levies.

count.note: Educated guess. Artillery played a very small role apart from camel-mounted swivel guns (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durrani_Empire); the 2,000 zamburaks are counted as light cavalry, not as pieces. The 50-60 guns at Panipat belonged to the ally Shuja-ud-Daula.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: few, light pieces; outranged by the Maratha French-made guns at Panipat.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5 minus.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5-0.75. Evidence: ghulam core with tribal contingents loyal to the shah's success and plunder.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75 minus. Evidence: recent victories in India; troops wanted to return home with their plunder, which ended the campaign in 1761.

weapons.note: Anchor: 5 (1600, arquebus/musket, field cannon). Evidence: lance, sword, matchlocks, blunderbusses and camel swivel guns; little field artillery.

ships.note: Anchor: 0-1. Evidence: landlocked; ferries and boats on the Indus only.

logistics.note: Anchor: 4-5. Evidence: camel and horse transport, foraging and plunder; cut the Maratha supply lines at Panipat while keeping his own open via Rohilkhand.

communications.note: Anchor: 4-5. Evidence: mounted couriers.

Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: caravan routes and passes, almost no engineered road.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: camels, horses and pack animals of a pastoral country (about 10% of the population); no count found.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

durrani-empire-1761.notes: Snapshot = January 1761, Ahmad Shah's army at the Third Battle of Panipat. Personnel: the royal army and the tribal cavalry in the field are activePersonnel; the Rohilla and Awadh allies at Panipat are separate states and not counted; uncalled tribal contingents are trainedReserves. Territory and population = the world_1783 Afghanistan polygon (Afghanistan, Khorasan, Baluchistan); Punjab, Kashmir, Multan and Sind were held or tributary in 1761 but are outside the border and the population, and includes is empty. Weakest values: population mid (composite), artillery, and the economy and logistics guesses; Maddison has no series for the region before 1950. Doctrine archetype-steppe-nomad: a cavalry army of raids, blockade and mounted firepower rather than a linear gunpowder army.

areaKm2.note: world_1650 Dutch Republic polygon = 32,996 km2 on the sphere. High allows for Generality Lands possibly drawn outside it.

population.note: HYDE via OWID: Netherlands 1,543,183 (1600) and 2,000,000 (1700); interpolated ~1.85M for 1672. The Military Revolution article gives 1.5M for c. 1650 and the Dutch States Army article "about 1.5 million in the 17th century". Generality Lands (Staats-Brabant, Staats-Vlaanderen, Maastricht) included.

urbanization.note: OWID urban share: Netherlands 22.0% (1600), 33.6% (1700) (de Vries, towns 10,000+); with the 5,000+ convention Holland exceeded 45%. Mid 38%: the most urbanised state in Europe.

activePersonnel.note: States Army establishment for 1672: 90,000 (Dutch States Army article, strength table), raised in haste from a peacetime ~30,000-40,000; the Franco-Dutch War article gives 80,000 and notes that contracts to exceed 80,000 took months to fill. Effective field army in June 1672 was far smaller (~22,000 under William III at the IJssel). Plus navy ~25,000 (28,000 personnel in 1670, Dutch States Navy table). Mid 76,000 = ~50,000 effective soldiers + ~26,000 navy.

trainedReserves.note: Schutterij civic militia: the cities provided 12,000 men in 1672 (Franco-Dutch War article); 50,000 militia backed 70,000 regulars in 1629 (Dutch States Army article).

supportPersonnel.note: Navy personnel 28,000 in 1670 (Dutch States Navy table after Rodger, Glete and others) incl. marines (Regiment de Marine, 1665), plus artillery and engineers (~1,500).

mobilizationRatio.note: Includes the mercenary market: the Republic hired Germans, Scots, English and Swiss (Dutch States Army article: without the open market for soldiers 1.5M people could not have competed). 90,000 army + 28,000 navy = ~6% of population in 1672-73; ceiling ~9-12% with foreign recruitment.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Infantry companies of the States Army, much of it in fortress garrisons; strongly expanded with raw recruits in 1672 (Dutch States Army article). Effective count, not the 90,000 paper.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: matchlock and early flintlock muskets with pikes; Liege and Amsterdam arms industry

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: the army had decayed during the stadholderless period; many 1672 recruits untrained; garrisons surrendered quickly

count.note: Cuirassier-type horse companies (~15% of the army).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: well-equipped

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: neglected before 1672

count.note: Educated guess: dragoons and light horse (dragoons counted as light cavalry).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: era-typical

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: new units

count.note: Educated guess: field pieces; Dutch fortress artillery (thousands of guns) excluded.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Dutch gun founding and Swedish iron guns among the best

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional gunners

count.note: Ships of the line: De Ruyter had 61 ships of the line (plus 14 frigates) at Solebay, 7 June 1672 (Battle of Solebay article, Blok 1928 and Van Nimwegen 2020); the Dutch States Navy table counts 110 warships of all classes in 1670.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: shallow-draught 60-80 gun ships, lighter than English first rates (Dutch States Navy article: 60-80 vs 70-100 guns)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: veteran crews of the Second Anglo-Dutch War (Medway 1667); De Ruyter the best admiral of the age

count.note: Frigates, fireships and yachts: 110 warships in 1670 (Dutch States Navy table) minus ships of the line; Solebay alone saw 14 frigates and ~24 fireships.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: good frigates

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75-1.0. Evidence: veteran crews

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.75. Evidence: De Ruyter at sea the best of the era (0.95); on land William III untested in 1672 and the field army collapsed before the Water Line held; De Witt brothers murdered Aug 1672

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: mercenary regiments and provincial particularism (each province paid its own troops); navy cohesion high

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.25-0.5. Evidence: Rampjaar panic: towns surrendered without fighting, Orangist riots; recovered after Solebay and the inundations

weapons.note: Anchor: 5.3. Evidence: Maurician drill tradition, matchlock and pike, early flintlocks

armor.note: Anchor: 5.1. Evidence: cuirassiers, pikemen's corselets

ships.note: Anchor: 5.45. Evidence: two-deck ships of the line, line-of-battle tactics audit 2026-10-30: mid 5.45 -> 5.35, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 1672 (5.351); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

fortification.note: Anchor: 5.4. Evidence: Old Dutch bastioned system and the Dutch Water Line inundations

logistics.note: Anchor: 5.6 above 5 (magazines, canal transport). Evidence: canal and river network, trekschuit services, the most advanced military contracting and credit system of the era audit 2026-10-30: mid 5.6 -> 5.35, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 1672 (5.351); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

communications.note: Anchor: 5.4. Evidence: dense postal and newspaper network

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years as the anchor table (1600 -> 5, 1805 -> 6). Evidence: cavalry screens, spies and merchant reports only; no aerial or signal intelligence

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (2011 int$): Netherlands 1670 = 3,476, 1672 = 2,923 (the war-year collapse), 1680 = 3,549. Mid 3,200: the richest economy per head in the world.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: The Dutch States Army article (financing section) describes army and navy as the bulk of the Generality budget; Holland's debt service and war spending in 1672-73 reached ~8-12% of GDP (wartime mid, peacetime low ~4%).

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: textiles (Leiden), shipbuilding (Zaan), sugar refining, brewing; services and trade large.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - a / s (a = agricultural share of employment, s = calorie self-sufficiency). a: the earliest fetched figure is Herrendorf et al. via OWID, Netherlands agriculture share of employment 1807 = 43.1% (1849 = 40.3%), https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/employment-by-economic-sector.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true. The Republic at its 1670s commercial peak was probably no more agrarian; a ~0.42 (0.35-0.50) assumed. No self-sufficiency figure fetched, so s = 1 is assumed, which overstates the value: Holland imported much of its bread grain from the Baltic (the moedernegotie) and its farms specialised in dairy. Grade D: a extrapolated over 135 years. audit 2026-10-30: was 0.05/0.1/0.15 (read as import dependence); recomputed with the formula.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.009-0.011 (mid 0.0095): in a pre-transition age structure (Wrigley and Schofield type, life expectancy ~30-35) males reaching 18 each year are about 0.9-1.1% of total population. Males only.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: few roads; ~650 km of trekvaart canals plus rivers carried passengers and freight.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Hellevoetsluis, Middelburg, Flushing, Enkhuizen, Hoorn, Harlingen, Den Helder.

merchantTonnage.note: Merchant fleet ~400,000-600,000 tons burden c. 1670, the largest in Europe (estimates after Vogel and de Vries/van der Woude summarised in the Dutch Republic literature); converted roughly to deadweight. Grade C.

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War (isbn:0-521-54657-5) ch. 1: 17th-18th c. armies tied to magazines and bread ovens, operating ~5 marches (~100-150 km) beyond the nearest magazine or navigable river; requisition extends it in rich country. Defensive war on interior water lines. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: horses for 1.85M people; transport mostly by boat.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: 1.2 row plus inundation: fortified cities and the Water Line (flooding stopped the French in June 1672); rated 1.3 for the water defence rather than climate.

dutch-republic-1672.notes: Snapshot = June 1672, the Rampjaar (French, Munster and Cologne invasion; Anglo-French naval attack; Solebay 7 June). Population: the Seven Provinces plus Generality Lands; VOC/WIC colonies are bases only (VOC troops excluded). Personnel convention: States Army regiments (largely foreign mercenaries) and navy are active; schutterij civic militia is trainedReserves. The 90,000 army figure is the 1672 establishment, not effectives; the effective field army in June was ~22,000-25,000 plus garrisons. Merchant tonnage is a conversion from tons burden, grade C.

areaKm2.note: Official GDR area 108,333 km2 incl. East Berlin (mid). The world_1960 East Germany polygon measures ~113,400 km2 on a spherical approximation (high).

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1989 = 16,630 thousand (mid-year, incl. East Berlin). Low = end-1989 ~16.43M after ~340,000 people left during 1989.

urbanization.note: OWID/HYDE urban share Germany 1989 = 73.1% (whole Germany). GDR official statistics (towns of 2,000+) gave ~77% (high).

activePersonnel.note: Crane, RAND, East Germany's Military (1989) p. 34, citing IISS Military Balance 1987: 176,000 excluding border troops (army 120,000, navy 16,000, air force 40,000) plus 49,000 Border Troops. NVA article: 175,300 at the 1987 peak. Mid 173,000 allows the 10,000-man cut announced in January 1989. High 225,000 includes the Border Troops; COW NMC v7 milper 1989 = 262,000 also counts security troops.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: about 2.5 million men served 1956-1990 (NVA article); mobilisation planned four mobilisation divisions and two reserve divisions plus fillers (Land Forces article; Crane p. 34 notes four motor rifle divisions formed from reserves). IISS gave ~300,000 reserves (not fetched). Workers' militia Kampfgruppen (~200,000) excluded as paramilitary.

supportPersonnel.note: Active 173,000 minus infantry P roles (~34,000): navy 16,000, air force/air defence 40,000-44,000 (Crane p. 38; LSK article infobox 44,000), and the army's tank, artillery, air defence, engineer, signals and rear services. audit 2026-10-30: mid 139,000 -> 138,500 so that P roles (34,500) + support <= active 173,000.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: same reasoning as the FRG: a 1989 general war would be short; the GDR could field ~0.5M in uniform plus militia (3%) at once, total war more.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess: dismounted motor rifle infantry of four motor rifle divisions and the motor rifle regiments of two tank divisions (Land Forces article: 1st, 4th, 8th, 11th MRD, 7th and 9th Panzer divisions); ~120,000 army personnel (Crane p. 34).

JG-3 converted to 24 MiG-29 in 1988-89 (LSK article; 24 MiG-29 passed to the Luftwaffe in 1990, NVA article). The LSK infobox figure of 800 combat aircraft counts trainers and helicopters.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: tight ground-controlled interception, low flying hours.

count.note: Fighter-bomber wings JBG-37 (MiG-23BN) and JBG-77 (Su-22M-4) and naval MFG-28 (Su-22M-4), two squadrons each (LSK article), ~12-15 aircraft per squadron; Crane Table 12 shows 35 Su-22 added by 1987.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript ground crews, limited low-level training.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison 2023 (OWID CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) Germany 1989 = 26,393 (2011 int$), split East/West with a per-capita ratio of 0.5 (range 0.4-0.6): CIA 1990 GDR GNP per capita $9,679 (Economy of East Germany article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_East_Germany) against FRG ~$19,000-20,000. With COW populations 62.06M/16.63M: East = r x 26,393 x 78.69 / (62.06 + r x 16.63) = 12,090-17,298.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Crane p. 33: reported defence budget 4.3% of GNP in 1980 (Collier estimate), 6.0% with state security; real spending grew faster than GNP into 1987-88 then flattened.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: CIA 1990 (Economy of East Germany infobox): 90% of GNP outside agriculture; industry was ~60-70% of net material product, ~50-55% of a Western-style GNP.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of the labour force (share of food output not eaten by the farm population; no calorie self-sufficiency adjustment). CIA World Factbook 1990 (Project Gutenberg #14) labour force, GDR: 10.8% agriculture and forestry (1987). Share 10.8% (range 9.0-13.0%) -> 0.892 (0.87-0.91).

annualCohort.note: Educated guess: males reaching 18 in 1989 = 1971 birth cohort (~235,000 GDR births) x 0.513, minus mortality. Crane ch. IV: the GDR would need to conscript nearly all 18-year-old males in the early 1990s. Males only (conscript pool).

artillery.note: Educated guess: light weapons and some artillery ammunition and components only.

ifv_apc.note: Educated guess: no indigenous AFV lines; licence or repair capacity only. Tanks, aircraft and most weapons were imported from the USSR, CSSR and Poland (Crane ch. II: CSSR and Poland built T-72s under licence).

ships_minor.note: Educated guess: Peene-Werft Wolgast built Parchim corvettes and minesweepers at a few a year (Crane p. 38).

roadKm.note: Educated guess: ~47,000 km classified roads incl. ~1,850 km Autobahn; high includes municipal roads.

railKm.note: Educated guess: Deutsche Reichsbahn route network ~14,000 km in 1989, dense and heavily used for military transport.

majorPorts.note: Rostock (overseas port opened 1960, Economy of East Germany article), Wismar, Stralsund, Sassnitz/Mukran (rail ferry to the USSR from 1986).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Deutsche Seereederei Rostock fleet ~1.3-1.5M GRT, x1.5 dwt/GRT.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: Warsaw Pact front logistics, rail-fed, NVA divisions attached to Soviet armies.

east-germany-1989.notes: Snapshot date mid-1989 (IISS Military Balance 1989-90 reference date 1 July 1989), before the November 1989 collapse. Main source: Keith Crane, East Germany's Military: Forces and Expenditures, RAND Arroyo Center report (Oct 1989, isbn 0-8330-1033-6), fetched as DTIC ADA221839 full text on archive.org; it quotes IISS Military Balance 1987-88 figures. Equipment totals cross-checked with the 1990 handover inventory (NVA article, BICC Brief 3): 767 aircraft, 208 ships, 2,761 tanks, 2,199 artillery pieces. The January 1989 Warsaw Pact force data statement was not fetched. Border Troops (~47,000-49,000) and Kampfgruppen militia excluded from active (border troops in the high range). The 19-20 Soviet divisions of the GSFG (~380,000 troops) stationed in the GDR are counted in ussr-1989. Population includes East Berlin.

ecuador-2026.notes: AUTO-GENERATED BASE SNAPSHOT. Population, economy, personnel and infrastructure from the World Bank (grade A/B). Force mix, ratings and tech copied from researched regional analogues (Argentine Republic, Federative Republic of Brazil, Republic of Chile, Republic of Colombia, Republic of Cuba, Republic of Peru, Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela) and graded D. Replace with a researched snapshot when one exists.

areaKm2.note: Official area 1,001,450 km2 incl. Sinai; hb:1960 Egypt polygon computes to ~1,000,600 km2 on the sphere. Gaza Strip (Egyptian-administered) excluded.

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1967 = 30,892k (mid). Low: 1966 census 30.08M grown 2%. High: OWID/UN 32,196,366 and World Bank 1967 (32.2M).

urbanization.note: HYDE (OWID) urban share 1967 = 42.3%; 1966 census urban share ~40% (low).

activePersonnel.note: COW NMC v7 milper 1967 = 220,000 (mid). CIA memo 26 June 1967: ground forces ~217,000 incl. 35,000 in Yemen; CIA/DIA table 26 May: ground forces 175,000 before mobilisation. Plus air force and navy ~25,000 -> 200,000-242,000. Pollack 2004 p. 59 via Six-Day War article: 160,000 total, 100,000 in Sinai.

trainedReserves.note: Reservists called up in May 1967. CIA/DIA 26 May: ground forces 175,000 before mobilisation, 200,000 at M+15 (+25,000, low) and "limited reserves at home". High allows the wider reserve call-up reported in May 1967. Grade C.

supportPersonnel.note: Active 220,000 minus P roles ~92,000: air force (~20,000), navy (~11,000), armour, artillery, air-defence, logistics and staff. Grade C.

mobilizationRatio.note: Egypt fielded ~0.65-0.85M in 1973 (Yom Kippur War infobox) from ~35M people = 1.9-2.4%; a total-war ceiling of 4-8% is assumed given limited conscript training capacity. Grade C.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Infantry of 9 divisions and 28 independent brigades (CIA 26 June 1967; ground forces 217,000), incl. ~35,000 troops in Yemen. Infantry share ~40% of ground forces. Reconstruction, grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: Soviet small arms (AK, SKS) and RPG-2, little night equipment.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: conscripts, poor flexibility and improvisation (CIA 26 May 1967); reservists barely trained (Pollack ch. 1).

count.note: Educated guess: Sa'iqa commandos and paratroop battalions (two commando battalions flown to Jordan in June 1967).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: volunteer commandos with Yemen experience.

count.note: Six-Day War article (Pollack 2004 p. 59): 1,000 artillery pieces in Sinai; plus guns west of the canal and in Yemen. CIA/DIA table also lists 200 SP antitank/assault guns (SU-100).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Soviet 122 mm and 130 mm guns, outranging Israeli artillery.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: rigid pre-planned fire, weak observation.

count.note: CIA memo 26 June 1967: ~1,000 tanks before the war (350 T-34, 400 T-54, 123 T-55, plus IS-3, PT-76, Centurion and Sherman); CIA/DIA table 26 May: 1,007. Pollack 2004 p. 59: 900-950 in Sinai.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: T-54/55 era-typical, but over a third were WWII T-34/85.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: poor gunnery and maintenance; ~500 tanks lost in Sinai (CIA June 1967).

count.note: Six-Day War article (Pollack 2004 p. 59): 1,100 APCs in Sinai; total incl. units west of the canal and Yemen somewhat higher. BTR-152, BTR-40, Walid.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: wheeled open-topped BTR-152.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5.

count.note: CIA/DIA memo 26 May 1967: 239 operationally assigned jet fighters, primarily MiG-17 and MiG-21. ~300 of ~430 combat aircraft were destroyed, mostly on the ground (CIA 26 June).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: MiG-21F-13/PF Mach 2 interceptors; MiG-17 obsolescent.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: low sortie rates, no hardened shelters, caught on the ground in Operation Focus.

count.note: CIA 26 June 1967: ~430 available combat aircraft before hostilities; CIA/DIA 26 May: 70 operational jet bombers (Tu-16, Il-28). 430 - 239 fighters = ~190 incl. Su-7 fighter-bombers and MiG-15/17 ground-attack (high).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Tu-16 with AS-1 cruise missiles, Il-28 obsolescent.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5.

count.note: Educated guess: Mi-4 and Mi-6 transport helicopters, used extensively in Yemen.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5.

count.note: CIA/DIA 26 May 1967: six destroyers (Skoryy class, ex-RN Z-class El Nasser/El Fateh); high adds 2-3 frigates and escort vessels.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: 1950s Soviet destroyers.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: CIA rates Egyptian ships ~80% as effective as Israeli due to poor maintenance and sea time.

count.note: CIA/DIA 26 May 1967: 18 missile patrol boats (Osa, Komar) (low); plus torpedo boats, submarine chasers and minesweepers (~20-40). Grade C.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Styx-armed Komar sank INS Eilat in October 1967, the first anti-ship missile kill (Egyptian Navy article).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5.

count.note: CIA/DIA 26 May 1967: 12 submarines (Soviet W and R class).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Whiskey/Romeo diesel boats.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5.

count.note: Educated guess: SA-2 battalions defending the Suez Canal and Cairo areas (CIA 26 May 1967: of limited effectiveness; few AAA defences on the four Sinai fighter bases); count not given in the fetched sources.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: SA-2 high-altitude SAM, useless against low-level attack.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.25. Evidence: Amer's politicised command, contradictory deployment orders in May 1967, general withdrawal order of 6 June collapsed the Sinai army (Pollack, Arabs at War ch. 1).

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.25-0.5. Evidence: national conscript army but deep officer-soldier divide; units disintegrated in the retreat.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.5. Evidence: high pre-war public confidence, but 35,000 men tied down in Yemen; collapsed after 6 June.

weapons.note: Anchor: between 8 (1943) and 9 (1985). Evidence: SA-2 SAMs, Styx anti-ship missiles, Mach 2 MiG-21; no ATGMs.

armor.note: Anchor: 8 = RHA. Evidence: T-54/55 steel armour, a third still T-34.

ships.note: Anchor: 8 = radar, submarines. Evidence: Osa/Komar missile boats, 12 submarines, WWII-era destroyers.

fortification.note: Anchor: 8. Evidence: Soviet-style layered field defences at Abu Ageila and Rafah; no hardened aircraft shelters.

logistics.note: Anchor: 8 = motor transport. Evidence: motorised supply, but sustained 60,000 men in Yemen (CIA 26 May 1967).

communications.note: Anchor: 8 = company radio. Evidence: Soviet radio sets, but centralised, slow reporting.

isr.note: Anchor: 8 = radar. Evidence: early-warning radar network (blind at low level); no satellites.

air.note: Anchor: air 8 = 1943, 9 = 1985. Evidence: MiG-21, Su-7, Tu-16 jets.

cyber.note: No military computer-network capability before ~1985 (cyber anchor 9 = 1990 networks).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (OWID CSV): Egypt 1967 = 1,835 (2011 int$). Range +/-10%.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via OWID: 1966 = 8.7% (low, last peacetime), 1967 = 8.9% (mid), 1968 = 11.1% (high).

industrialShare.note: World Bank NV.IND.TOTL.ZS: industry (incl. construction) 23.8% of GDP in 1967.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of the labour force (share of food output not eaten by the farm population; no calorie self-sufficiency adjustment). World Bank WDI Database Archives (version 1999 Apr), SL.AGR.TOTL.ZS "Labor force in agriculture (% of total)" (ILO-based) Egypt 1967 = 53.7% (1989 Apr vintage 53.8%). Egypt was a wheat importer; that does not lower this value. Share 53.7% (range 50.0-57.0%) -> 0.463 (0.43-0.5).

annualCohort.note: World Bank SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y and SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/ISR;EGY/indicator/SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y?date=1967:1973&format=json): 16,144,385 x 10.23% / 5 = ~330,300 males per year; only men were conscripted. audit 2026-10-30: males only, the conscript-pool convention of all other snapshots (derived:cohort-from-agegroup applied to the male term only); was 645,700 for both sexes.

artillery.note: Educated guess: Factory 99 etc. produced mortars, ammunition and small arms; guns came from the USSR.

aircraft_fighter.note: Educated guess: Helwan HA-300 programme abandoned 1969; licence assembly of trainers only.

missiles.note: Educated guess: al-Zafir/al-Kahir rockets under development with German engineers; CIA: not deployed.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: paved roads of the Nile valley and delta plus coastal and canal roads; Sinai mostly tracks.

railKm.note: Educated guess: Egyptian National Railways ~4,500-4,800 km incl. the El Qantara-El Arish line.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: Alexandria, Port Said, Suez, Safaga.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: small national merchant fleet (~200-300k GRT) x 1.5.

supplyRangeKm.note: CIA 26 May 1967: Egypt fed and armed up to 60,000 men in Yemen at the end of a thousand-mile supply line (sea route; high). Overland in Sinai ~200-250 km from the canal (mid). Grade C.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: buffaloes, cattle, donkeys and camels on Egyptian farms; negligible military use.

nuclearWarheads.note: Egypt never possessed nuclear weapons.

homeDefense.note: 1.1 row: familiar terrain and local supply in Sinai; the Nile valley behind the canal adds fortified cities and population support (1.2).

egypt-1967.notes: Snapshot date 5 June 1967. Official name United Arab Republic (Egypt), kept after Syria left the union in 1961. Territory: hb:1960:Egypt incl. Sinai; the Egyptian-administered Gaza Strip is excluded. Personnel: activePersonnel = standing conscript and regular forces incl. ~35,000 in Yemen (listed as a base abroad), trainedReserves = reservists called up in May 1967. Key sources: CIA/DIA memo "Military Capabilities of Israel and the Arab States" 26 May 1967 (UAR: 175,000 ground forces before mobilisation, 1,007 tanks, 200 SP guns, 239 jet fighters, 70 jet bombers, 6 destroyers, 12 submarines, 18 missile boats); CIA memo of 26 June 1967 on Soviet resupply (217,000 ground forces, ~1,000 tanks, ~430 combat aircraft before the war); Six-Day War article quoting Pollack, Arabs at War p. 59. IISS Military Balance 1967-68 not fetched (paywalled). Weakest: air-defence battery count, reserves, helicopter count.

areaKm2.note: Official area 1,001,450 km2 (hb:1960 polygon ~1,000,600 km2), which includes the Sinai (~61,000 km2) occupied by Israel since 1967; low = area actually held on 6 Oct 1973.

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1973 = 35,366k (mid). Low: censuses 1966 (30.1M) and 1976 (36.6M) interpolated = ~34.5M. High: OWID/UN 37,102,044 and World Bank 1973 (37.1M).

activePersonnel.note: Standing conscript and regular forces. COW NMC v7 milper 1973 = 390,000 (mid). Low ~300,000 reflects estimates of the pre-mobilisation regular force (IISS Military Balance 1973-74 order of magnitude, not fetched). High allows the extended service of conscripts held since 1967.

trainedReserves.note: Yom Kippur War infobox: Egypt 650,000 (Rabinovich 2004 p. 54) to 850,000 (Herzog 1975 p. 239) troops after mobilisation; minus ~390,000 standing = 260,000-460,000 reservists. Reservists were called up in batches from 27 Sep (Shazly p. 207). High ~500,000 trained reserve pool.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.03 -> 0.72. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/EGY/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 17.52% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.62 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.62-0.63). Mid 1 - 0.175/0.62 = 0.72. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.62 = 0.63. High: s 0.63 = 0.72. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 62% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. World's largest wheat importer; Nile agriculture feeds most of the rest.

areaKm2.note: The infobox gives 650,000 km2 for 1000 (J.P. Martin 2023, The Mali Empire). The world_1000 Ghana polygon measures 202,000 km2 (low). The page notes that written sources are vague about the extent; oral traditions name Gajaaga, Soso and the Hodh among subject areas.

population.note: No scholarly estimate for Ghana was found. HYDE via OWID (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population): Mali 722,000 (1000) and 776,150 (1100), Mauritania 172,000 and 184,900, Senegal 121,508 and 151,885, about 1.1 million in 1068 for the three modern countries, most of it outside Ghana or in desert; low assumes Ghana held half. High: the Seshat density of the Mali Empire (4-5 million over 1.7-1.9 million km2, as in mali-empire-1330, about 2.5 per km2) x 650,000 km2 = 1.6 million. Mid between.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Koumbi Saleh held 15,000-20,000 by Mauny's estimate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koumbi_Saleh), with Walata and other caravan towns; a rural Sahel population.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. Royal household troops, slave soldiers and the provincial garrisons of the king. al-Bakri (1067/1068): "The king of Ghana, when he calls up his army, can put 200,000 men into the field, more than 40,000 of them archers" (Hopkins trans., Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History, 1981, pp. 78-87, via https://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/history/worldspring09/paperdemo/albakri.html) describes the full levy, not a standing force, and exceeds the plausible population share; it is noted here and not used.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Clan and vassal levies called up for war. The high end is half of al-Bakri's 200,000 and still above the mobilizable mid.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Smiths, herders of the royal horses and caravan staff.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. General levy of free Soninke men and vassal contingents; al-Bakri's call-up of 200,000 would be 12-40% of the population range, beyond any plausible ratio, so it is not used.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. Archers, the arm al-Bakri singles out (40,000 of 200,000, i.e. one in five of the levy).

empire-of-ghana-1068.notes: Snapshot = 1067/1068, the date of al-Bakri's description, under Tunka Manin (king from 1063), after the Almoravids took Awdaghust (1054) and before the disputed 1076 events. Population is the weakest value: no scholarly estimate was found, so it is bracketed by HYDE country totals and the Seshat density of the later Mali Empire (grade D). Every force count is an educated guess; al-Bakri's 200,000 men and 40,000 archers is an informant's report of the full levy and is not used as a count. Border: world_1000 Ghana is the file at or before the year (202,000 km2, the core between the upper Senegal and the Inner Niger Delta); areaKm2 uses the published 650,000 km2. The identification of Koumbi Saleh as the capital is disputed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Empire).

areaKm2.note: The world_1000 England polygon measures 112,547 km2 on the sphere (low); modern England is ~130,000 km2 and the 1066 kingdom held all of it bar Cumbria (mid).

population.note: Darby: the 268,984 Domesday households (1086) indicate 1.2-1.6 million; the Economy of England article gives ~1.5 million in 1086; higher estimates up to ~2.25 million allow for omitted landless and subtenants (Postan). 1066 was probably slightly higher than 1086 (harrying of the North 1069-70).

urbanization.note: About 5.5% of the population lived in urban areas in 1086.

activePersonnel.note: Standing element: royal and earls' housecarls ("as many as 3,000" by the late 11th century; Cnut kept 3,000-4,000) plus royal thegns in attendance.

trainedReserves.note: Select fyrd: "England could furnish about 14,000 men" (one man per five hides). Harold's army at Hastings is put at 5,000-13,000, most agreeing on 7,000-8,000 (Norman Conquest article); Norman chroniclers' 400,000 and 1,200,000 are rejected. Per the feudal-host convention the fyrd is reserve, not standing force.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Butsecarls and crews of royal ships, household officials.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The great fyrd of all free men for local defence on top of the select fyrd.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Housecarls and thegns fighting dismounted in a shield wall with Dane axe, spear and sword (Housecarl article: up to 3,000 royal housecarls).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: mail byrnie, helm, kite shield, Dane axe; but no cavalry arm.

training.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: paid professional household warriors.

training.note: Rubric 0.5.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: defending the homeland, victorious at Stamford Bridge (25 Sept).

england-1066.notes: Snapshot = September 1066, Harold II between the Norwegian landing and Stamford Bridge (25 Sept) and before Hastings (14 Oct). The shares above follow the feudal-host convention: activePersonnel = housecarls and thegns in royal service; the select fyrd (~14,000) is trainedReserves. Modern estimates of Harold's army at Hastings run 5,000-13,000 (most 7,000-8,000), William's 7,000-12,000 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest). Population convention: the kingdom south of the Tweed-Solway line excluding Wales and Cumbria.

areaKm2.note: England and Wales ~151,000 km2 + Gascony ~20,000-30,000 + Calais Pale ~700 + the Irish Pale (mid). The world_1400 "English territory" polygon measures 287,393 km2 because it draws all of Ireland (high).

population.note: England fell from 4-5 million in 1300 by roughly half in the Black Death and later plagues (Economy of England article), giving ~2.0-2.5 million c. 1400; HYDE/OWID UK 1400 = 2.9M including Scotland. Adds Wales (~0.2M) and Gascony (~0.2-0.3M, educated guess).

urbanization.note: Urban share rose to up to 10% by 1377 (Economy of England article).

activePersonnel.note: Paid troops under arms in August 1415: Henry V's indentured expedition of at least 2,300 men-at-arms and 9,000 archers at Harfleur (Curry 2005, p. 70; infobox 11,300), plus Calais garrison (~1,000), Scottish March, Welsh castle and Gascon garrisons (~2,000-5,000, educated guess). These are contract soldiers, the standing force of the moment, not a feudal levy.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Further retinues raised by indenture and county levies under commissions of array; Henry raised ~10,000 again for 1417.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Gunners, miners, carpenters, surgeons and armourers with the expedition and crews of the ~12 royal ships.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Commissions of array could call all able men 16-60, but only a fraction were useful.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Men-at-arms: at least 2,300 with the expedition (Curry) + ~1,000 in garrisons. They rode to battle but fought dismounted at Agincourt.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: full plate harness c. 1415, the era's best.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: veterans of Wales and Scotland in indentured retinues.

count.note: Archers: 9,000 with the expedition (Curry) + ~2,000 in garrisons. About 7,000 longbowmen stood at Agincourt (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: the English longbow massed in the field was the era's best missile weapon.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: trained archers on contract, many veterans.

count.note: Educated guess. Great guns of the Harfleur siege train (Allmand: artillery barrages forced Harfleur's surrender, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England); exact count not found.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: early bombards, among the best siege guns of 1415.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: specialist gunners.

count.note: Educated guess. Royal ships (cogs, carracks, balingers) in 1415, before the build-up to ~30-40 by 1418-20 (Grace Dieu). The 1,500 vessels of the 1415 crossing (Allmand via Henry V article) were hired and impressed merchantmen, counted in merchantTonnage.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75 minus: cogs and carracks.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: Henry V, proven in Wales, won Agincourt against superior numbers by choice of ground and use of archers.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.75 minus: indentured retinues with strong captain loyalty; the Southampton Plot (July 1415) shows noble disaffection.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: motivated, but dysentery at Harfleur sent ~1,330 home (Curry).

weapons.note: Anchor 4 (longbow, crossbow) plus early bombards towards anchor 5.

armor.note: Anchor 4 plus: full white plate harness, beyond the 1250 plate-and-mail anchor.

ships.note: Anchor 4: cogs, carracks and balingers.

fortification.note: Anchor 4: concentric castles, Calais walls, first gunports.

logistics.note: Anchor 4: sea transport across the Channel, purveyance and supply contracts.

communications.note: Anchor 4: royal messengers and written orders.

isr.note: Anchor 4 minus: scouts and spies in France.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 (via OWID): United Kingdom 1400 = 1,717, 1450 = 1,683 (2011 int$). Post-plague real wages were high; Gascony lower (low).

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Wartime: Henry V pawned crown jewels and borrowed to fund the 1415 expedition; low = peacetime crown spending share.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Woollen cloth industry, tin and lead mining.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Post-plague land abundance; pastoral shift.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; medieval age structures were similar (high mortality, young population).

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Roman road network maintained by local obligation.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. London, Southampton, Bristol, Sandwich, Dover, Plymouth, Dartmouth, Hull, King's Lynn, Calais, Bordeaux.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Some 1,500 vessels assembled in the Solent for the 1415 crossing (Allmand, via the Henry V article), many foreign hires; English merchant shipping estimated at tens of thousands of tons.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies with carts and pack animals operated ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses and oxen; the 1415 army alone took up to 20,000 horses (Agincourt article).

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: island position, castles, walled towns and population support.

england-1415.notes: Snapshot = August 1415, Henry V at Harfleur. Unlike the feudal levies of other snapshots, the 1415 army was paid indentured troops, counted as activePersonnel because they were under arms on the snapshot date. Curry (Agincourt: A New History) puts the English at ~9,000 at Agincourt vs 12,000 French; Barker, Sumption and Rogers prefer ~6,000 English (5,000 archers, 900-1,000 men-at-arms) vs 14,000-15,000 French plus up to 10,000 armed valets (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt). Population convention: England, Wales, Calais and Gascony; the Irish lordship counted only for the Pale. Same nationId as england-1066.

activePersonnel.note: Mid 201,750: the long-standing IISS figure, matched by World Bank MS.MIL.TOTL.P1 202,000 (2020). trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Citizens up to age 59 are recallable (CIA Factbook 2025); decades of universal national service give a very large trained pool. IISS gives no figure.

supportPersonnel.note: Active 201,750 minus infantry P roles (15,000 + 160,000) = 26,750: crews, navy, air force, logistics; many conscripts work in national-service economic roles.

mobilizationRatio.note: Regional analogy with near-total mobilization states: universal service 18-40 with recall to 59 (CIA Factbook 2025); in the 1998-2000 war Eritrea fielded ~300,000 of ~3.5 million. Educated judgement.

gdpPerCapita.note: GDP 5,603,494,898 2011 int$ / population 3,607,003 (World Bank 2025) = 1,554. Population estimates for Eritrea are themselves uncertain (no census since independence).

gdp.note: No World Bank PPP GDP for Eritrea. IMF WEO PPP GDP 2019 (last value) 6.369 bn current int$ (https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/api/v1/PPPGDP/ERI) x FRED GDPDEF 2011/2019 = 91.478/103.975 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPDEF) = 5,603,494,898 2011 int$. Range -20%/+25% for growth since 2019 and PPP uncertainty.

milSpendShare.note: Last SIPRI/World Bank value 20.9% of GDP (2003, high; https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/ERI/indicator/MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS?format=json). No figure since; mid is an educated guess for a garrison state with 200,000 under arms.

industrialShare.note: asOf 2009: industry incl. construction (and mining/oil where present) 21.8% of GDP (NV.IND.TOTL.ZS). +/-2 points.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.0 -> 0.08. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/ERI/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 55.48% (2025). Educated guess for s: Eritrea is absent from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets and no current cereal balance was fetchable; s = 0.6 (0.45-0.75) for a chronic cereal deficit (FAO GIEWS reports poor 2026 rains, https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=ERI&lang=en). Mid 1 - 0.555/0.60 = 0.08. Low: a x 1.2, s 0.45 gives below 0, floored at 0.01. High: s 0.75 = 0.26. Low floored at 0.01 (formula below 0): never 0 while agriculture exists. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 60% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Chronic food deficit; cereal yield 638 kg/ha (World Bank 2024). No surplus.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 1,781,275 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share aged 15-19 12.135% / 5 = 43,231. Males only (conscript-pool convention). Range +/-10%.

roadKm.note: Road list (2018): 16,000 km total (high), 1,600 km paved (mid). World Bank IS.ROD.TOTL.KM 4,010 km (2000).

railKm.note: CIA Factbook: 306 km (2018); no World Bank value. Low allows for disused track. Italian-era 950 mm Massawa-Asmara line, mostly heritage use.

majorPorts.note: CIA Factbook 2024: 2 small ports (Massawa, Assab).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. CIA Factbook: 9 ships under the Eritrean flag (2023). (context page: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/factbook/factbook.json/master/africa/er.json)

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Short interior lines; little motor transport.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Camels and donkeys widely used (not from FAO data).

nuclearWarheads.note: Non-nuclear-weapon state (NPT); not listed by FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.3: mountainous escarpment, fortified border lines, harsh climate and total-defence society.

eritrea-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2025 World Bank data (population; no PPP GDP), 2026 order of battle. Eritrea publishes nothing: active strength is the IISS/World Bank ~200,000 with a 2026 IISS figure of 301,750 as quoted (high); equipment is from Wikipedia lists based on old deliveries (grade C/D). Population convention: World Bank figure for everything inside ne:ERI (3.6 million; other estimates run higher; no census). GDP is a composite from IMF 2019 (derived:snapshot-composite). Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Tension with Ethiopia over sea access (2024-26) and Eritrea's role in the Tigray war (2020-22) make it a likely belligerent. People's Militia excluded from active.

eswatini-2026.notes: AUTO-GENERATED BASE SNAPSHOT. Population, economy, personnel and infrastructure from the World Bank (grade A/B). Force mix, ratings and tech copied from researched regional analogues (Republic of Angola, Democratic Republic of the Congo, State of Eritrea, Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Republic of Kenya, Federal Republic of Nigeria, Republic of South Africa, Republic of the Sudan, United Republic of Tanzania, Republic of Uganda) and graded D. Replace with a researched snapshot when one exists.

areaKm2.note: Statesman's Year-Book 1913: 432,432 sq mi = 1.12 million km2 (high), close to the world_1914 Abyssinia polygon (about 1.14 million km2 on the sphere) used as the border. Kaffa (1897), Beni Shangul (1898) and the southern and Ogaden marches were taken or fixed after Adwa, so 1896 lies below that (mid, low: reduction by educated guess). The 1880/1900 basemaps draw only the northern highlands ("Ethiopia", about 277,000 km2, without Shewa or Addis Ababa) and are not used.

population.note: Low: estimated 8 million for the 1913 empire (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1913/Abyssinia). 12,180,600 for 1900 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population_in_1900, footnote not checked). High: OWID Ethiopia 1890 = 17.86M, 1900 = 17.72M (Gapminder v7, modern borders, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population), likely high. Mid 11 million between the contemporary and the list figure. The 1899 Year-Book's 3.5 million covers only the 150,000 sq mi of Abyssinia proper (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia). No census.

urbanization.note: Statesman's Year-Book 1899: almost no towns over 5,000 (Ankober 7,000, Aksum and Gondar 5,000, Adwa 3,000; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia); 1913: Addis Ababa 40,000-50,000 and Harar 50,000 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1913/Abyssinia). Towns of 5,000+ held about 60,000-150,000 people of 8-11 million.

activePersonnel.note: Army mobilized by Menelik's awaj (call to arms) of September 1895 and assembled at Adwa: 73,000-100,000 (McLachlan 2011 p. 20; Ahmad and Pankhurst 1998 pp. 158-62), over 100,000 in the Petrides and Pankhurst breakdown (via Uhlig); mid just above 100,000 to fit the force split below. High: regular army about 150,000 men drawn from provincial contingents (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia). Camp followers, about as many again, are not counted.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: provincial troops and territorial levies not marched north, and the unknown number of armed peasants McLachlan notes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Adwa).

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess: gunners of about 42 guns and the imperial household's armourers; muleteers are camp followers and not counted.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: the awaj called every able-bodied man of the Christian highlands; the 1896 army of 73,000-150,000 was about 1% of 8-11 million people, and the wider levy pool is set at 2-4%, near the Mughal 3% armed-peasantry analogy used for South Asia.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Riflemen of the regional contingents (McLachlan 2011 p. 42, via the article): Shewa 25,000, Semien 3,000, Gojjam 5,000, Harar 15,000, Tigray 12,000, Wollo 6,000, Gondar 8,000, Lasta 6,000 = 80,000 rifles (high); mid deducts the mounted riflemen counted as cavalry.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) minus. Evidence: imported breech-loading rifles of mixed patterns, mostly single-shot, against Italian Vetterli and Carcano rifles; ammunition supply uneven.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: experienced warriors of the provincial retinues, good shots, but no formal drill or regimental training.

count.note: About 20,000 spearmen and swordsmen (McLachlan 2011 p. 42, via the article) (mid); high adds part of the armed peasants of unknown number.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25 or below. Evidence: spears, swords and shields in a rifle war.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: retainers and levies with no drill.

count.note: Horses listed by McLachlan 2011 p. 42: Shewa 3,000, Semien 600, Wollo 5,000 = 8,600 (low); Petrides and Pankhurst (via Uhlig): 8,000 cavalry under Menelik and 5,000 Oromo cavalry under Ras Mikael = 13,000 (high). Both via the article.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: small highland horses, lances and some rifles.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Oromo horsemen under Ras Mikael, effective in the pursuit at Adwa.

count.note: Guns listed by McLachlan 2011 p. 42 (via the article): Shewa 32, Semien 4, Tigray 6 = 42. High allows for guns of contingents whose entries list rifles only.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: imported mountain and field guns, comparable with the Italian mountain batteries at Adwa.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: few trained gunners; artillery a small arm of the army.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Menelik united rival rases, concentrated an army over 1,000 km and let Baratieri attack into prepared positions at Adwa.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5, between a feudal host (0.25) and a national army. Evidence: regional contingents under their own rases, held together by the emperor; the army would melt away once local food ran out (Battle of Adwa article).

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75-1.0. Evidence: defence against invasion; victories at Amba Alagi (December 1895) and Mekelle (January 1896).

weapons.note: Anchor: 6 (1805) to 7 (1905, magazine rifle, QF artillery). Evidence: breech-loading rifles and imported guns, few magazine rifles and machine guns; spears for a fifth of the army.

armor.note: Anchor: 5 (half-armour) to 6 (none). Evidence: hide shields only; no body armour. Set below 6 because shields, not drill and entrenching, were the protection.

ships.note: Anchor: 0. Evidence: landlocked after Italy took Massawa (1885); no navy.

fortification.note: Anchor: 4-5. Evidence: amba hill strongholds and walled Harar; besieged the Italian fort at Mekelle by cutting its water rather than by artillery.

logistics.note: Anchor: 4 (granaries, pack animals). Evidence: army lived off the land with mules and camp followers and had to fight or disperse when local supplies ran out (Battle of Adwa article).

communications.note: Anchor: 5-6. Evidence: runners and mounted couriers; a telegraph line Addis Ababa-Harar existed by 1899 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Statesman%27s_Year-Book_1899/Abyssinia), whether it worked in early 1896 was not checked.

isr.note: Anchor: 5. Evidence: local spies and guides; the Italians marched on Adwa with poor maps and misled by informants.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023: Ethiopia's first value is 1950 = 622 (2011 int$); held back to 1896 on the stagnation assumption, mid about that. High reflects the Sub-Saharan Africa regional average (1870 = 1,286, which SOURCES.md notes overstates the region) scaled down; low near subsistence.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. War-year value (low = peacetime). Soldiers were paid mainly through land grants (gult) and quartering on peasants, so a cash share is not documented.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: crafts (weaving, smithing) only; all rifles and guns were imported.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Plough agriculture of the highlands, weakened by the Great Famine of 1888-92; a concentrated army exhausted a district within weeks.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: In 1913 roads were mostly mere tracks with only a few miles of metalled road in and near the capital; in 1896 there were fewer still.

railKm.note: The Jibuti-Harar line was still a project in 1899 (70 of 186 miles surveyed, 12 miles laid, starting from Jibuti); none in Ethiopia in 1896.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess: no coast; imports came through Italian Massawa, French Obock/Jibuti and British Zeila.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: no merchant shipping.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. The army foraged where it stood; it marched from Shewa to Tigray (about 800 km) by living off successive districts, not on a supply line.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: mules, donkeys, horses and plough oxen of a highland farming country (about 10% of the population); no count found.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2-1.3: mountainous highlands, amba strongholds and population support; long, exposed supply lines for an invader from the coast. Below the full 1.3 row because the highland climate did not defeat the Italians.

ethiopia-1896.notes: Snapshot = February 1896, Menelik's army concentrated at Adwa before the battle of 1 March. Personnel: the mobilized army (riflemen, spearmen, cavalry, gunners) is activePersonnel; territorial levies and armed peasants not marched north are trainedReserves; camp followers are not counted. Force figures from the Battle of Adwa article (McLachlan 2011 regional breakdown, Petrides and Pankhurst). Population is the weakest value (8 to 17.7 million; no census) and the border (world_1914 Abyssinia) postdates the snapshot by 18 years, so area and population include lands annexed 1897-1900. Economy and logistics are educated guesses except roads and railways. Doctrine archetype-feudal-host: provincial contingents of the rases raised by the emperor's call.

milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via World Bank: 0.49% of GDP in 2025. The official figure likely understates wartime spending (Tigray war, Fano/OLA COIN); high 1.5% is an educated allowance.
