The historical-basemaps world_bc100 "Parthia" polygon covers only Parthia proper (473,839 km2 computed on the sphere) and leaves Mesopotamia and Media inside its "Seleucid Kingdom" polygon, so it is not used for the area.

population.note: Seshat codes Parthian Empire I at 5,450,000 for 100 BCE (low) and gives three disputed values for 1 CE: 7,500,000, 15,000,000 and 25,000,000. Mid ~8 million for 53 BCE, after the conquest of Mesopotamia and Media but before later growth; the 25 million figure is treated as an outlier. Everything inside the realm including the vassal kingdoms (Characene, Elymais, Persis, Adiabene, Osroene); Armenia, at war with Parthia in 53, is not counted.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/125) codes the largest settlement at 300,000 for 100 BCE (Seleucia on the Tigris). Mesopotamia was highly urban (Seleucia, Ctesiphon, Babylon), the Iranian plateau and Parthia proper much less.

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. No standing army; this is the force under arms in the 53 BCE campaign season: Surena's ~10,000 horsemen (Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001)), the royal army in Armenia, eastern frontier forces and city garrisons (see forces) + the camel and baggage train (supportPersonnel). Mid = P roles 50,000 + support 4,000, rounded. Convention: noble retinues already called up for the 53 BCE campaign are counted as active (wartime snapshot at campaign start); retinues not called up are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Noble retinues not called up in 53; Justin (41.2, quoted by Wiesehofer p. 137, https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001) gives 50,000 horsemen against Antony in 36 BCE (ancient figure), which bounds what the nobility could field within a season.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Camel drivers, grooms and baggage servants: Surena alone travelled with 1,000 baggage camels (Plutarch Crassus 21, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Crassus*.html) and the camels carrying spare arrows at Carrhae (Crassus 25) needed handlers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. No standing army: the king called up the nobles, who brought retinues of dependants (Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001): "The richer someone is, the more horsemen he provides for the king", Justin 41.2). Justin's 50,000 horsemen against Antony in 36 BCE (ancient figure) would be ~0.6% of an 8 million population; 0.025 allows for a fuller call-up including foot levies.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Surena's 1,000 cataphracts at Carrhae (Plutarch Crassus 21, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Crassus*.html; accepted by Koselenko, Wolski and von Gall as summarised by Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001)) + the cataphracts of the royal army that Orodes II led into Armenia and of other noble retinues (unknown; 1,000-7,000 estimated).

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: fully armoured men and horses with the kontos, "Margianian steel" (Plutarch, quoted by Wiesehofer p. 148), the era's best heavy cavalry.

training.note: Noble warriors trained from childhood (rubric 0.75); no unit drill on the Roman pattern.

count.note: Surena's horse archers: ~9,000 (Wolski) to 10,000 (von Gall) per Wiesehofer, Ancient Persia from 550 BC to 650 AD (2001), pp. 137-138, 147-148 and n. on p. 279-280 (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001), from Plutarch's "no fewer than ten thousand" horsemen, vassals and slaves (Crassus 21, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Crassus*.html) + mounted archers of the royal army in Armenia (Plutarch: Orodes attacked Armenia "with an overwhelming force", Crassus 22; size unknown, 5,000-30,000 estimated) + eastern frontier and satrapal horse (1,000-10,000 estimated).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: powerful composite bows and an arrow resupply by camel train at Carrhae (Plutarch Crassus 25), which made the horse archers decisive.

training.note: Dependants trained in riding and archery from childhood (Justin 41.2, quoted by Wiesehofer p. 137); not drilled as units.

count.note: Educated guess. Foot levies with javelins and spears of the royal army and vassal kings; Wiesehofer (https://archive.org/details/AncientPersiaFrom550BcTo650Ad2001, p. 148) calls infantry "of secondary importance" and cites only the Chronicle of Arbela's 20,000 foot against the Alans in 136 CE.

quality.note: Lightly equipped levies (rubric 0.25-0.5).

training.note: Levies (rubric 0.25).

count.note: Educated guess. Foot archers and slingers of the levies and of the hill peoples (Elymaeans, Mardians); no figure survives.

quality.note: Composite bows, unarmoured (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Levies and hill tribes.

count.note: Educated guess. Garrisons and militias of the Greek cities (Seleucia, Babylon, Susa) and mercenaries of the king; close-order infantry played almost no role in Parthian field armies.

quality.note: Hellenistic-style equipment, era-typical.

training.note: City militia and mercenaries.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75 for Surena (proven commander: the camel arrow resupply and combined cataphract/horse-archer tactics at Carrhae) but no staff system and royal distrust (Orodes executed Surena soon after); mid 0.7.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: feudal host of noble retinues (Wiesehofer p. 137: pelatai and douloi of the aristocracy); retainers loyal to their lord rather than the king, dynastic strife frequent.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: defending Mesopotamia against invasion, confident in cavalry superiority over Roman infantry in open country.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (iron weapons) with powerful composite bows and the kontos; no torsion artillery in field use.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail) plus full horse armour of the cataphracts, anticipating anchor 4 barding; horse archers unarmoured.

ships.note: No navy. Anchor 1-2: river craft on the Tigris and Euphrates; Gulf shipping belonged to the vassal kingdom of Characene.

fortification.note: Anchor 2-3: mudbrick and Hellenistic city walls (Seleucia, Nisa); the Parthians rarely conducted or resisted formal sieges.

logistics.note: Anchor 2-3: camel and pack-horse trains (Surena's 1,000 camels), living off grazing; the Achaemenid depot system was not maintained.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): royal roads with stations (stathmoi) listed by Isidore of Charax.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts and guides (the Arab chief Ariamnes misled Crassus, Plutarch Crassus 21).

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE values for Iran and Iraq are 1,116 (2011 int$), Turkey 897. Applied to Parthian Mesopotamia and Iran with a slightly lower mid for the pastoral north-east.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Military service was owed by the nobility and their dependants in return for land, so little of the military burden passed through a royal treasury; share of output devoted to horses, arms and retinues estimated.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian and pastoral economy; crafts and caravan trade (Silk Road via Merv and Seleucia).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated Mesopotamian agriculture produced large surpluses; the plateau and the north-east much less.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Royal roads inherited from the Achaemenids and Seleucids: the Zeugma-Seleucia-Ecbatana-Merv-Arachosia route described by Isidore of Charax ran several thousand km; no engineered network on the Roman pattern.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Charax Spasinou and the river ports of Seleucia/Ctesiphon; no war fleet to supply.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gulf and river shipping of the Characene and Mesopotamian merchants; no source gives a tonnage.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Cavalry armies living off grazing with camel trains could operate further from depots than infantry (Engels, isbn:0520042727, ch. 1 for the infantry baseline of 1-2 weeks); desert stretches limited them.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.08-0.2 horses, camels, mules and donkeys per inhabitant x population (horse-breeding aristocracy, Nisaean horses of Media, camels of Mesopotamia).

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.3 elements: deep strategic depth and a hot, dry climate the Roman infantry was not adapted to (Plutarch Crassus 22 on the waterless desert march), plus local supply and population support; few fortified cities, hence mid 1.25.

parthia--53.notes: Snapshot = spring-summer 53 BCE, Crassus' invasion: Orodes II split his forces, invading Armenia himself while Surena met Crassus at Carrhae with ~10,000 horse. Border: historical-basemaps world_bc100 (latest file at or before -53) has only Parthia proper as "Parthia" (473,839 km2) and still shows Mesopotamia and Media as "Seleucid Kingdom"; world_bc1 ("Parthian Empire", ~1.93 million km2) is closer to the real 53 BCE extent but post-dates it. areaKm2 is researched (Seshat). All force numbers are reconstructions: Plutarch's figures for Surena are accepted by modern scholars (Wolski, Koselenko, von Gall as summarised by Wiesehofer), but nothing is known about the size of the royal army in Armenia or the eastern forces, so the total active strength is an educated guess. Sheldon (Rome's Wars in Parthia, 2010) and Overtoom (Reign of Arrows, 2020) were not fetched. Population convention: inside the real 53 BCE realm incl. vassal kingdoms; Armenia excluded.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 3.8-4.325 million km2 for 450-331 BCE (low, mid). The historical-basemaps world_bc400 polygon measures 6.02 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, high); it includes Egypt and the nominal Indus and Central Asian satrapies.

population.note: Seshat codes 20-26 million for 500 BCE and 17-35 million for 400 BCE (range used). Egypt, in revolt 404-343, was reconquered by Artaxerxes III and is counted. Everything inside the imperial border, including Egypt, Babylonia, Anatolia, Bactria and the eastern satrapies.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/107) codes the largest settlement at 200,000 (Babylon) for 550-331 BCE. Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Levant and western Anatolia urbanised; the Iranian plateau and Central Asia much less. Same as persia-achaemenid--480.

activePersonnel.note: Field forces of 334-333 (57,000 / 110,000 / 200,000, see forces) + fleet crews (60,000 / 70,000 / 80,000, see supportPersonnel) + garrisons left across the empire (40,000 / 60,000 / 100,000; educated guess: satrapal guards, citadels such as Sardis, Babylon, Memphis, Elephantine, and the eastern satrapies that sent troops only for Gaugamela). Convention: satrapal contingents already assembled for the 334-333 campaigns, garrisons and fleet crews are counted as active; eastern levies that joined only in 331 are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Iranian and eastern cavalry and levies (Bactrians, Saka, Arachosians) that reached the royal army only in 331 for Gaugamela; reachable within ~30 days only from the western satrapies.

supportPersonnel.note: Fleet crews: 300 / 350 / 400 warships (see ships_major) x ~200 men (oarsmen, deck crew, marines). Excludes transports, the royal baggage train and court.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Agrarian empire levying satrapal contingents and military colonists; the 334-333 field forces plus fleet were already ~0.7% of the population. Same convention as persia-achaemenid--480.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Line infantry = Greek mercenary hoplites (Arrian: ~20,000 at the Granicus, 30,000 at Issus; modern estimates mostly 10,000-20,000 in total) + kardakes and Persian spearmen including the 1,000 apple-bearer guards (Arrian 2.8.6 gives 60,000 kardakes, rejected). Mid 20,000 mercenaries + 20,000 Iranian line infantry.

quality.note: Greek mercenary hoplite panoply era-typical (0.5) to good; kardakes lighter. No sarissa phalanx.

training.note: Greek mercenaries professional (0.75); kardakes semi-trained young Persians (0.5).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Archers and slingers of the satrapal and royal levies ~27% of the field force.

quality.note: Composite bows and wicker shields, little armour; era-typical missile troops but outranged by nothing and outclassed in close combat (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Mostly satrapal levies (rubric 0.25-0.5).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Javelinmen and hill levies (Arrian 2.8.5: 20,000 light-armed sent across the Pinarus) ~14%.

quality.note: Light, often traditional equipment (rubric 0.25).

training.note: Levies (rubric 0.25).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Armoured Iranian noble and royal kinsmen cavalry, Bactrian and Hyrcanian heavy horse; the Persian army's main arm (Arrian: ~20,000 horse at the Granicus, 30,000 at Issus) ~40% of the cavalry.

quality.note: Scale-armoured riders with javelins and short spears, horse armour for some (Xenophon's cavalry ideal); good but outmatched by the Companions' xyston in close combat.

training.note: Aristocratic riders trained from youth (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Light horse and mounted archers (Saka, Dahae, Medes, satrapal horse) ~60% of the cavalry.

quality.note: Mounted archers and javelinmen, era-typical (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Iranian and steppe riders raised in the saddle.

count.note: Educated guess. Scythed chariots were part of the royal army (200 at Gaugamela 331 per Arrian 3.8.6, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_III/Chapter_VIII, ancient); none at the Granicus or Issus. Number on hand in 334 unknown.

quality.note: Scythed chariots were defeated by opening lanes at Gaugamela; below era-typical.

training.note: Royal crews; little combat record.

count.note: Arrian 1.18.5 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XVIII) gives about 400 Persian ships at Miletus in summer 334 against Nicanor's 160 (ancient figure, high). Mid 350 allows for undermanned or detached ships; Phoenician, Cypriot and Cilician triremes with some larger polyremes. Disintegrated in 333-332 when Alexander took the Phoenician bases.

quality.note: Phoenician and Cypriot ships among the era's best (rubric 0.75); Arrian 1.18 has Alexander refuse battle with the "disciplined fleet of the Cyprians and Phoenicians".

training.note: Professional Phoenician and Cypriot seafarers; Memnon an able commander.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: divided satrapal command at the Granicus (Memnon's scorched-earth advice rejected), Darius III an average-to-poor field commander; strong staff for musters and logistics. Memnon competent at sea.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: multi-ethnic host plus mercenaries; core Persian guard and cavalry better.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5 average; the empire had just suppressed Egypt (343) but faced court turmoil (Bagoas, accession of Darius III in 336).

weapons.note: Close to anchor 3 (300 BCE: iron weapons, torsion artillery): iron weapons general, Greek mercenary hoplites; torsion artillery used defensively at Halicarnassus but no sarissa.

armor.note: Anchor 2-3: scale and linen armour for elites and mercenaries, many levies unarmoured.

ships.note: Anchor 3: triremes plus early quadriremes and quinqueremes in the Phoenician and Cypriot squadrons.

fortification.note: Anchor 3: ashlar city walls (Tyre, Halicarnassus, Babylon) able to resist Macedonian siege towers for months.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 plus: Royal Road and depot system documented in the Persepolis Fortification tablets (Briant, isbn:1575060310, ch. 9); huge treasuries. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.1 -> 2.97, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -334 (2.969); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

communications.note: Anchor 3: mounted relay posts (angareion) on the royal roads. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.1 -> 2.97, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -334 (2.969); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts and spies; before Issus the two armies passed each other on opposite sides of the Amanus without either detecting the other (Livius, https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/).

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE values for Iran, Iraq, Egypt, Israel and Jordan are 1,116, Turkey 897 (2011 int$). Applied to the empire three centuries earlier with a wider range; Central Asian and plateau satrapies were poorer than Mesopotamia and Egypt. Same convention as persia-achaemenid--480.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Most service still paid in land grants (hatru) and satrapal levies, but mercenary armies were paid in coin; Alexander later found ~120,000 talents at Persepolis (Diodorus 17.71, ancient), showing that much revenue was hoarded rather than spent.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian empire with craft centres in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Phoenicia and Lydia.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated Mesopotamian and Egyptian agriculture produced large surpluses stored in royal granaries.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Sardis-Susa Royal Road ~2,500 km (Herodotus 5.52-53) is the low bound; the Persepolis tablets attest further royal routes to Persepolis, Ecbatana, Bactra, Arachosia and Egypt (Briant, isbn:1575060310, ch. 9). Same as persia-achaemenid--480.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Phoenicia (Sidon, Tyre, Arwad, Byblos), Cyprus (Salamis), Cilicia, Egypt, Ionia and Caria; count of ports able to supply a fleet is an estimate by analogy with persia-achaemenid--480.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Phoenician and Egyptian merchant shipping; same order as persia-achaemenid--480.

supplyRangeKm.note: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander, ch. 9: Persian armies moved along royal roads with pre-stocked depots and a huge baggage train (Darius left his at Damascus before Issus); away from roads and depots the range was short. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.07 / 0.09 / 0.11 draft and pack animals (incl. camels) per inhabitant x population.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2 (local supply, fortified cities); deep strategic depth and desert climate argue for 1.3, weak loyalty of subject peoples (Egypt welcomed Alexander) for less.

persia-achaemenid--334.notes: Snapshot = spring 334 BCE, Alexander crossing the Hellespont. Forces are the field forces the empire put into the field in 334-333 (the Granicus satrapal army and the royal army mustered for Issus), not a single simultaneous order of battle; garrisons are in activePersonnel only. Arrian's figures (600,000 at Issus, 1,040,000 at Gaugamela, 400 ships) are cited in notes but not used as mid values except the ship count, which modern historians broadly accept. The 15 Indian elephants at Gaugamela (Arrian 3.8.6) arrived only in 331 and are not counted. Population convention: everything inside the bc400 polygon, Seshat range; Egypt (reconquered 343) included.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 4.8-5.5 million km2 for 500-451 BCE. The historical-basemaps world_bc500 polygon measures 5.95 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, high).

population.note: Seshat codes 20-26 million for 500 BCE (mid = 23 million) and 17-35 million for 400 BCE (range). Everything inside the 480 BCE imperial border incl. Egypt, Babylonia, Ionia, Bactria and the Indus satrapy.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat codes the largest settlement at 200,000 (Babylon). Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Levant and Ionia were urbanised; the Iranian plateau and Central Asia much less. Scaled below the Roman 10-25% (Hanson & Ortman 2017).

activePersonnel.note: Invasion land army (80,000 / 152,000 / 300,000) + fleet crews (102,000 / 150,000 / 241,000, see supportPersonnel) + garrisons across the empire left behind (40,000 / 60,000 / 100,000; educated guess: Elephantine, Babylon, Sardis, satrapal guards). Garrisons are not broken down by role in `forces`.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: Iranian and satrapal cavalry and levies reachable within ~30 days; the empire's distances make most levies slower than that.

supportPersonnel.note: Fleet crews: triremes (600 / 750 / 1,207) x ~170-200 men (oarsmen, deck crew, the ~30 marines per ship that Herodotus mentions). Excludes the transport crews.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess for an agrarian empire levying satrapal contingents (hatru land-for-service system): the 480 expedition plus fleet (~300,000 men) was already ~1.3% of the population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Land army of the 480 invasion: low 80,000 (Shahbazi 2012, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 129: 80,000-100,000 or fewer), mid 150,000, high 300,000 (Munro and Macan, from six marshals and 29 myriarchs). Herodotus 7.60-99 gives 1,700,000 infantry and 80,000 cavalry (rejected). Split by role on the composition in Herodotus' muster list (Iranian archer infantry dominant): Iranian and Saka archer infantry incl. the 10,000 Immortals (Herodotus 7.83) ~46%. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.15 -> 0.7. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/PER/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 23.13% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.78 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.77-0.79). Mid 1 - 0.231/0.78 = 0.7. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.77 = 0.61. High: s 0.79 = 0.71. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 78% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Exports fruit/vegetables (avocados, blueberries, asparagus) and fishmeal but imports cereals; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/PHL/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 20.5% (2025). s proxied by the rice self-sufficiency ratio 0.77 (2022, PSA via https://businessmirror.com.ph/2023/10/10/rice-sufficiency-level-falls-to-24-year-low/), rice being the main calorie source. Mid 1 - 0.205/0.77 = 0.73. Low: a x 1.3 (larger rural households), s 0.72 = 0.63. High: s 0.815 (2021) = 0.75. Import dependence: world's largest rice importer; wheat fully imported. Audit follow-up 2026-10-29: 0.0 -> 0.73, rule changed: value is the share of production not eaten by the farm population, import dependence goes in the note.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.25 -> 0.94. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/POL/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 6.22% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 1.13 (mean 2021-2023, range 1.09-1.17). Mid 1 - 0.062/1.13 = 0.94. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 1.09 = 0.93. High: s 1.17 = 0.95. Net exporter: production is about 113% of domestic calorie supply. foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.1 -> 0.94. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/PRT/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 2.78% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.44 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.42-0.45). Mid 1 - 0.028/0.44 = 0.94. Low: a x 1.5 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.42 = 0.9. High: s 0.45 = 0.94. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 44% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Net food importer (cereals), exporter of wine, fish products.

prussia-1866.notes: Snapshot = Kingdom of Prussia in mid-June 1866 after mobilisation. Territory and population = Prussia plus Schleswig under Prussian administration; North German allies and Italy (200,000) excluded; includes is empty. Personnel: line army incl. recalled reservists = active (the mobilisation was complete by the snapshot date); Landwehr and Ersatz = trainedReserves. Strengths from the Austro-Prussian War page (Clodfelter 2017 p. 182: 437,262) and the Koeniggraetz page (220,984 at the battle); branch split is a reconstruction (grade C).

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 1,000,000 km2 for 305-217 BCE (polity 109, high) and 833,000 km2 for 200 BCE (polity 207, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/207), after Coele-Syria was lost. The historical-basemaps world_bc300 polygon measures 549,000 km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, low): it covers Egypt and Cyrenaica only and misses Coele-Syria, Cyprus and the Aegean and Anatolian holdings.

population.note: Seshat codes Ptolemaic Egypt at 4,000,000 for 217-151 BCE (polity 207) and 7,000,000 for 305-217 BCE (polity 109, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/109, high). Fischer-Bovet (isbn:9781107007758, ch. 3) works with ~4 million for Egypt, reporting Rathbone (under 3 to almost 4 million in the 3rd century) and Manning (3.5-4.5 million). Mid 4.5 million = Egypt ~4 million + Cyrenaica, Cyprus and the Aegean and Anatolian possessions (~0.5 million, educated guess). Coele-Syria, occupied by Antiochus in 218-217, not counted.

urbanization.note: Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/207) codes Alexandria at 300,000 for 217-150 BCE, alone ~7% of a 4.5 million population; Memphis, Ptolemais, Cyrene, Salamis and the nome capitals add an estimated 3-9% (educated guess).

activePersonnel.note: Raphia field army (62,800 / 75,000 / 84,500, see forces) + navy crews, mahouts and staff (10,000 / 20,000 / 35,000, see supportPersonnel) + garrisons in Egypt, Cyprus, Cyrenaica and the Aegean (10,000 / 17,000 / 25,000; Fischer-Bovet's wartime land army of 89,000-94,000 (https://www.worldhistory.org/Ptolemaic_Army/) less the ~75,000 at Raphia). Convention: cleruchs and the newly armed Egyptian machimoi were already called up for Raphia and are counted as active; the few not called up are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Fischer-Bovet (https://www.worldhistory.org/Ptolemaic_Army/) gives 50,000-55,000 in peacetime and 89,000-94,000 in wartime: in 217 nearly all cleruchs and the newly armed machimoi were already called up, leaving few reserves.

supportPersonnel.note: Navy: decked warships (30 / 60 / 120) x ~250 + light craft x ~50; + ~2 mahouts and attendants per elephant; + ~2,000 staff, engineers and supply officials. Transport crews (400+ transports in 218, Polybius 5.68) not counted.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The Raphia mobilisation (land army 89,000-94,000 per Fischer-Bovet) was ~2% of the population, achieved only by arming 20,000 native Egyptians; total-war ratio slightly above that.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Polybius 5.65 and 5.79 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/5*.html): Ptolemy marched from Alexandria with 70,000 foot, 5,000 horse and 73 elephants; composition: royal guard 3,000, peltasts 2,000, Macedonian-style phalanx 25,000, Greek mercenaries 8,000, guard cavalry 700 + Libyan and native horse (~3,000 together), Greek and mercenary cavalry (~2,000), Cretans 3,000, Libyans in Macedonian arms 3,000, native Egyptian heavy infantry ~20,000, Thracians and Gauls 6,000. Fischer-Bovet (isbn:9781107007758; summarised at https://www.worldhistory.org/Ptolemaic_Army/) accepts the Raphia army at ~70,000 including 11,000 mercenaries and 20,000 machimoi, and puts the wartime land army at 89,000-94,000. Line infantry = phalanx 25,000 + native Egyptian phalanx 20,000 + royal guard 3,000 + Greek mercenaries 8,000 + Libyans 3,000 + Thracians and Gauls 6,000 = 65,000. Low allows for Polybius' totals being paper strength. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

Further squadrons held Cyprus, Thera and the Aegean bases; Ptolemy II's mid-century navy of over 300 warships (Athenaeus 5.203d, ancient) had declined. Includes polyremes; Ptolemy IV's showpiece "forty" (Athenaeus 5.203e) not a combat unit.

fortification.note: Anchor 3: walled Alexandria and Pelusium; Pelusium plus deliberate flooding of the Delta (Polybius 5.62) held off Antiochus in 218.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 plus Nile transport, royal granaries and a dense bureaucracy; the 400 transports of 218 (Polybius 5.68) supplied the Syrian front by sea.

communications.note: Anchor 3: royal postal relay along the Nile (papyri), mounted couriers.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts, spies; Sosibius hid the Alexandrian preparations from Antiochus' envoys (Polybius 5.66).

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Fischer-Bovet (https://www.worldhistory.org/Ptolemaic_Army/) estimates army and navy at 4,500-5,700 talents, 34% of the royal budget in peacetime; with royal revenue at an assumed 12-25% of output, defence was ~4-9% of GDP. Wartime 217 higher.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy with large royal textile, papyrus and oil monopolies and Alexandrian crafts; somewhat above other Hellenistic kingdoms.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Nile-irrigated agriculture; Egypt was the largest grain exporter of the eastern Mediterranean.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Transport ran on the Nile and canals; desert roads to the Red Sea ports (Berenice, Myos Hormos) and the coastal road through Sinai.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Alexandria, Pelusium, Salamis and Paphos (Cyprus), Berenice on the Red Sea, Ephesus and Aegean bases; analogy with persia-achaemenid--480 port counting.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. More than 400 transports supported the 218 campaign (Polybius 5.68.4) at an assumed ~50-100 t each, plus the Alexandrian grain and trade fleet.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): one to two weeks' march from depots; the Sinai crossing to Raphia (Pelusium to Raphia in five days, Polybius 5.80) relied on pre-positioned water and sea supply.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.05 / 0.07 / 0.1 draft and pack animals (oxen, donkeys, camels, horses) per inhabitant x population; river transport reduced the need.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2 plus: the Sinai desert, Pelusium and floodable Delta (Polybius 5.62) protect the core; 1.3 not reached since the population was not loyal (Great Revolt 206).

ptolemaic-egypt--217.notes: Snapshot = spring 217 BCE, the Raphia campaign. Forces are Ptolemy IV's field army as listed by Polybius (5.65, 5.79), accepted by Fischer-Bovet; garrisons only in activePersonnel. The border polygon (bc300) covers Egypt and Cyrenaica only; Cyprus, the Aegean and Anatolian holdings and Coele-Syria (contested, partly occupied by Antiochus III in 218) are outside it. Population convention: Egypt plus Cyrenaica, Cyprus and the overseas possessions; Coele-Syria not counted. Fleet size and native population are the weakest numbers.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.0 -> 0.65. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/QAT/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 1.62% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.05 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.04-0.05). Mid 1 - 0.016/0.05 = 0.65. Low: a x 1.5 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.04 = 0.38. High: s 0.05 = 0.68. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 5% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Imports ~90% of food despite post-2017 dairy self-sufficiency push.

The union of the world_bc300 Qin and Zhou states polygons (the states Qin had conquered by 221) measures 2.47 million km2 on the sphere (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_bc300.geojson).

population.note: Seshat codes 40 million for 207 BCE (mid). The first census (2 CE, Han) counted 57.7M (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty) after two centuries of growth; the unification wars killed and displaced many, so the low end is well below. No Qin census survives.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Xianyang ~200,000-350,000 (Seshat 250); Linzi, Handan and Ying were large cities; >90% rural (Lewis 2010 p. 102).

activePersonnel.note: Field army of 600,000 (Wang Jian against Chu 224-223, and Wang Ben's 600,000 in 225, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin%27s_wars_of_unification) + ~100,000 garrisons in the conquered states = 700,000. Shiji figures repeated by modern narratives; in 214 BCE ~100,000 held the north and 500,000 went south (Morton 1995 p. 47, on the Qin dynasty page); Meng Tian led 300,000 against the Xiongnu (215). Chronicle-derived; modern scholars (Lewis) accept armies of hundreds of thousands under universal service. Mid 700,000 for the armies still mobilised at unification; grade C.

qin--221.notes: Snapshot at unification, 221 BCE, when the conquest armies were still mobilised. Army sizes come from the Shiji as repeated in modern narratives (Morton, Bodde); they are chronicle claims and the grade stays C. The 1,200,000 vs 1,500,000 strengths in the Wikipedia infobox are uncited and not used. Border: the union of world_bc300 Qin and Zhou states, i.e. the lands Qin had conquered; it omits the later southern (Baiyue) conquests of 214. Population convention: everything inside that border. GDP per capita is a regional analogy (grade D). Personnel: active = conscripts actually under arms in the conquest armies and garrisons at unification; trainedReserves = registered men who had served and were demobilised; mobilizable = population x ratio.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 13.1 million km2 for the Early Qing (1644-1796). High = the ~14.7 million km2 peak usually quoted for c. 1790; low allows for loosely held Tibet and Mongolia. The world_1715 union (Manchu Empire + Tibet, protectorate from 1720) lacks Dzungaria and the Tarim basin, conquered 1755-59, which sit in the "central Asian khanates" polygon.

qing-1760.notes: Snapshot = 1760, Qianlong after the conquest of Dzungaria and Altishahr (1755-59) and before the Burma war (1765-69). Personnel convention: the salaried Eight Banners (>200,000) and Green Standard Army (600,067) are activePersonnel; Mongol jasagh levies, tusi native troops and banner supernumeraries are trainedReserves. The split of the 800,000 into roles is an educated reading of the banner/Green Standard structure (Elliott, The Manchu Way, 2001; Waley-Cohen, The Culture of War in China, 2006), neither consulted directly. Border: nearest file containing the polity is world_1715; it lacks Xinjiang. Population convention: China proper, Manchuria, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang; vassals (Korea, Vietnam, Burma later) excluded.

areaKm2.note: world_1880 polygon "Manchu Empire" = 11.01M km2 on the sphere; Qing claims incl. Mongolia, Tibet, Xinjiang and Taiwan ~11.4M km2.

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1894 = 421,000k; HYDE/Gapminder (OWID) China 1894 = 384M (modern borders). Qing figures are uncertain.

activePersonnel.note: First Sino-Japanese War page, table of Qing army size by source (Olender 2014 p. 89): actual totals 375,000 (Gawlikowski) to 998,500-1,255,000; Olender 1,070,000-1,220,000; Green Standard 450,000-600,000 actual, Bannermen ~100,000 actual of 250,000. Japanese General Staff expected no more than 350,000 effectives. COW milper 1894 = 1,000,000.

trainedReserves.note: Provincial militia (tuanlian): Olender gives at most 300,000 (page table).

supportPersonnel.note: Artillery and fortress gunners ~30,000, navies ~15,000, arsenals and transport. Reconstruction.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: the Qing state could not raise more than a few million men in total; effective modern forces stayed in the hundreds of thousands. audit 2026-10-30: kept at 0.006 (2.4M): the cited page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Sino-Japanese_War) gives 1.07-1.22M under arms plus at most 300,000 militia, so the ceiling is 1.6-2x the forces actually raised; no fetched source supports the 0.02-0.03 (8-12M) an era-median comparison suggests.

republic-of-the-congo-2026.notes: AUTO-GENERATED BASE SNAPSHOT. Population, economy, personnel and infrastructure from the World Bank (grade A/B). Force mix, ratings and tech copied from researched regional analogues (Republic of Angola, Democratic Republic of the Congo, State of Eritrea, Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Republic of Kenya, Federal Republic of Nigeria, Republic of South Africa, Republic of the Sudan, United Republic of Tanzania, Republic of Uganda) and graded D. Replace with a researched snapshot when one exists.

areaKm2.note: Peninsular Italy south of the Arno-Rubicon line ~130,000 km2 (the low bound Seshat codes for 264 BCE, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/183) + Sicily outside Hiero's kingdom ~20,000 + Sardinia 24,100 and Corsica 8,700 (modern island areas) = ~183,000; high adds the ager Gallicus and the Cisalpine land conquered in 225-222. The historical-basemaps world_bc300 polygon (37,893 km2, Latium and Campania only) badly understates the 218 extent and is used for the map only.

population.note: Seshat codes the Middle Republic at 3.5-4.0 million for 264-133 BCE (low). De Ligt (Peasants, Citizens and Soldiers, 2012, as reviewed at https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/?p=37690) reads the Polybian manpower list of 225 (Polybius 2.24, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/2*.html) as 4.2 million for Italy; Brunt (isbn:0198142838, ch. 5) has ~3 million free in peninsular Italy plus slaves. Added: the provinces of Sicily (outside Hiero's kingdom) and Sardinia-Corsica, ~0.3-0.6 million (educated guess). Covers Rome, the Latin colonies and the Italian allies south of the Apennines; Cisalpine Gaul (in revolt in 218) and Syracuse are not counted.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/183) codes Rome at 210,000 in 200 BCE; Capua, Tarentum, Neapolis, Syracuse (outside) and the Latin colonies were the other towns of 5,000+. ~0.5 million urban of ~4.5 million.

activePersonnel.note: Field armies of 218 (70,200 per Livy 21.17) + fleet crews (supportPersonnel, ~66,000) + garrisons in Sicily, Sardinia and Tarentum (0-15,000, estimate; Polybius 2.24.13 records two legions of 4,200 in Sicily and Tarentum in 225). Livy 21.17 (https://archive.org/stream/livybook2125seco00livy/livybook2125seco00livy_djvu.txt): six legions voted for 218, 24,000 Roman infantry and 1,800 cavalry, 40,000 allied infantry and 4,400 allied cavalry; Sempronius 2 legions + 16,000 allied foot + 1,800 allied horse, Scipio 2 legions + 14,000 + 1,600, the praetor Manlius in Gaul 2 legions + 10,000 allied foot + 1,000 allied and 600 Roman horse. Brunt, Italian Manpower (isbn:0198142838, Appendix 26, legions by year) and Lazenby (isbn:0806130040, ch. 3) accept six legions for 218. Convention: the six legions and allied contingents levied for 218 are under arms at the snapshot date and counted as active; men on the census rolls who must still be levied are in trainedReserves. audit 2026-10-30: grade B -> C: rests on an ancient chronicler's figure (SOURCES.md: at most C), accepted by modern historians.

trainedReserves.note: Polybius 2.24 lists 250,000 Roman and Campanian foot and 23,000 horse and ~450,000 allied men on the rolls of 225 (ancient figures; Brunt, isbn:0198142838, ch. 4, accepts their order of magnitude). Many had served in the Gallic war of 225-222. Callable within ~30 days: Rome raised 8 legions for Cannae (216); range is an estimate of men already trained.

roman-republic--218.notes: Snapshot = spring 218 BCE, the outbreak of the Second Punic War; forces are the six legions and allied contingents voted for 218 (Livy 21.17) and the 220-quinquereme fleet. Population convention: Rome, the Latin colonies and the Italian allies (socii) south of the Apennines, plus the provinces of Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica; Hiero's Syracuse (an ally), Massalia and Cisalpine Gaul are not counted (includes = []). Polybius 2.24's manpower list of 225 (700,000 foot and 70,000 horse able to bear arms) is used only for reserves; the population debate (Brunt's low count vs high counts) is reflected in the range. Border uses historical-basemaps world_bc300 (nearest file at or before 218), whose Roman Republic polygon shows only Latium and Campania (37,893 km2): the map polygon understates the 218 extent by about a factor of five; areaKm2 is researched separately. audit 2026-10-30: border left at hb:bc300:Roman Republic (37,893 km2, Latium and Campania): the nearer hb:bc200:Rome (~518,000 km2) adds eastern Spain, Cisalpine Gaul and the Po valley, Carthaginian or Gallic in 218, so it is not better; neither matches the ~190,000 km2 area.

Range +/-10% for PPP benchmark uncertainty and the relative-price drift the rebase ignores.
