milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS: 2.28% of GDP in 2025 (mid), 2.17% in 2024, 1.86% in 2021. Low is the lowest of those years; high allows ~5% for NATO-definition spending above SIPRI.

industrialShare.note: asOf 2025: industry incl. construction 25.3% of GDP (NV.IND.TOTL.ZS). Range +/-1.5 pp for year-to-year variation.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.25 -> 0.92. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/ROU/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 10.95% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 1.42 (mean 2021-2023, range 1.22-1.64). Mid 1 - 0.109/1.42 = 0.92. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 1.22 = 0.88. High: s 1.64 = 0.93. Net exporter: production is about 142% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Large grain exporter.

annualCohort.note: asOf 2025. Males reaching military age per year = male population 9,211,812 (SP.POP.TOTL.MA.IN) x share of males aged 15-19 6.095% (SP.POP.1519.MA.5Y) / 5 = 112,295. Males only (conscript-pool convention); about double if women are counted. Range +/-10%.

ifv_apc.note: Educated guess. Moreni plant assembles Piranha V; Lynx deal planned.

roadKm.note: As quoted: 86,847 km of which 65,315 paved (2026 row).

railKm.note: asOf 2021: 10,769 route-km (IS.RRS.TOTL.KM). Low allows for closures since.

majorPorts.note: CIA Factbook 2024: 0 large + 2 medium (Constanta is the largest Black Sea port).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Not in the quoted UNCTAD table; CIA Factbook lists 127 Romanian-flag vessels (2023), mostly small. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_merchant_navy_capacity_by_country)

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. By analogy to NATO mechanized brigade sustainment (truck-based, depots every ~150-200 km).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Horses, mules and donkeys, not from FAO data. Militarily irrelevant in 2026.

nuclearWarheads.note: Non-nuclear-weapon state (NPT); FAS Status of World Nuclear Forces 2026 lists only nine nuclear-armed states. FAS lists the five US B61 host states (Belgium, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Turkey); this state is not one of them.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: Carpathian arc, familiar terrain, population support.

romania-2026.notes: Modern snapshot, asOf 2025 World Bank data with an Oct 2026 order of battle. Population convention: everything inside ne:ROU. Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011. Force counts from the Wikipedia Romanian Land Forces equipment list, active Romanian military aircraft list and naval forces article; drones = Group 2+ only. Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Personnel figures disagree (70,000-90,000).

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes the late Republic at 1.95-3.5 million km2 (133-31 BCE) and the Principate (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/70) at 4.5 million km2 in 1 CE. The 27 BCE empire already held Egypt, all Gaul and Syria but not yet Galatia (25 BCE), Raetia/Noricum (15 BCE) or Moesia; mid 3.4 million. The border polygons used (historical-basemaps world_bc100: two "Roman Republic" polygons 1,059,280 + 164,959 km2 plus "Ptolemaic Kingdom" 607,216 km2, computed on the sphere) total only ~1.83 million km2: they miss Gallia Comata, Syria and parts of Anatolia, so they are not used as the low bound.

population.note: Seshat codes the Principate at 50 million for 1 CE (high) and the late Republic (polity 184, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/184) at 25-35 million for 133-31 BCE, i.e. before Egypt (30 BCE) and before the Gallic provinces were fully counted. Frier 2000 (Cambridge Ancient History XI, isbn:0521263352, p. 814 table 6) gives 45.5 million for 14 CE; the 27 BCE empire lacked Raetia, Noricum, Moesia, Galatia and NW Spain, so mid ~43 million. Brunt (https://archive.org/details/p.-a.-brunt-italian-manpower-225-b.-c.-a.-d.-14-clarendon-press-1971, ch. on the Augustan census) reads the 28 BCE census of 4,063,000 citizens (Res Gestae 8) as all citizens incl. women and children (low count) against Frank's ~12 million (high count); either way citizens are a minority of the empire. Everything inside the border, slaves included.

urbanization.note: Hanson & Ortman 2017 (JRA 30, pp. 301-324) put ~20-25% of the 2nd-century CE population in cities above 5,000; the Augustan empire was slightly less urbanised (Gaul and Spain just being urbanised). Seshat codes Rome itself at 900,000-1,100,000 in 1 CE (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/70).

activePersonnel.note: Legions + Praetorian cohorts 150,000-176,000 (Brunt, https://archive.org/details/p.-a.-brunt-italian-manpower-225-b.-c.-a.-d.-14-clarendon-press-1971, p. 337: by 25 BCE 27 legions which "with the praetorian cohorts" made 176,000 men at full strength "or more probably 150,000"; 28 legions in 27 BCE before XVII-XIX were counted twice) + auxiliaries and allied contingents 80,000-140,000 (Tacitus Ann. 4.5, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Tacitus/Annals/4A*.html, for 23 CE: auxilia "in not much inferior strength" to the legions; in 27 BCE they were still partly ad hoc allied levies, so mid ~100,000) + navy and staff (see supportPersonnel). Mid = 160,000 + 100,000 + 30,000. Convention: legions, praetorians, auxilia and allied levies in service are counted as active; recallable veterans (evocati) are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Recently discharged veterans settled in colonies and on Italian allotments after Actium: Brunt (p. 337) gives two estimates of men entitled to allotments in 30 BCE, 85,000 or 145,000; Augustus settled or sent home "something more than 300,000" over his reign (Res Gestae 3, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Augustus/Res_Gestae/1*.html). Mid assumes about half of the post-Actium veterans recallable as evocati within a month.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Fleet crews at Misenum, Ravenna and Forum Iulii (Tacitus Ann. 4.5 for the three bases, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Tacitus/Annals/4A*.html): ~120-200 major ships and liburnians x 150-200 men; plus ~2,000-3,000 staff, engineers and officers excluded from unit totals. Many rowers of the Actium fleets had been discharged.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Octavian and Antony together had at least 250,000 men under arms in 31-30 BCE (Brunt, https://archive.org/details/p.-a.-brunt-italian-manpower-225-b.-c.-a.-d.-14-clarendon-press-1971, p. 337: "can hardly be put under 250,000"), and Augustus says ~500,000 citizens swore the military oath to him over his career (Res Gestae 3, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Augustus/Res_Gestae/1*.html). That was ~0.6% of the empire in arms at the civil-war peak; 0.04 assumes an emergency levy on the Republican pattern, mostly from citizens and frontier peoples.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Legionary infantry: 28 legions x ~4,800-5,300 (Brunt p. 337 total of 150,000-176,000 with the praetorians, less ~3,400 legionary cavalry) = ~145,000, + 9 Praetorian cohorts (~4,500-9,000; formalised 27 BCE, Tacitus Ann. 4.5 lists nine in 23 CE) + close-order auxiliary and allied infantry (~30,000-55,000, share of the auxilia estimated from Tacitus Ann. 4.5, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Tacitus/Annals/4A*.html).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: the legion kit that the rubric names as the era's best c. 100 CE was already standard (mail, scutum, gladius, pilum); allied infantry lighter, mid 0.9.

training.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: long-service civil-war veterans; many legions had fought for 10-15 years. Allied infantry lower.

count.note: Educated guess. Allied and auxiliary javelinmen and slingers (Balearic, Spanish caetrati, African) of the client kings and provincial levies; no total survives.

quality.note: Era-typical javelins and slings (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Semi-regular ethnic contingents between levy and professional.

count.note: Educated guess. Cretan and eastern archers (Ituraean, Commagenian) among the auxilia; scaled from the ~1 in 12 archer units of the 2nd-century auxilia (Holder 2003, doi:10.1111/j.2041-5370.2003.tb01979.x) applied to ~100,000 auxiliaries.

quality.note: Composite bows from eastern recruiting grounds (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Specialist mercenary and allied archers.

count.note: Educated guess. Gallic, German, Spanish and Thracian alae of the auxilia (heavy-ish shock cavalry with mail, spear and shield) + ~3,400 legionary cavalry (28 x 120). The alae were still largely ethnic contingents under native officers in 27 BCE; the total is scaled from Tacitus Ann. 4.5 (https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Tacitus/Annals/4A*.html) "cavalry divisions" of 23 CE.

quality.note: Mail-armoured Gallic and German horse with spears; good but below the later Roman alae and Parthian cataphracts (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Experienced civil-war cavalry; still ethnic contingents (rubric 0.5-0.75).

count.note: Educated guess. Numidian, Moorish and eastern light horse and horse archers from client kingdoms and auxilia; no total survives.

quality.note: Unarmoured javelin and bow horse, era-typical (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Raised in the saddle; semi-regular.

count.note: 28 legions x ~30-65 bolt-throwers and stone-throwers: Vegetius (Epitoma 2.25) gives 55 carroballistae + 10 onagri per legion for the late empire; Caesar's legions already used scorpiones in numbers. Low allows for smaller late-Republican establishments.

quality.note: Torsion artillery of Hellenistic design, era's best (rubric 0.75-1.0).

training.note: Crewed by veteran legionaries.

count.note: Educated guess. Augustus captured 600 ships larger than triremes or equal (Res Gestae 3, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Augustus/Res_Gestae/1*.html) and burned most of Antony's fleet after Actium; the captured warships sent to Forum Iulii (Tacitus Ann. 4.5, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Tacitus/Annals/4A*.html) and the Misenum and Ravenna fleets being organised. Triremes, quadriremes and some quinqueremes.

quality.note: Liburnian-heavy Agrippan fleet that won Naulochus and Actium; unchallenged after 30 BCE (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Crews with recent fleet battle experience (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Educated guess. Liburnians and patrol craft of the Italian fleets and Nile/Egyptian squadrons; the provincial fleets (Germanica, Pannonica) did not exist yet.

quality.note: Liburnians were the decisive light warship of the era.

training.note: Standing professional crews being formed.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75: proven commanders (Agrippa, Statilius Taurus, Augustus' legates) and an officer corps hardened by twenty years of civil war; no formal staff system beyond the legionary hierarchy.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: legionary identity strong (numbered legions with eagles), but the army had just been merged from Octavian's and Antony's forces and loyalty was personal to the commander.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: victorious (Actium 31, Alexandria 30), paid from the Egyptian treasure; war-weary after two decades of civil war.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (iron weapons, torsion artillery) with Roman refinements (pilum, gladius Hispaniensis, scorpio); slightly below the Trajanic ~3.3.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail): lorica hamata standard, Montefortino/Coolus helmets; segmented plate not yet introduced. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.3 -> 3.18, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -27 (3.176); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

ships.note: Anchor 3 (triremes, quinqueremes) plus Agrippa's harpax and towered ships; liburnians.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 (ashlar walls, siege towers); Caesar's siege works at Alesia; no permanent stone legionary fortresses yet.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (engineered roads, depot system): Italian viae, sea-borne grain supply; the Augustan reorganisation of provincial roads just starting. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.3 -> 3.18, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -27 (3.176); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): Augustus founded the cursus publicus later in his reign (Suetonius Aug. 49), so couriers and dispatch riders only in 27 BCE.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: exploratores and speculatores.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 (2011 int$) values for year 1 CE in Roman territory: Italy 1,407, Greece 1,275, Egypt/Levant/Tunisia 1,116, France 956, Turkey 897, Spain 886. Mid ~1,050 is a rough population-weighted average; Italy (~7-8 million of 43 million, with Rome's tribute inflows) pulls it above the Trajanic snapshot's 1,000.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994), ch. 3: army cost ~600-650 million HS a year in the 2nd century for ~30 legions + auxilia; the Augustan army of similar size with lower pay (225 denarii) would cost ~400-500 million HS against a GDP of ~15-18 billion HS (Scheidel & Friesen 2009, doi:10.3815/007543509789745223: ~260 HS per head) -> ~3%. Post-Actium land and cash for veterans (Res Gestae 16: 600 million HS for Italian land in 30 and 14 BCE) pushed the real burden higher. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy, ~75-85% of output agricultural; mining (Spain), textiles, ceramics (Arretine ware) and construction make up the rest. Same basis as rome-117.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. GDP ~1.7-1.9x bare subsistence (Scheidel & Friesen 2009) implies a modest surplus feeding ~15% urban population and the army. Egypt's grain now went to Rome.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (Scheidel & Meeks 2012) models 84,631 km of principal roads and desert tracks c. 200 CE (high). In 27 BCE the network outside Italy, Narbonensis, Macedonia (Via Egnatia) and Asia was largely unbuilt, so mid ~60,000 km.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites c. 200 CE; ports able to supply a fleet or army in 27 BCE (Ostia, Puteoli, Misenum, Ravenna, Brundisium, Forum Iulii, Massilia, Carthage, Alexandria, Seleucia Pieria, Ephesus, Corinth, Gades...) estimated at ~15.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Rome already imported ~200,000 t of grain a year (scaled down from the Trajanic estimate); Mediterranean shipping as in the rome-117 snapshot, somewhat smaller.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying their own grain and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; same value as the rome-117 snapshot.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.05-0.12 draft and pack animals per inhabitant x population, as for the rome-117 snapshot.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: familiar terrain, local supply, fortified cities and colonies of veterans; not 1.3 (no harsh climate). Gaul and Spain were not yet fully pacified, which lowers the low end.

rome--27.notes: Snapshot = January 27 BCE, the "first settlement" (Octavian becomes Augustus), after the post-Actium demobilisation: 28 legions retained (Brunt, Italian Manpower, archive.org text; Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army, isbn:1566193591, ch. 6, not fetched). Border uses historical-basemaps world_bc100 (latest file at or before -27): the two "Roman Republic" polygons plus "Ptolemaic Kingdom" (Egypt annexed 30 BCE, Cyrene and Cyprus already Roman); the union misses Gallia Comata, Syria and much of Anatolia, so areaKm2 is researched, not computed. Population convention: everything inside the real 27 BCE border, slaves included; client kingdoms (Judaea, Galatia until 25 BCE, Mauretania, Commagene, Thrace) not counted. Auxiliary numbers are the weakest: no Augustan list exists and Tacitus' "not much inferior" (23 CE) is an ancient statement, used only to scale. Ship counts are guesses.

areaKm2.note: Cited page, table of empires at their greatest extent: Roman Empire 5.0 million km2 in 117 (Turchin, Adams and Hall 2006; Taagepera 1979) (mid). Seshat codes 5.8 million km2 for 100 CE (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/70, high). The historical-basemaps world_100 polygon measures 4.62 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, low); it predates Trajan's eastern annexations of 114-117. audit 2026-10-30: mid was Taagepera not fetched; now read from the fetched list, which cites him.

population.note: Seshat codes the Principate at 50-60 million for 100 CE and 55-70 million for 200 CE. Frier 2000 (Cambridge Ancient History XI, isbn:0521263352, p. 814 table 6) gives 45.5 million in 14 CE and 61.4 million in 164 CE; geometric interpolation to 117 CE gives ~56 million, used as mid. High end covers Scheidel's 59-72 million for c. 165 CE and the 70 million upper Seshat value. Everything inside the imperial border, slaves included.

urbanization.note: Hanson & Ortman 2017 (JRA 30, pp. 301-324) put ~14 million people in ~600 cities above 5,000 inhabitants, i.e. 20-25% of a 56-70 million population (high end). Mid and low allow for stricter urban definitions; Seshat codes Rome itself at 1.0-1.2 million in 100 CE.

activePersonnel.note: Holder 2003 (BICS 46, 101-145) reconstructs the army of c. 130 CE as 30 legions (165,000 infantry + 3,600 cavalry) and 381 auxiliary units (152,260 infantry + 71,468 cavalry) = 392,328, excluding ~4,000 officers. Added: Praetorian and urban cohorts (~10,000-20,000), numeri (~5,000-20,000) and the navy (30,000-46,000). Trajan in 117 also had 30 legions (II Traiana and XXX Ulpia raised, IX Hispana and XXII Deiotariana still extant). Vigiles (~7,000) excluded as paramilitary.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. No formal reserve; recalled veterans (evocati) and recently discharged veterans in colonies. 30 legions x ~150-200 survivors of 25-year service discharged per year = ~5,000-6,000 legionaries a year; a few recent year classes recallable.

supportPersonnel.note: Navy 30,000-46,000 (John Lydus gives 45,562 sailors for the fleet before Diocletian's expansion; ancient figure, late) + ~4,000 centurions and higher officers excluded from Holder's unit totals (Holder 2003, doi:10.1111/j.2041-5370.2003.tb01979.x). Mid = 40,000 navy + 4,000 officers.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The standing army was ~0.8% of the population; the Republic during the Second Punic War mobilised a far larger share of its citizen body, but provincials could not be levied at that intensity. 0.04 assumes an emergency levy on the Republican pattern restricted to citizen and frontier populations.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Legionary infantry 30 x ~5,500 = 165,000 + auxiliary infantry 152,260 less ~12,000 archers (Holder 2003, as tabulated for c. 130 CE) + Praetorian and urban cohorts in Rome (~10,000-20,000, estimate). Auxiliary cohorts fought as close-order armoured infantry, hence line.

quality.note: Rubric quality 1.0 row names Roman legion kit c. 100 CE as the era's best (mail/segmented armour, scutum, gladius, pilum); auxiliaries slightly lighter, so mid 0.95.

training.note: Rubric training 0.75-1.0: long-service professionals (25-year terms), drill and fortified-camp routine; auxiliaries slightly below legionaries.

count.note: Archer units (sagittarii) were about 1 in 12 auxiliary units with an official total of ~17,600 men including mounted archer alae (high); infantry share estimated at ~12,000.

quality.note: Composite bows from eastern recruiting grounds; among the era's best (0.75).

training.note: Professional auxiliary units (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Educated guess. Irregular numeri and allied light troops (e.g. Lusius Quietus' Moors in the Dacian and Parthian wars); Goldsworthy, The Complete Roman Army, chapter on the auxilia, describes the units but gives no total.

quality.note: Era-typical javelins/slings (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Semi-regular ethnic units; between conscript and professional.

count.note: Alae: 88 units (7 milliary) ~46,500 men, i.e. Holder's 71,468 auxiliary cavalry less ~25,000 riders of cohortes equitatae (70% of cohorts assumed equitate), + 3,600 legionary cavalry + ~1,000 equites singulares Augusti.

quality.note: Mail-armoured cavalry with spears and shields; among the era's best but not superior to Parthian cataphracts (rubric 0.75-1.0).

training.note: Long-service professionals (rubric 0.75-1.0).

count.note: Mounted men of the cohortes equitatae (~25,000 under Holder's 70% assumption) + Moorish and other irregular light horse (2,000-5,000, estimate).

quality.note: Lighter equipment than the alae (rubric 0.5-0.75).

training.note: Professional auxiliaries (rubric 0.75).

count.note: 30 legions x 65 pieces: Vegetius (Epitoma 2.25) gives 55 carroballistae + 10 onagri per legion. Late-4th-century source applied to the 2nd century; low allows for lower 2nd-century establishments.

quality.note: Torsion artillery at its ancient peak (rubric 1.0 row: Roman kit c. 100 CE).

training.note: Crewed by trained legionaries.

count.note: Educated guess: triremes and larger (one hexeres flagship at Misenum) of the two praetorian fleets. Navy 30,000-46,000 men divided between major ships (~200 men) and liburnians/river craft (~60-100 men).

quality.note: Unchallenged Mediterranean fleet, standard trireme/liburnian designs.

training.note: Standing professional fleets with 26-year service.

count.note: Educated guess: liburnians and patrol/river craft of the provincial fleets (Britannica, Germanica, Pannonica, Moesica, Pontica, Syriaca, Alexandrina); same manpower split as ships_major.

quality.note: Liburnians formed the bulk of the provincial fleets.

training.note: Standing professional fleets.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75: trained staff system (legates, tribunes, centurionate), proven commanders (Trajan's Dacian and Parthian campaigns).

cohesion.note: Rubric 1.0 row names legionary identity; auxiliaries somewhat lower, mid 0.9.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75: motivated, recent victories (Dacia 106, Parthian war 114-116), though the 115-117 Jewish diaspora revolt and eastern unrest weighed on 117.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 (300 BCE: iron weapons, torsion artillery) plus refinements (pilum, gladius, carroballista); SOURCES.md names Rome 117 CE weapons ~3.3.

armor.note: Anchor 3 (iron cuirass, mail) exceeded: segmented plate and mail standard issue; well short of anchor 4 plate-and-mail. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.5 -> 3.27, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 117 (3.269); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

ships.note: Anchor 3: triremes, liburnians, a few larger polyremes.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 (ashlar walls, siege towers) plus permanent stone legionary fortresses and a fortified limes. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.4 -> 3.27, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 117 (3.269); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 (engineered roads, depots) plus empire-wide granaries, annona shipping and river transport (part of anchor 4). audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.5 -> 3.27, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 117 (3.269); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): cursus publicus.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: exploratores, speculatores, frontier watchtowers.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 (2011 int$) values for year 1 CE in Roman territory: Italy 1,407, Greece 1,275, Egypt/Levant/Tunisia 1,116, France/Belgium/Portugal 956, Turkey 897, Spain 886. Mid ~1,000 is the rough population-weighted provincial average (Italy is ~1/8 of the population). Cross-check: Scheidel & Friesen 2009 (doi:10.3815/007543509789745223) put output at ~1.7-1.9x bare subsistence, consistent with this range.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994), ch. 3: army cost ~600-650 million HS a year in the 2nd century; GDP ~18 billion HS (Scheidel & Friesen 2009, doi:10.3815/007543509789745223: ~260 HS per head) -> ~3.5%. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

industrialShare.note: Educated guess for an agrarian economy where ~75-85% of output was agricultural; mining, textiles, ceramics and construction make up the rest.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: GDP ~1.7-1.9x bare-bones subsistence (Scheidel & Friesen 2009) implies a modest surplus that fed ~15-20% urban population and the army.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (Scheidel & Meeks 2012) models 84,631 km of principal roads and desert tracks c. 200 CE; it reproduces arterial routes only, so the full engineered network was larger (high).

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites; ports able to supply a fleet or army (Ostia/Portus, Puteoli, Misenum, Ravenna, Alexandria, Carthage, Seleucia Pieria, Caesarea, Ephesus, Corinth, Massilia, Aquileia, Byzantium, Gades, Londinium...) estimated at ~20.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Rome alone imported ~200,000-300,000 t of grain a year; at ~2 voyages a season that needs ~100,000-150,000 t of shipping, and the annona was perhaps a quarter to a third of seaborne trade.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying their own grain and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; the Roman soldier carried ~3 days' rations plus mule-borne reserves.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: ~0.05-0.11 draft and pack animals (oxen, mules, donkeys, horses, camels) per inhabitant x population.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: familiar terrain and local supply plus fortified cities, the limes and broad population support; not 1.3 because the core is not protected by harsh climate.

rome-117.notes: Snapshot = August 117 CE, at Trajan's death, the territorial peak. Population convention: everything inside the imperial border, slaves included; Armenia and Mesopotamia (annexed 114-116, abandoned by Hadrian in 118) are inside the border but their population is not counted in the mid. Border uses historical-basemaps world_100 (closest file), which shows the empire before the eastern annexations. Force numbers are Holder's c. 130 CE reconstruction (published unit lists, Hadrianic) applied to 117; the totals at Trajan's death were within a few percent (same number of legions). Navy numbers and ship counts are weak (no surviving order of battle). GDP per capita from the Maddison Project year-1 values for Roman provinces; all ancient GDP figures are reconstructions.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 4.0-4.5 million km2 for 285-394 CE (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/71). Border: the world_400 Western Roman Empire (2,361,040 km2) and Eastern Roman Empire (1,829,503 km2) polygons (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_400.geojson, computed on the sphere) total 4.19 million km2 (mid); northern Britain beyond York is outside them. audit 2026-10-30: border changed from the four world_300 tetrarchy polygons (95 years off, 4.30M km2) to world_400 (5 years off); mid follows the new polygon.

population.note: Seshat codes the Dominate at 40-70 million for 300 CE; the high end is trimmed because the Antonine and Cyprian plagues and the 3rd-century crisis left the late-4th-century empire below its 2nd-century peak (rome-117 snapshot: ~56 million). Seshat codes the Eastern empire alone at 15 million for 400 CE (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/72), which implies a West of 25-35 million for the mid. Everything inside the border, slaves included; federate Goths settled in Thrace and Moesia in 382 are included.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Below the 2nd-century 20-25% of Hanson & Ortman 2017 (doi:10.1017/S1047759400074134): western cities had shrunk behind 3rd-century walls, while eastern cities (Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople at ~300,000 per Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/72) still flourished.

activePersonnel.note: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964), vol. 2 ch. XVII "Numbers", pp. 679-684 (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02): applying unit establishments to the Notitia Dignitatum gives East field armies 104,000, Eastern limitanei ~250,000, scholae 3,500 (East total ~357,500), Western field armies 113,000 and limitanei 135,500 c. 425, which Jones raises for the late 4th century (Rhine garrison comparable with the Upper Danube 81,000 or Lower Danube 64,000; Africa ~30,000). Empire-wide paper total ~600,000, "roughly consonant" with Agathias' figure of 645,000 for the old army (ancient, high). Jones stresses this is a paper strength well above effectives (dead men, deserters, fictitious soldiers on the rolls), and the Eastern field army had lost heavily at Adrianople (378) and both halves at the Frigidus (394), so mid ~505,000 and low 400,000 (cf. Strobel's ~435,000 for Diocletian, cited by Treadgold, Byzantium and Its Army 284-1081, isbn:0804731632, ch. 2, not fetched). Convention: comitatenses, limitanei and scholae (all salaried) are counted as active; Gothic and other federates called up under their own leaders are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Gothic federates settled under the 382 treaty, called up under their own leaders (Theodosius led some 20,000 Goths at the Frigidus in 394 according to Jordanes and Orosius, ancient figures), plus other federate and allied bands. Jones (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, ch. XVII) describes the growing use of federates without a total.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Fleets: John Lydus gives 45,562 men in Diocletian's fleets (as quoted by Jones, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 679; ancient figure, high). The Notitia fleets (Misenum, Ravenna, river flotillas on the Danube and Rhine) were smaller by 395, and some fleet units are already inside Jones' limitanei totals at 500 men each. Plus ~5,000 staff of the magistri militum and duces.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The late empire struggled to recruit (conscription levies on landowners, commutation to gold, ever-greater use of barbarian recruits and federates; Jones vol. 2 ch. XVII, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02). The paper army of ~600,000 was already ~1.2% of the population; 0.025 assumes an emergency levy roughly doubling it.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Legions (comitatenses at ~1,000, old frontier legions at ~3,000 per Jones) and auxilia palatina, plus limitanei infantry (milites, cohortes): ~55-60% of the paper army in Jones' Notitia reconstruction (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, pp. 681-683) scaled to the active mid; the infantry/cavalry split is not given by Jones and is estimated from his unit-type establishments (cavalry units at 500).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: mail or scale, ridge helmets, oval shields, spatha, plumbatae; still well equipped from state fabricae but lighter than the Principate legion; frontier units worse equipped.

training.note: Comitatenses professional (0.75), limitanei partly part-time soldier-farmers (0.5); weighted toward the limitanei majority.

count.note: Educated guess. Lanciarii, exculcatores and light auxilia skirmishers; Vegetius describes light-armed troops in every late legion but no total exists.

quality.note: Era-typical javelins and darts (rubric 0.5).

training.note: Mixed professional and frontier troops.

count.note: Educated guess. Sagittarii units in the field armies and frontier commands (several listed in the Notitia) plus archers inside legions (Vegetius says a third to a quarter of recruits trained as archers); no total exists.

quality.note: Composite bows (rubric 0.75 for eastern archers).

training.note: Professional units, frontier archers lower.

count.note: Educated guess. Scholae palatinae (3,500 East + 2,500 West per Jones, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 683), cataphractarii and clibanarii vexillations and heavier equites of the field armies, at Jones' 500 per cavalry unit.

quality.note: Clibanarii in full horse armour on the Persian model, among the era's best (rubric 0.75).

training.note: Guard and field-army professionals (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Educated guess. Equites sagittarii, Dalmatae, Mauri, promoti, scutarii and the many cunei equitum of the limitanei (cavalry units dominate the Notitia lists of the eastern frontier). Total cavalry (heavy + light) ~25-30% of the army is an estimate; Jones gives no cavalry total.

quality.note: Era-typical light horse and horse archers (rubric 0.5-0.75).

training.note: Field-army cavalry professional, frontier cunei lower.

count.note: Educated guess. Vegetius (Epitoma 2.25, written c. 390) gives 55 carroballistae + 10 onagri per legion, but late legions were 1,000-3,000 strong; ballistarii units appear in the Notitia and fortress walls carried mounted engines. Scaled to ~150-200 legion-sized formations and fort garrisons.

quality.note: Torsion artillery still the era's best; onager now standard.

training.note: Specialist ballistarii.

count.note: Educated guess. Liburnians of the Italian and eastern fleets listed in the Notitia (classis Misenatis, Ravennatium, Venetum...); no Mediterranean naval rival existed, so the sea-going fleets were small.

quality.note: Era-typical oared warships, no innovation since the Principate.

training.note: Peacetime crews.

count.note: Educated guess. River patrol boats (lusoriae) of the Danube and Rhine flotillas; the Theodosian Code (CTh 7.17.1, AD 412) orders 225 new or rebuilt lusoriae for Moesia and Scythia alone (ancient legal figure, later date).

quality.note: Purpose-built river craft.

training.note: Frontier crews.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: a structured command system (magistri militum, comites, duces, the Notitia hierarchy) and a capable emperor and general (Theodosius, Stilicho), but Adrianople (378) showed poor coordination and the system was riven by usurpations.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5: regimental identity survived in the field units, but frontier troops were tied to their land, the army had just fought a civil war (Frigidus, 394), and federates served under their own chiefs (rubric 0.25 for those).

morale.note: Rubric 0.5 average: victory at the Frigidus in 394 but the Adrianople disaster (378) still recent, heavy losses on both sides of the civil war, and recruitment by compulsion.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 plus late refinements: spatha, plumbatae, widespread composite bows, onager and arcuballista; short of anchor 4 (no true crossbow or trebuchet in use).

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail) plus scale and lamellar, ridge helmets and fully armoured clibanarii horse; segmented plate gone, so not above the Trajanic 3.5.

ships.note: Anchor 3: liburnians and river lusoriae; the dromon had not yet appeared.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 exceeded toward anchor 4: late Roman walls with projecting towers, thick curtain walls and city circuits (Aurelian Walls rebuilt), quadriburgia on the frontiers. The Theodosian Land Walls of Constantinople came after 404. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.6 -> 3.45, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 395 (3.448); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 plus annona militaris in kind, state fabricae, granaries and river transport; network partly degraded in the West.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): cursus publicus fully developed.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: exploratores, agentes in rebus, frontier watchtowers.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true has no 4th-century values; year 1 CE values for Roman territory (Italy 1,407, Greece 1,275, Egypt 1,116, France 956, Turkey 897, Spain 886) and Egypt 730 CE (1,164) bracket it. The late empire is placed slightly below the 1st-2nd-century average (rome-117: 1,000) for the shrunken western economy; the East was probably at or above its earlier level.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Jones (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 684) stresses that pay and allowances were issued for ~645,000 men, by far the largest item of the imperial budget (commonly put at half to two-thirds of state spending); with the late Roman tax take at ~6-10% of GDP that implies ~3-7%.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy; state fabricae for arms, mints, mines, textiles and construction. Slightly below the Principate.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Egypt and Africa still produced large tax-grain surpluses for Rome and Constantinople and the annona militaris; the West was weaker than in the 2nd century.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (Scheidel & Meeks 2012) models 84,631 km of principal roads and desert tracks (c. 200 CE network, mid); still maintained in 395 apart from Dacia and the Agri Decumates (low), with secondary roads beyond the ORBIS network (high).

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites; ports able to supply a fleet or army (Constantinople, Ostia/Portus, Ravenna, Aquileia, Thessalonica, Alexandria, Carthage, Seleucia Pieria, Ephesus, Corinth, Arelate, Gades...) estimated at ~20.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Grain fleets now served both Rome and Constantinople (the Egyptian annona went east after 330); estimate as for rome-117, lowered for the decline of western trade.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying grain and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; same as the rome-117 snapshot.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.06-0.11 draft and pack animals per inhabitant x population; cursus publicus and annona transport were large users.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: fortified cities and frontier forts, local supply via the annona; weakened by Gothic federates already inside the empire and limited popular support for a conscript army.

rome-395.notes: Snapshot = 17 January 395, death of Theodosius I at Milan, the last ruler of the united empire; the empire was divided between Arcadius (East) and Honorius (West, under Stilicho) immediately afterwards. Capital set to Constantinople (Theodosius' main residence); Milan held the western court. Border: historical-basemaps world_400 Western and Eastern Roman Empire polygons (5 years after the snapshot, matching the division of 395). (audit 2026-10-30) Army figures are Notitia Dignitatum reconstructions (Jones 1964); the Notitia lists units, not men, so every total rests on assumed unit establishments, and it is a paper strength. Treadgold (Byzantium and Its Army, ch. 2) and Elton (Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425) give similar orders of magnitude but were not fetched. Agathias' 645,000 is an ancient figure shown only as the high bound. The infantry/cavalry split is the weakest part of the force table. Federates are counted as trainedReserves, not active forces.

areaKm2.note: asOf 2024. Surface area 17,125,190 km2; low is land area 16,376,870 km2. Internationally recognised territory; occupied Ukrainian territory (Crimea and parts of four oblasts, ~100,000+ km2) not included.

population.note: asOf 2025 (World Bank 143,513,328, declining ~0.1%/yr). High allows for Russian official statistics that include annexed Crimea (a few million higher; not fetched). Population of occupied Ukrainian territories excluded.

activePersonnel.note: IISS Military Balance 2026 p.188 as quoted: 1,264,000 active (plus 569,000 paramilitary, excluded). CIA Factbook 2025: 1.1-1.2 million (low); September 2024 decree sets 1.5 million servicemen (high, a target). Wartime: high casualties (~1 million killed and wounded by mid-2025 per the Russian Armed Forces article, Western estimates) are replaced by contract recruitment.

trainedReserves.note: IISS Military Balance 2026: 1,500,000 reserves (mid). Low is what was actually called up in the 2022 partial mobilization (~300,000, IISS Feb 2023 as quoted on the Russian Ground Forces article), i.e. the realistic 30-day intake. High: "close to two million" reservists (Russian Armed Forces article).

supportPersonnel.note: Active 1,264,000 minus infantry P roles (300,000 + 100,000). Aerospace Forces, Navy, Strategic Rocket Forces, crews, artillery, drone units (Unmanned Systems Forces), logistics, staff, and the ~20,000 deployed in other former Soviet states/Africa (CIA Factbook 2025).

mobilizationRatio.note: Analogy to the USSR in WWII (roughly 34 million mobilized from ~195 million, ~17%) scaled down for a smaller, older population, emigration since 2022 and a labour-short war economy. Ukrainian C-in-C Syrskyi (Apr 2025, a party to the war) claimed Russia could mobilize 20 million (14%), 5 million with military training (Russian Armed Forces article).

count.note: Educated guess. The grouping in Ukraine was ~623,000 in April 2025 and growing 8-9,000/month (Syrskyi, as quoted; CIA Factbook 2025: ~600,000 in Ukraine). The war is infantry-heavy (motor-rifle and "assault" units of contract soldiers and mobilized men); about half of the grouping taken as line infantry. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Armed_Forces)

quality.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: era-typical small arms and drones, but many units ride MT-LB/old BMPs or go on foot; a generation behind NATO in protection.

training.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: short training for contract recruits (weeks), offset by combat experience of survivors.

count.note: Educated guess. Airborne Forces (VDV), naval infantry, Spetsnaz, Storm-Z/Storm-V penal assault units, plus foreign contingents (North Korean troops deployed 2024-25 excluded). (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Ground_Forces)

quality.note: Rubric 0.5 era-typical.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: elite VDV/naval infantry cadres largely destroyed in 2022-23 and refilled; penal units 0.25.

count.note: Highly uncertain wartime figure. High: ~3,460 tanks in service per the new IISS Military Balance edition (as reported by www1.ru, May 2026; the same 3,460 appears on the Ground Forces equipment list: T-54/55 120, T-62 600, T-64 50, T-72 1,470, T-80 600, T-90M 620), with ~2,100 left in storage. Low: 1,750 active (IISS 2024, mind.ua). Losses since 2022 exceed 3,000 (IISS 2024).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: T-90M/T-80BVM/T-72B3M current, but a large share are refurbished T-62/T-55 (obsolete, 0.25).

training.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5.

count.note: IISS as quoted on the equipment list: IFVs 1,950 (BMP-1 750, BMP-2 550, BMP-3 650; IISS 2025) + APCs BTR-60 800, BTR-70 200, BTR-80 1,200, MT-LB 2,500 (IISS 2024) = ~6,650. BMD airborne vehicles not counted (high). Up to 3,000 BMP-1/2 and 1,000 MT-LB in storage excluded.

quality.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: mostly Soviet-era designs.

training.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5.

count.note: IISS 2025 as quoted: SP 1,675 (2S1 400, 2S3 600, 2S19 450, 2S5 100, 2S7 125) + towed 152mm 370 + D-30 200 + MLRS 1,181 = ~3,426 active. ~4,800 more in storage (SP 1,900, towed 152mm 1,650, MLRS 1,250) feed refurbishment (high). Artillery advantage over Ukraine fell from ~10:1 to ~2:1 by 2025 (Syrskyi, as quoted).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5 era-typical; Tornado-S/2S19M2 modern, many barrels worn.

training.note: Rubric 0.5 plus combat experience in counter-battery and drone-spotted fires.

count.note: Active-aircraft list (World Air Forces 2025 / IISS 2022 as quoted): Su-27/30/35 combined "<422", naval Su-30SM 22, Su-57 29, MiG-29 ~87, MiG-31 128+ and 32 naval, MiG-35 6 = ~726; list subtotal ~1,069 double-counts across tables (high).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75 band minus: Su-35S/Su-30SM2 modern 4+ generation, only ~29 Su-57.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: low peacetime flying hours, but extensive stand-off combat sorties since 2022.

count.note: World Air Forces 2025 as quoted: Su-24 259, Su-25 175, Su-34 142-163, Tu-22M3 55, Tu-95MS 46, Tu-160 17 = ~700 (high). Mid discounts the Su-24 count (many retired/stored) and combat losses; Bulletin 2026: ~60 heavy bombers active.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: Su-34 and glide bombs (UMPK) effective; Su-24/Su-25/Tu-95 old airframes.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75.

count.note: World Air Forces 2025 as quoted: attack Ka-52 135 + Mi-28 94 + Mi-24 323 = 552; transport/utility Mi-8/17 777 + Mi-26 45 + Ka-226 36 + Ansat-U 50 = 908; total ~1,460 (high). Mid allows for war losses.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: Ka-52M/Mi-28NM modern, Mi-24/Mi-8 old.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75.

count.note: Educated guess. Reusable Group 2+ UAVs (Orlan-10/30, Zala, Supercam, Orion, Forpost) in service; no fetched inventory. FPV drones (millions per year) and one-way attack drones (Geran) are munitions and excluded. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Armed_Forces)

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: mass-produced, combat-iterated designs; few large MALE drones.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: Unmanned Systems Forces formed from combat-experienced units (Rubikon).

count.note: Convention: carriers + cruisers + destroyers + frigates. Active list (statuses partly 2021-24): cruisers 2 + destroyers 6 + frigates 9-12 (mid 11) = 19; high adds the non-operational carrier Kuznetsov, battlecruiser Admiral Nakhimov on trials and damaged/refit hulls. Moskva and other Black Sea Fleet ships lost 2022-24.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: Admiral Gorshkov frigates modern (Zircon), destroyers/cruisers 1980s.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75.

count.note: Active list tallies: corvettes ~47 operational (8 large + ~39 small missile ships; page summary c. 79 incl. reserve), landing ships ~10-17, mine countermeasures 42+, patrol ships 5 (patrol boats excluded). Mid ~110.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: Karakurt/Buyan-M corvettes carry Kalibr; old landing ships and MCM.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75.

count.note: Active list: operational SSBN 12 + SSGN 4 + SSN 10 + SSK 16 = 42 (low); page summary incl. refit/reserve 57 (high). Bulletin Nuclear Notebook (Mar 2026): 13 operational SSBNs.

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: Yasen-M and Borei-A among era best; older Akula/Oscar/Kilo.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: submarine force is the best-maintained navy branch.

count.note: Launchers: ~324 ICBMs (Yars ~207, Voevoda ~40, Topol-M, Avangard; Bulletin Nuclear Notebook Mar 2026) + 162 Iskander-M launchers (IISS 2025 as quoted on the equipment list) = ~486. High allows for Bastion/Bal coastal anti-ship launchers (not counted).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75-1.0: Iskander-M, Kinzhal, Zircon, Oreshnik IRBM (used Nov 2024); Sarmat not on combat duty.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: Strategic Rocket Forces are well-trained long-service units.

count.note: Educated guess in batteries: Ground Forces SAM systems 1,029+ (Strela-10 300, Tunguska 190, Osa 100, Tor 129+, Buk 310; IISS 2025) / ~4 per battery = ~260, plus Aerospace Forces S-300/S-400/S-350 battalions (~80-120, not fetched). Several S-300/S-400 units destroyed in Crimea/occupied areas 2023-25. (context page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_equipment_of_the_Russian_Ground_Forces)

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: S-400, Pantsir-SM, Tor-M2 among era best; older Osa/Strela.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5 (competent staff, average generalship): failed 2022 opening, then effective defensive operations (2023) and slow attritional advances; centralized command, generals purged/killed; reportedly improving drone-artillery integration.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: national army but filled with pay-motivated contract volunteers, mobilized men, convicts and foreign recruits; units repeatedly reconstituted after losses; ~250,000+ draft evaders fled (Russian Armed Forces article).

morale.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: high signing bonuses rather than enthusiasm, heavy casualties; would rise toward 0.75 for defence of Russian territory proper.

weapons.note: Anchor 10 partly: hypersonic Kinzhal/Zircon, Oreshnik IRBM, glide bombs, mass drones; precision-munition stocks limited; much Soviet-era equipment.

armor.note: Anchor 9 composite/ERA armour; Arena-M APS fielded only in small numbers; field-improvised anti-drone cages.

ships.note: Anchor 9 (nuclear subs) with Yasen-M/Zircon toward 10; surface fleet aging, no networked USV fleet.

fortification.note: Anchor 10: layered air defence (S-400, Pantsir), deep fortified lines in occupied Ukraine (2023 "Surovikin line").

logistics.note: Between anchor 8 (motor transport + rail) and 9: rail-dependent, truck-poor (forces operate ~90 miles from railheads, War on the Rocks 2021); limited airlift.

communications.note: Anchor 9 satellite comms and data links, but chronic shortages of secure tactical radios (use of commercial phones/Starlink terminals reported 2022-24).

isr.note: Anchor 9-10: dense tactical drone ISR, limited satellite and AEW (few A-50 left).

air.note: Anchor 9-10: Su-35/Su-34 4+ generation; Su-57 5th generation in small numbers only.

cyber.note: Anchor 10 state cyber forces: GRU units (Sandworm etc.), FSB, SVR.

gdpPerCapita.note: asOf 2025. World Bank NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD 42,358.0 (2021 int$) x 0.8005 = 33,908 2011 int$. Range +/-15%. Corrected 2026-10-29: values x1.0376 because the rebase factor was an arithmetic error (0.8005); the right factor is 0.8306 (FRED GDPDEF, 2017=100: 2011 91.478 / 2021 110.130). Figures quoted above are before the correction.

gdp.note: asOf 2025. World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.PP.KD (constant 2021 int$) 6,183,071,354,160 x 0.8005 (US GDP deflator 2011/2021) = 4,949,548,619,005 2011 int$. Range +/-15% for PPP benchmark uncertainty and the relative-price drift the rebase ignores. Corrected 2026-10-29: values x1.0376 because the rebase factor was an arithmetic error (0.8005); the right factor is 0.8306 (FRED GDPDEF, 2017=100: 2011 91.478 / 2021 110.130). Figures quoted above are before the correction.

milSpendShare.note: SIPRI via World Bank: 7.50% of GDP in 2025 (wartime, mid), 6.87% 2024, 3.60% 2021 (pre-war peacetime, low). The field is defined as peacetime share; mid is the current wartime value because the 2026 snapshot is at war. High allows for classified spending.

industrialShare.note: asOf 2025: industry incl. construction 29.7% of GDP; 32.2% in 2022.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.3 -> 0.96. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/RUS/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 5.11% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 1.30 (mean 2021-2023, range 1.23-1.35). Mid 1 - 0.051/1.30 = 0.96. Low: a x 1.3 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 1.23 = 0.95. High: s 1.35 = 0.96. Net exporter: production is about 130% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess: world's largest wheat exporter and self-sufficient in most staples; not computed from FAO balance sheets.

russia-2026.notes: WARTIME snapshot (4th year of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine), asOf 2025 economic data with a 2026 order of battle. All equipment counts are highly uncertain: IISS figures as quoted are from the 2023-2026 editions and mix active and refurbished stock; losses since 2022 exceed 3,000 tanks (IISS 2024) and the force is sustained by drawing down Soviet-era storage (~2,100 tanks left per the new IISS edition as reported May 2026). Population convention: internationally recognised territory inside ne:RUS (World Bank); occupied Crimea and parts of Ukraine, and their populations, excluded; forces deployed there are counted. Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011 (+/-15%). ships_major = carriers + cruisers + destroyers + frigates; ships_minor = corvettes, landing ships, MCM, patrol ships; drones = reusable Group 2+ UAVs only. Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Rosgvardiya (~350,000) and other paramilitary (IISS 569,000) excluded. North Korean troops sent in 2024-25 excluded. Figures from Ukrainian officials (Syrskyi) are from a party to the war and used only as ranges.

Cited page: the peasantry was 80% of the population at the turn of the 20th century; Collectivization in the Soviet Union page: 82% peasants in 1928. Population share used as a proxy for the agricultural employment share: 1 - 0.80 = 0.20 (mid). Russia was Europe's largest grain exporter in 1913.

homeDefense.note: 1.3 row: familiar terrain, fortresses, deep strategic depth and a continental winter that invaders were not adapted to.

russian-empire-1914.notes: Snapshot date August 1914 after mobilisation (general mobilisation 30-31 July). Bukhara and Khiva protectorates excluded. Forces are the whole army; on the German front in August the 1st and 2nd Armies had ~30 divisions, the four armies against Austria-Hungary ~53. Aircraft in aircraft_strike (no fighters in 1914). Ship convention per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries: battleships, carriers, cruisers and destroyers = ships_major, torpedo boats and smaller craft = ships_minor (role split per SOURCES.md naval role boundaries). Book figures (Stone, Conway's, Ferguson) not fetched online, graded at most B.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/RWA/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 35.05% (2025). s = 1 assumed: no self-sufficiency figure is fetched for auto-base states, which overstates the value for a net food importer. Mid 1 - 0.351/1 = 0.65. Low: a x 1.2 (farm households larger than the employed count) = 0.58. High: kept at mid (no s range).

rwanda-2026.notes: AUTO-GENERATED BASE SNAPSHOT. Population, economy, personnel and infrastructure from the World Bank (grade A/B). Force mix, ratings and tech copied from researched regional analogues (Republic of Angola, Democratic Republic of the Congo, State of Eritrea, Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Republic of Kenya, Federal Republic of Nigeria, Republic of South Africa, Republic of the Sudan, United Republic of Tanzania, Republic of Uganda) and graded D. Replace with a researched snapshot when one exists.

areaKm2.note: Infobox 2.9 million km2 for 1630 (high; Seshat 2.7M for 1501-1722, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/374). In 1600 Tabriz, Shirvan and Georgia were still Ottoman (1590 treaty) and Kandahar Mughal; the world_1600 polygon measures ~1.61 million km2 (low).

population.note: Infobox 8-10 million for 1650 (Blake 2013); Seshat codes 9 million (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/374); OWID/HYDE Iran 1600 = 5.0M plus western Afghanistan (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true). Lower in 1600 with Azerbaijan under Ottoman rule.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Isfahan up to ~200,000 (Seshat largest settlement), Qazvin, Tabriz (Ottoman in 1600), Mashhad, Shiraz.

activePersonnel.note: Abbas's crown-paid army: 10,000-15,000 ghulam cavalry, 12,000 musketeers, 12,000 artillerymen and a 3,000 bodyguard, ~37,000-40,000 in all (Roemer 1986 p. 265, Savory 1980, via the article), plus ~12,000 qurchis/Shahsevans (Blow via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Iran). In 1600 the reforms (Allahverdi Khan from 1600) were still in progress, hence low 30,000.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Qizilbash tribal cavalry raised by the provincial amirs from tuyul land grants, plus Kurdish, Lur and Georgian contingents.

supportPersonnel.note: Tupchi artillery corps: 12,000 at full strength (Roemer via the article); smaller in 1600, low/mid educated.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Tribal cavalry society plus the new crown army.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: 10,000-15,000 ghulam cavalry (Caucasian slave soldiers) and the 3,000 bodyguard (Roemer, Savory via the article), plus part of the ~12,000 qurchis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Iran).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: mail, lance, bow and some muskets.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: palace-trained ghulams.

count.note: Tufangchi musketeer corps, 12,000 at full strength (Roemer 1986 p. 265 via the article); still forming in 1600.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: matchlocks.

training.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: recruited from Iranian peasants, drilled with English help (Shirley brothers).

count.note: Abbas increased his cannon so that he could field 500 in a single battle (Nahavandi and Bomati 1998 via the article) (high, later in the reign); mid for 1600.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: new corps.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.75: Abbas I and Allahverdi Khan retook Herat (1598) and would take Tabriz (1603) and Yerevan (1604).

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: ghulams loyal to the shah; Qizilbash factionalism (civil wars of the 1580s) only recently curbed.

morale.note: Rubric 0.75 minus: recovery after the losses of 1578-90.

weapons.note: Anchor 5 (1600): matchlocks and cannon alongside composite bows.

armor.note: Anchor 4-5: mail and plate-and-mail (chahar aina), helmets.

ships.note: Anchor 2-3: no navy; Caspian and Gulf boats only; Hormuz was taken in 1622 with English ships.

fortification.note: Anchor 4: mudbrick and stone citadels, no bastioned trace.

logistics.note: Anchor 4-5: caravanserai network and Abbas's road building.

communications.note: Anchor 4-5: chapar courier posts.

isr.note: Anchor 4: tribal scouts and spies.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

cyber.note: No computer networks before ~1990.

gdpPerCapita.note: No Maddison value for Iran before 1820 (877). Analogues: Turkey 1500 = 768, 1650 = 832 (Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true). Silk exports lift Iran slightly.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Crown army paid from khassa (crown) lands converted from Qizilbash provinces; low = peacetime.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Silk, carpets, textiles, metalwork.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Qanat-irrigated oases and Caspian rice.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Caravan routes with caravanserais; Abbas's paved causeway in Mazandaran.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. No Gulf port in Safavid hands in 1600 (Hormuz Portuguese, Gombroon taken 1614); Caspian landings only.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Caspian craft; Gulf trade in Portuguese hands.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Cavalry armies foraging across the plateau; scorched-earth defence against the Ottomans.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Camels, horses, mules.

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2-1.3: high arid plateau, long Ottoman supply lines and Safavid scorched-earth defence (Tahmasp vs Suleiman).

safavid-empire-1600.notes: Snapshot = 1600, Shah Abbas I in the middle of his military reforms, capital newly moved to Isfahan (1598), Herat retaken, Tabriz still Ottoman. Personnel convention: the crown-paid ghulam, musketeer and artillery corps and the qurchi guard are activePersonnel; Qizilbash tribal cavalry raised by provincial amirs are trainedReserves. Corps sizes are end-of-reign establishment figures (Roemer, Savory, Blow via the Abbas the Great and Safavid Iran articles); Matthee and Floor (Safavid Government Institutions) not consulted directly. Population convention: lands under Safavid rule in 1600 (without Ottoman-held Azerbaijan, Shirvan and Georgia).

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 2.60-2.96 million km2 for 600 CE (low to mid). The historical-basemaps world_600 polygons measure 3.20 million km2 ("Sasanian Empire") + 0.34 million km2 ("Sasanian dependencies", Yemen, a Sasanian province since c. 570) on the sphere, computed from the GeoJSON (high).

population.note: Seshat (Sasanid Empire II) codes 12.7 million for 551-619 CE (mid), 8.9 million for 499-550 (low ~9 million) and 22.1 million for 620-642 when the occupied Roman East was included. High 18 million allows for a larger Mesopotamian population than Seshat assumes. Everything inside the border incl. Mesopotamia, Khuzestan, the plateau, Khorasan, Persarmenia and Yemen; Lakhmid and Arab client tribes outside.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Mesopotamia and Khuzestan were heavily urbanised (Seshat largest settlement Ctesiphon 400,000-500,000 for 499-642, https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/130), the plateau and the east much less; set below the late Roman East.

activePersonnel.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 69-72: standing professional army c. 588-603 = 70,000 savaran on the warrior-caste rolls (al-Tabari's 70,000, reinterpreted; Mas'udi has Khosrow II review 50,000 horse c. 603) + ~50,000 (max 60,000) regular infantry (Daylamites, tirbad archers), i.e. ~120,000; plus vassal contingents in service (up to 30,000) and support. Howard-Johnston 1995 (cited by Soto p. 63) estimated ~180,000 for Khosrow I (high side). Counted here: savaran, regular infantry, vassal light horse on duty, garrison levies and support. The peasant levy (paighan) is in trainedReserves. Low allows for a smaller warrior roll after the 589-591 civil war.

trainedReserves.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 73-74: the Chronicle of 1234 gives 120,000 "peasants" with Khosrow I before Dara in 573; Soto puts the ceiling of the paighan levy at ~150,000 (high), usable only for short campaigns. Mid assumes about half can be raised within a campaign season; untrained, but counted here per the levies-in-reserves convention.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Grooms, baggage train, elephant mahouts and crews, engineers, staff and the small Gulf flotilla crews; no source gives a figure.

mobilizationRatio.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 72-74: in great need and for a limited time Persia could field at most ~300,000 men (70,000 savaran, 50,000 regular infantry, 30,000 vassal troops, 150,000 peasant levies, paighan). 300,000 / 12.7 million = 0.024 (mid); low and high bracket a smaller levy and a larger population.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 69-70: 70,000 savaran on the rolls in 588 (high); attested single-front concentrations of 15,000 (531), 23,000 and 40,000 (573), and 50,000 horse at Khosrow II's review. Mid 60,000 allows for losses in the civil war of 589-591 and nobles on garrison duty counted as unavailable.

quality.note: Rubric 1.0: lamellar/mail-armoured lancer-archers on armoured horses, the model the Romans copied (clibanarii); era best with the Roman bucellarii.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: hereditary warrior caste trained from youth, periodic royal reviews (Soto p. 69-70 on the 40-day reviews).

count.note: Soto Chica, "Los efectivos del ultimo ejercito de la Persia sasanida (572-642)", Gladius 35 (2015) pp. 61-76, doi:10.3989/gladius.2015.0004, pp. 72-73: vassal contingents (Lakhmid Arabs, Armenian, Albanian and Iberian nobles, settled Hephthalites and Turks) never exceeded ~30,000 in all (high); the largest single contingent was ~15,000 Lakhmids in 531. Mid assumes half on call in peacetime 600.

Split ~60/40 between shielded close-order infantry (Daylamites, highland peoples; 3,000-4,000-man contingents attested in 554, 573, 642) and archers.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: experienced generals (Bahram Chobin, Shahrbaraz, Shahin) and a structured command (spahbeds of the four quarters), but the 589-591 civil war had just removed or alienated leading commanders.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: savaran loyal to their noble houses; Bahram Chobin's revolt split the army in 589-591 and Khosrow II was restored only with Roman help.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: peace with Rome since 591; elite cavalry confident, levies unwilling.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 plus refinements: heavy composite bows, lance and mace cavalry, stirrups arriving c. 600; below anchor 4 (crossbow, counterweight trebuchet).

armor.note: Above anchor 3 (mail): lamellar and mail with horse armour for the savaran; short of anchor 4 plate-and-mail.

ships.note: Anchor 3 lower end: coastal and Gulf craft, no oared war fleet.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 plus long frontier walls (Gorgan ~195 km, Derbent) and fortified cities (Nisibis, Ctesiphon).

logistics.note: Anchor 3: royal roads and depots, irrigated Mesopotamian granaries; levies limited by agricultural calendar (Soto p. 73-74).

communications.note: Anchor 3: mounted relay posts on the royal roads (later the Abbasid barid).

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts, spies, frontier informants.

air.note: No aircraft before 1903.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Savaran were partly paid (Khosrow I's reforms introduced state pay and equipment) and partly supported by land; levies unpaid (Soto p. 73).

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy with silk weaving, metalwork and caravan trade.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated Mesopotamian (Sawad) agriculture produced large tax surpluses; the plateau far less.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Royal roads inherited from the Achaemenids and Parthians (Ctesiphon-Hamadan-Rayy-Nishapur-Merv, Ctesiphon-Istakhr); total length not documented.

railKm.note: No railways before 1825.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Ubulla, Rev-Ardashir, Siraf, Hormuz on the Gulf; the river ports of Ctesiphon.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Gulf and Indian Ocean shipping (Persian merchants dominated the Ceylon trade per Procopius); no tonnage figure exists.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1) for infantry armies, extended for a cavalry army living off grazing; Sasanian field armies operated ~1-3 weeks from Mesopotamian bases.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.08-0.14 horses, camels, mules and donkeys per inhabitant x population (horse-breeding nobility, Mesopotamian camels).

nuclearWarheads.note: No nuclear weapons before 1945.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: local supply and fortified cities with population support; the plateau gives depth and an arid climate (1.3 at most), but Heraclius showed in 624-628 that the Mesopotamian core was reachable.

sasanian-empire-600.notes: Snapshot = 600 CE, Khosrow II (590-628) between his restoration with Roman help (591) and the great war against Rome (603-628). Force convention: activePersonnel = standing savaran heavy cavalry, regular infantry, vassal contingents on duty, garrison levies and support; the peasant levy (paighan) is in trainedReserves. Army figures follow Soto Chica 2015 (Gladius 35), the most detailed source-based reconstruction; medieval Arabic and Persian figures (al-Tabari, Mas'udi, Firdausi) and the Chronicle of 1234 are ancient and are only used through Soto's critique. Border is the historical-basemaps world_600 Sasanian Empire plus "Sasanian dependencies" (Yemen). Lakhmid al-Hira was a client kingdom until 602 and its population is not counted; its horsemen are in cavalry_light. Elephant, ship and siege-engine counts are educated guesses.

foodSurplus.note: Recomputed 2026-10-29 under the definition: 0.02 -> 0.88. Formula: surplus = 1 - a/s, a = farm population share of consumers (proxy: agricultural employment share, World Bank SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS, ILO modelled, https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/SAU/indicator/SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS), s = domestic production / consumption (calorie self-sufficiency). a = 2.50% (2025). s from FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_All_Data.zip): production / domestic supply summed over all FBS items, each weighted by kcal per tonne (world median of food kcal / food tonnes per item); feed, processing and non-food uses stay in domestic supply. s = 0.21 (mean 2021-2023, range 0.18-0.26). Mid 1 - 0.025/0.21 = 0.88. Low: a x 1.5 (farm households larger than the employed count), s 0.18 = 0.8. High: s 0.26 = 0.91. Import dependence: domestic production covers about 21% of domestic calorie supply. Earlier net-trade reading: Educated guess. Imports ~80% of food; some dates/dairy/poultry self-sufficiency.

saudi-arabia-2026.notes: WARTIME-adjacent snapshot: attacked by Iran in the 2026 Iran war and retaliated (war article), and hit by Houthi missile/drone waves since the Bab al-Mandab crisis (Sept-Oct 2026). asOf 2025 economic data, 2026 order of battle. Population: everything inside ne:SAU incl. ~40% expatriates; the mobilization ratio is set low for that reason. Money in 2011 int$ via derived:ppp-rebase-2011. Counts from Wikipedia inventory tables (Army equipment list, RSAF, Navy, RSADF, SANG); some figures include equipment on order and are flagged. ships_major = frigates (11); corvettes and FAC in ships_minor. Infantry P-role splits are educated guesses (grade D). Paramilitary (24,500, IISS) excluded.

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 3.6 million km2 for 312-201 BCE (high) and a declining range of 2.3 million to 475,000 km2 for 200-147 BCE (mid = start of that range). The historical-basemaps world_bc200 polygon measures 1.75 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, low); it omits Coele-Syria (taken at Panium in 200) and the tributary upper satrapies.

population.note: Seshat codes two disputed values for 312-63 BCE: 16 million and 30 million. In 200 the empire had lost nothing yet to Rome and had just regained Coele-Syria (Panium), but the upper satrapies (Bactria, Parthia) were only tributary after the anabasis of 212-205; low 14 million allows for their exclusion, high 30 million is the larger Seshat value. Everything inside the border; Bactria and Parthia (vassal kings) not counted in the mid.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/108) codes the largest settlement at 50,000-100,000 for 312-63 BCE (Antioch, Seleucia on the Tigris). Dense Greek city foundations in Syria and Babylonia, rural plateau; scaled below Roman 117 CE (10-25%).

activePersonnel.note: Royal field army (49,500 / 66,000 / 89,000, see forces) + fleet crews, mahouts, engineers and staff (15,000 / 28,000 / 40,000, see supportPersonnel) + city and fortress garrisons from Sardis to Susa (20,000 / 30,000 / 50,000; educated guess). Convention: the royal army, guards and garrisons under arms are counted as active; military settlers (katoikoi) and vassal contingents not called up are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Military settlers (katoikoi) of Syria, Mesopotamia, Media and Lydia not called up for Panium, plus vassal contingents (Bactria, Armenia, Cappadocia) callable within weeks; Bar-Kochva (isbn:9780521206679, ch. 2) treats the settlers as the phalanx reserve. audit 2026-10-30: ISBN corrected from 9780521200745 (resolves to The Agrarian History of England and Wales) to 9780521206679 (Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army, Open Library work OL2927924W) throughout this file.

supportPersonnel.note: Fleet: decked ships (40 / 70 / 100) x ~250 crew + lighter craft (100 / 150 / 200) x ~50; plus ~2-3 mahouts and attendants per elephant and ~2,000-4,000 engineers, staff and royal pages.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Maximum field armies (~70,000) plus garrisons were ~0.5% of the population; the Macedonian-armed core depended on a limited pool of military settlers (Bar-Kochva, isbn:9780521206679, ch. 2). Total-war ratio assumes wide levying of native and allied contingents.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Three documented field armies bracket the 200 BCE royal army: Raphia 217 (Polybius 5.79, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/5*.html): 62,000 foot, 6,000 horse, 102 elephants; Magnesia 190 (Livy 37.40, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/From_the_Founding_of_the_City/Book_37): phalanx 16,000, 6,000 cataphracts, agema 1,000, royal cavalry 1,000, 54 elephants, ~70,000 in all; Daphne parade 166 (Polybius 30.25, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/30*.html): 20,000 Macedonian-armed, 5,000 Roman-armed, ~20,000 allies and mercenaries, ~8,500 cavalry. Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (isbn:9780521206679, ch. 2-3 and the battle chapters) accepts these figures as broadly reliable musters of the royal army (ancient figures, hence grade C). Line infantry = Macedonian-armed phalanx (16,000-20,000) + argyraspides guard (~10,000 picked men in Macedonian arms, Polybius 5.79.4) + Greek and Galatian mercenary heavy infantry (3,000-10,000).

quality.note: Sarissa phalanx and silver-shield guard: era-typical to among the era's best (rubric 0.75); mercenaries era-typical.

training.note: Argyraspides a standing guard (0.75); phalanx of settler-reservists called up for campaigns (0.5-0.75). Polybius 5.66 says the army was not exercised in winter 218/217.

Heavy cavalry = Companions and agema (1,000 each) + cataphracts, first attested for the Seleucids at Panium 200 (Polybius 16.18.6-8, https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/16*.html: the "mailed horsemen" of the younger Antiochus) and 6,000 strong at Magnesia.

quality.note: Fully armoured cataphracts on armoured horses and the guard cavalry; the era's best heavy cavalry (rubric 1.0). Panium was won by the cataphract charge.

training.note: Guard units professional (0.75-1.0); cataphracts newly raised after the anabasis.
